questions.q: D, driving a delivery truck, carelessly knocks over a fire hydrant. The gushing water runs two blocks downhill and floods the basement of an antique shop whose owner, P, was never in any physical danger. P sues D for the destroyed inventory. The claim most likely fails at which negligence gate?
options: Duty — a driver owes no duty to property owners he cannot see.
Breach — knocking over a hydrant is not careless.
Proximate cause — P was an unforeseeable plaintiff beyond the foreseeable zone of danger.
Damages — destroyed inventory is pure economic loss, unrecoverable in negligence.
questions.explain: Duty, breach, cause-in-fact and damages are all satisfied — destroyed inventory is property damage, not pure economic loss. The killer is proximate cause: P was an unforeseeable plaintiff outside the foreseeable zone of danger. This is the Palsgraf rule.

questions.q: A offers to sell his motorcycle for $4,000, 'this offer is open until Friday.' On Wednesday, B mails a letter accepting the offer. Also on Wednesday, A sends a telegram revoking the offer, which reaches B on Thursday morning — before B's letter arrives. Is there a contract?
options: No — the revocation reached B before the acceptance did, so the offer was dead.
Yes — B's acceptance was effective when mailed on Wednesday, before the revocation arrived.
No — an offer stated to stay open until Friday cannot be revoked.
Yes — but only because a telegram is not a valid revocation.
questions.explain: The mailbox rule: acceptance is effective on dispatch. B's mailed acceptance formed the contract on Wednesday, and the revocation arriving Thursday came too late. An ordinary offer is revocable any time before acceptance.

questions.q: P, a nurse, sees a stranger collapse and performs CPR, saving his life. The stranger's grateful family later promises P in writing that they will pay her $10,000 for 'saving his life.' P sues to enforce the promise. The promise is:
options: Enforceable — it was put in writing.
Enforceable — the rescue was valuable consideration.
Unenforceable — the rescue was past consideration, not bargained for.
Enforceable under promissory estoppel — P must have relied on the promise.
questions.explain: Past consideration is not consideration: the rescue was already done and never bargained for — the promise was gratitude, not exchange. Writing alone does not create consideration, and promissory estoppel fails because there was no reliance on the promise (the rescue came first).

questions.q: D manufactures a power drill. One drill leaves the factory with a misaligned chuck; the rest of the model line is fine. A buyer is injured when the bit flies out. The strongest theory is:
options: Design defect — the whole product line is dangerous as designed.
Failure to warn — D gave no warning about the chuck.
Manufacturing defect — this unit deviated from the intended design; strict liability applies.
No liability — a misaligned chuck is an open and obvious danger.
questions.explain: One unit deviated from its own design — the classic manufacturing defect. Under Restatement (Second) section 402A, a commercial seller of a defective, unreasonably dangerous product is strictly liable; the care D took is irrelevant.

questions.q: Owner and Manager orally agree: 'You will manage my restaurant for eighteen months, starting next month.' Three months in, Owner fires Manager, who sues for breach of the oral agreement. The agreement is:
options: Enforceable — it could have been performed within one year if Manager had died.
Unenforceable — it cannot possibly be performed within one year of its making.
Enforceable — employment contracts are outside the Statute of Frauds.
Unenforceable — but only because Manager was fired without cause.
questions.explain: The Year rule asks whether the contract could possibly be fully performed within one year of its making. A fixed 18-month term cannot — and death terminates a fixed-term contract; it does not perform it. So the oral agreement falls inside the Statute of Frauds and is unenforceable.

questions.q: Widow, 87, lives alone and depends entirely on her live-in caregiver of two years, who manages her finances and has cut off her contact with family. Widow signs a deed giving her house to the caregiver 'for love and affection.' Her niece sues to set the deed aside. The strongest ground is:
options: Duress — the isolation was an improper threat leaving Widow no reasonable alternative.
Undue influence — a confidential relationship plus an unfair transaction shifts the burden to the caregiver to prove fairness.
Fraud — the caregiver concealed the house's true market value.
Unconscionability — the deed's terms are grossly one-sided.
questions.explain: A confidential relationship (caregiver managing finances, isolation showing dominance) plus a facially unfair transaction (a house for 'love and affection') equals undue influence, and the burden shifts to the caregiver to prove fairness. Duress needs an improper threat — isolation is dominance, not a threat.

questions.q: A and B contract for the sale of A's cow. Both believe the cow is barren; the price is $80. Before delivery they learn she is pregnant and worth $1,000. A seeks rescission. The court should:
options: Deny rescission — this is a mere mistake of value, for which there is no relief.
Grant rescission — mutual mistake as to a basic assumption materially affecting the exchange, the risk of which A did not bear.
Deny rescission — only B was mistaken, so the mistake was unilateral.
Grant rescission — but only if B knew the cow was pregnant.
questions.explain: Sherwood v. Walker: both parties shared the mistaken basic assumption (the cow is barren), it went to the substance of the thing (breeding cow vs. beef cow — not mere value), and A did not bear the risk. Rescission is granted.

questions.q: Buyer and Seller sign a fully integrated written contract for the sale of a restaurant, containing a merger clause: 'This is the entire agreement of the parties.' Before signing, Seller orally promised the ovens were new. After closing, Buyer discovers twenty-year-old ovens and sues Seller for breach of contract, offering testimony of the oral promise. The testimony is:
options: Admissible — it is a consistent additional term of a partially integrated agreement.
Admissible — a merger clause is never conclusive of complete integration.
Inadmissible — a completely integrated writing bars prior oral terms, and the merger clause evidences complete integration.
Admissible — under the fraud exception, because Seller lied about the ovens.
questions.explain: A fully integrated writing with a merger clause bars prior oral terms in a breach-of-contract action. The fraud exception is the trap: it admits evidence when the plaintiff attacks formation (fraudulent inducement), but Buyer sued to enforce an added term — exactly what the parol evidence rule bars.

questions.q: Owner contracts Builder to build a house for $200,000, with final payment 'due upon architect's certificate of completion.' Builder finishes the house essentially perfectly — but installs Cohoes-brand pipe instead of the specified Reading-brand pipe. The pipes are identical in quality, price, and performance. The architect, annoyed at the substitution, withholds the certificate. Builder sues for the final $40,000. Who wins?
options: Owner — express conditions require strict compliance, and the certificate is missing.
Owner — the pipe substitution is a material breach, excusing payment.
Builder — he substantially performed; the certificate condition is excused to avoid forfeiture, and the breach was minor.
Builder — prevention doctrine: the architect's refusal is the owner's hindrance, so the condition drops out entirely.
questions.explain: The Jacob & Youngs pattern: Builder substantially performed — the deviation is trivial. Express conditions normally require strict compliance, but the certificate condition is excused to avoid disproportionate forfeiture: the house is complete and withholding $40,000 over identical pipe would be extreme forfeiture.

questions.q: Adaeze owns a flour mill. Its only crankshaft breaks. She hires Swift Carrier to rush the broken shaft to the manufacturer for a pattern, telling Swift only 'deliver fast — it's urgent.' Swift delays unreasonably by two weeks. The mill sits idle; Adaeze loses $30,000 in profits. Swift never knew the mill could not operate without the shaft, nor the profit figures. Result?
options: Adaeze recovers $30,000 — lost profits flow naturally from a carrier's delay.
Adaeze recovers $30,000 — she told Swift the shipment was urgent, which put Swift on notice.
Adaeze recovers nothing beyond the shipping charge — the lost profits were not foreseeable to Swift at formation.
Adaeze recovers $30,000 — a common carrier impliedly assumes all downstream losses.
questions.explain: Hadley v. Baxendale: consequential damages (lost profits) are recoverable only if reasonably in the contemplation of both parties AT FORMATION. Swift knew only 'urgent' — not that the mill would sit idle or the profit figures — so the $30,000 was not foreseeable. Urgency alone is not notice of specific profits.

questions.q: Buyer contracts with Seller for 1,000 bushels of wheat at $5/bushel, delivery June 1. On May 15 Seller unequivocally repudiates. Buyer promptly and in good faith covers on May 20 at $6/bushel. Market price on May 15 was $5.75/bushel. Buyer's damages under the UCC are:
options: $750 — the market-contract differential at the time of repudiation (section 2-713).
$1,000 — the cover-contract differential (section 2-712), because buyer actually covered in good faith.
$750 — buyer must take the lower of cover and market.
$1,000 — but only if buyer proves it could not have covered at $5.75.
questions.explain: UCC section 2-712: when the buyer actually covers in good faith without unreasonable delay, damages are (cover price minus contract price) times quantity — ($6 − $5) × 1,000 = $1,000. Section 2-713's market measure applies only when the buyer does NOT cover.

questions.q: Landscaper agrees to landscape Homeowner's small yard for $10,000. The contract states: 'If Landscaper fails to complete by June 1, Landscaper forfeits $50,000.' Landscaper finishes June 10; Homeowner's actual delay damages are $800. The clause is:
options: Enforceable — the parties agreed to it, and courts enforce bargains.
Enforceable — $50,000 was a reasonable forecast of delay damages at formation.
Void as a penalty — unreasonably large relative to probable loss; Homeowner recovers $800 actual damages.
Void as a penalty — and Homeowner therefore recovers nothing.
questions.explain: $50,000 on a $10,000 job is unreasonably large relative to the probable loss — a penalty, void under Restatement section 356 / UCC section 2-718. Reasonableness is judged at formation, and delay damages on a small yard were easily estimable and small. The clause falls, but Homeowner still recovers actual damages of $800.

questions.q: Police find D heavily intoxicated inside his own apartment. They drag him out onto the public sidewalk and arrest him for 'being drunk in a public place,' a misdemeanor. At trial, D moves for acquittal. How should the court rule?
options: Deny the motion — D was in fact drunk in a public place.
Grant the motion — the actus reus (being in public while intoxicated) was not D's voluntary act; the police put him there.
Deny the motion — D voluntarily became intoxicated, so the act requirement is satisfied.
Grant the motion — but only because the police lacked probable cause for the arrest.
questions.explain: Martin v. State: the actus reus the statute punishes — being in a public place while intoxicated — was not D's voluntary act; the police supplied the 'public place' element. Voluntary intoxication does not satisfy the voluntariness of the prohibited conduct itself.

questions.q: A statute provides: 'A person commits assault if he recklessly causes bodily injury to another.' D, annoyed at his neighbor V, fires a shot into the air near V's yard to frighten him, reasonably believing V is away at work. Unbeknownst to D, V is napping in a hammock behind the shed; the bullet grazes V's arm. D testifies, credibly, that it never occurred to him anyone could be in the yard. D is:
options: Guilty — firing a gun near a dwelling is inherently reckless conduct.
Guilty — his intent to frighten V transfers to the bodily injury.
Not guilty — recklessness requires conscious disregard of a perceived risk, and D perceived no risk to any person.
Guilty — the statute requires only causation, so negligence suffices.
questions.explain: Recklessness is SUBJECTIVE — conscious disregard of a perceived risk. D perceived no risk to any person (credible testimony plus a reasonable belief the yard was empty), so he lacked recklessness; at most he was negligent, which this statute does not punish. Transferred intent cannot convert negligence into recklessness.

questions.q: H, an expert swimmer, is hiking when he sees a stranger slip and fall into a deep river. H could have saved the stranger with no risk to himself, but keeps walking. The stranger drowns. H is charged with involuntary manslaughter based on his omission. Result?
options: Guilty — he could have saved the man with no risk to himself.
Guilty — his failure to act was the but-for cause of the death.
Not guilty — the law imposes no general duty to rescue a stranger; none of the five duty sources applies.
Not guilty — an omission can never supply the actus reus of a crime.
questions.explain: There is no general legal duty to rescue a stranger — moral duty is not legal duty — and none of the five duty sources (statute, status, contract, undertaking, creation of peril) applies to H. But-for causation is irrelevant where there was no duty to act.

questions.q: D, age 19, has consensual intercourse with V, age 15. V told D she was 18, showed a convincing fake ID, and looked 18; a reasonable person would have believed her. The jurisdiction's statutory-rape statute makes the victim's age a strict-liability element. Result?
options: Not guilty — D's mistake was both honest and reasonable.
Not guilty — D lacked the mens rea for the offence.
Guilty — as to the victim's age the offence is strict liability; even a reasonable mistake of fact is no defence.
Guilty — but only because the jurisdiction follows the common-law approach.
questions.explain: Strict liability as to age means no mens rea is required for that element, so no mistake-of-fact defence exists — not even a reasonable one. The honest-and-reasonable-mistake rule applies to malice and general-intent crimes, not strict-liability elements.

questions.q: During a heated argument in a parking lot, D reaches into his open car door, takes a pistol from the glove compartment, and within seconds shoots V dead. D says he never planned anything — it all happened in a flash. Under the common-law approach, D is guilty of:
options: Second-degree murder, because premeditation requires more than a few seconds of thought.
First-degree murder.
Voluntary manslaughter, because the heated argument was adequate provocation.
No homicide, because D lacked malice aforethought.
questions.explain: Deliberate plus premeditated intent to kill is first-degree murder. The golden trap: premeditation has no minimum thinking time — it can form in an instant, and reaching for the gun was reflection beforehand. A heated argument (mere words) is not adequate provocation under the majority rule.

questions.q: D, enraged at V over a debt, beats V with a baseball bat, intending to break his legs. V dies from the injuries. The prosecution charges felony murder, using aggravated assault as the underlying felony. D is properly guilty of:
options: Felony murder — the death occurred during an inherently dangerous felony.
Nothing — the assault merges with the homicide, leaving no charge.
Second-degree murder, on an intent-to-inflict-serious-bodily-injury theory.
Involuntary manslaughter, because D did not intend to kill.
questions.explain: The merger doctrine bars using the very assault that caused the death as the felony-murder predicate — the felony must be independent of the killing. But D intended serious bodily injury (broken legs), and death resulting from intended serious bodily injury is malice route two: second-degree murder.

questions.q: D, wanting to frighten people at a crowded street fair, fires his rifle several times into the air above the crowd. A falling bullet strikes and kills a bystander. D is guilty of:
options: First-degree murder — firing a rifle at a crowd shows premeditation.
Second-degree murder, on a depraved-heart theory.
Involuntary manslaughter — D was merely criminally negligent.
No homicide — D never intended to kill anyone.
questions.explain: Firing above a crowd is extreme recklessness manifesting extreme indifference to human life — the depraved (abandoned and malignant) heart, malice route three, second-degree murder. Malice aforethought does not require intent to kill.

questions.q: H walks into his bedroom and finds his wife in bed with another man. Enraged, H grabs a table lamp and immediately strikes the lover dead. H is guilty of:
options: First-degree murder — grabbing the lamp and striking was deliberate and premeditated.
Second-degree murder.
Voluntary manslaughter.
Involuntary manslaughter — the killing was unintentional.
questions.explain: Catching a spouse in the act of adultery is the classic adequate provocation. With actual passion, no cooling time, and a direct causal connection, the provocation negates malice: voluntary manslaughter. Grabbing the nearest object in immediate rage is the opposite of deliberation.

questions.q: D slips his hand into V's coat pocket intending to steal V's wallet, but the pocket is empty — V left the wallet at home. D is arrested with his hand still in the pocket. D is guilty of:
options: Nothing — the crime was impossible to complete.
Attempted larceny.
Completed larceny.
Conspiracy to commit larceny.
questions.explain: Classic factual impossibility — the pickpocket's empty pocket — which is never a defence. D had specific intent to steal and went beyond mere preparation (hand in the pocket). Larceny needs an actual taking, so the attempt stands; conspiracy needs an agreement, and D acted alone.

questions.q: D and U agree to rob a bank next Tuesday. U is an undercover officer who never intended to rob anything, and the two take no step toward the robbery. Under the Model Penal Code, D is guilty of:
options: Nothing — there was no genuine agreement and no overt act.
Conspiracy.
Attempted robbery.
Solicitation.
questions.explain: The MPC takes the unilateral approach: one genuine criminal mind suffices, so D's agreement with the feigning officer is conspiracy. The overt-act objection fails on MPC terms — section 5.03(5) requires no overt act for first- or second-degree felonies, and robbery is a second-degree felony under the MPC.

questions.q: D, fleeing the scene of a burglary, fires wildly at pursuing police officers to scare them off. A bullet grazes one officer, who survives. The prosecution charges attempted felony murder. D is:
options: Guilty of attempted felony murder.
Guilty of attempted depraved-heart murder.
Not guilty of either attempted charge, but guilty of aggravated assault.
Guilty only of the burglary.
questions.explain: There is no such crime as attempted felony murder or attempted depraved-heart murder — attempt requires specific intent to kill, and you cannot intend an unintentional killing. But the completed assault stands: firing at the officers to scare them off satisfies assault.

questions.q: D lends his car to two men, knowing they will use it as the getaway car for a burglary they have planned. D is not part of their plan and shares no agreement with them. During the burglary, one burglar shoots and kills a homeowner who confronts him. Under the common-law approach, D is guilty of:
options: Nothing — assistance without an agreement creates no liability.
Burglary as an accomplice, but not the homicide.
Burglary and murder as an accomplice.
Murder only, under Pinkerton liability.
questions.explain: D acted with dual intent — he lent the car knowing it was for the burglary and with the purpose of facilitating it — and gave actual aid. Under the common law the accomplice answers for the target crime and its natural and probable consequences; a killing during a burglary is foreseeable. Pinkerton needs conspiracy membership, which D lacks.

questions.q: At 2 a.m., Marcus hears glass break and finds a stranger climbing through his kitchen window holding a crowbar. Marcus's family is asleep upstairs. Marcus shoots the intruder dead. The intruder had made no verbal threat and had not seen Marcus. Under the majority rule, Marcus's best defense is:
options: He had a duty to retreat before using deadly force.
Castle doctrine — no duty to retreat in his own home, and deadly force was justified by a reasonable fear of imminent death or serious bodily injury.
Defense of property, because the intruder was committing burglary.
Imperfect self-defense, reducing the charge to manslaughter.
questions.explain: The castle doctrine: no duty to retreat in one's own home. A crowbar-wielding intruder at 2 a.m. with family asleep upstairs gives a reasonable fear of imminent death or serious bodily injury, justifying deadly force. Deadly force may never be used solely to defend property.

questions.q: Lena's ex-husband holds a gun to her six-year-old daughter's head and orders Lena to drive the getaway car for a bank robbery. Lena drives. She is charged with robbery. Her duress defense:
options: Fails, because duress requires the threat to be directed at the defendant herself.
Fails, because robbery is a serious felony.
Succeeds, because the threat was imminent death to a close family member and she had no reasonable escape.
Succeeds only if she can prove she would not have driven but for the threat.
questions.explain: Duress requires an imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury to the defendant or a close family member, with no reasonable escape. A gun to her daughter's head satisfies it. The threat need not target the defendant personally.

questions.q: Daniel, suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, kills a stranger because he genuinely believes God commanded the killing as a holy act. He understood he was ending a human life, but he believed the act was morally commanded and therefore not wrong. Under the M'Naghten test, Daniel is:
options: Sane, because he knew the nature and quality of his act.
Insane, because he did not know that what he was doing was wrong.
Sane, because schizophrenia is not a mental disease under M'Naghten.
Insane only under the irresistible-impulse test, not M'Naghten.
questions.explain: M'Naghten's two prongs are disjunctive — either one suffices. Daniel knew the nature of his act, but his deific decree meant he did not know it was wrong. Knowing the act is not enough; he must also know it is wrong.

questions.q: An undercover agent befriends Paul, a man with no criminal record, and over six weeks of daily calls begs him to find a drug supplier, finally offering triple the street price. Paul reluctantly arranges one sale and is arrested. Paul's entrapment defense under the federal (subjective) test:
options: Fails, because providing the opportunity to buy drugs is enough to defeat entrapment.
Succeeds, because the agent induced the crime and Paul showed no predisposition.
Fails, because Paul completed the sale voluntarily.
Succeeds only under the MPC objective test.
questions.explain: The federal subjective test asks two questions: did the government induce the crime, and was the defendant predisposed? Six weeks of begging plus triple the price is inducement, and a clean record with reluctance shows no predisposition. Entrapment succeeds.

questions.q: Contractor agrees to build Owner's fence for $5,000. Halfway through, Contractor says he will not finish unless Owner pays $7,000. Owner orally agrees. Contractor finishes and sues for $7,000. Result?
options: Contractor recovers $7,000 — Owner agreed to the modification.
Contractor recovers $5,000 — the modification lacks consideration under the pre-existing duty rule.
Contractor recovers $7,000 — UCC section 2-209 allows good-faith modification without consideration.
Contractor recovers nothing — the whole contract is void.
questions.explain: At common law (this is a services contract, not goods), a modification needs new consideration; doing what you were already bound to do is not consideration — the pre-existing duty rule. UCC section 2-209's no-consideration modification rule applies only to goods.

questions.q: Merchant Seller signs a writing: 'I will sell you 500 widgets at $10 each; this offer stays open for four months.' Two months later Seller revokes; Buyer accepts the next day. Result?
options: No contract — offers are revocable any time before acceptance.
A contract — the UCC firm-offer rule makes it irrevocable for up to three months without consideration; the four-month period is capped at three.
A contract — the offer is irrevocable for the full four months stated.
No contract — Buyer accepted after revocation.
questions.explain: UCC section 2-205: a merchant's signed writing holding an offer open is irrevocable without consideration, but the period of irrevocability can never exceed three months. Buyer's acceptance within two months therefore formed a contract.

questions.q: Buyer (a merchant) sends a purchase order for 1,000 bolts. Seller (a merchant) replies with an acknowledgment that adds a term requiring Buyer to acknowledge receipt of each shipment by email. Buyer's form said nothing about email acknowledgments. Under UCC section 2-207:
options: No contract — the mirror-image rule requires the forms to match exactly.
A contract is formed, and the email-acknowledgment term becomes part of the deal because it does not materially alter it and Buyer did not object.
A contract is formed, but the added term is automatically knocked out.
No contract — any additional term prevents formation.
questions.explain: The UCC rejects the mirror-image rule: a definite expression of acceptance forms a contract even with additional terms. Between merchants, additional terms become part of the deal unless the offer limited acceptance to its terms, they materially alter the deal, or objection was made. An email-acknowledgment term is not a material alteration.

questions.q: Buyer orders 100 red bicycles. Seller delivers 95 red and 5 blue bicycles. Buyer rejects the whole shipment the same day. Under the UCC:
options: Buyer may reject the whole shipment under the perfect-tender rule, but Seller may cure within the contract time.
Buyer must accept the 95 conforming bicycles under substantial performance.
Buyer may reject only the 5 blue bicycles.
Buyer may reject all, and Seller has no right to cure.
questions.explain: UCC section 2-601's perfect-tender rule: goods must conform exactly, so any non-conformity lets the buyer reject the whole shipment. But section 2-508 gives the seller the right to cure by making a conforming delivery within the contract time.

questions.q: On May 1, Seller tells Buyer he will not deliver the goods due June 1. Buyer may:
options: Do nothing until June 1, then sue.
Treat the repudiation as a breach immediately — suing now or covering now.
Demand adequate assurance of performance before taking any action.
Cancel the contract but recover no damages.
questions.explain: An unequivocal anticipatory repudiation lets the aggrieved party either await performance or treat it as an immediate breach — suing or covering right away. The adequate-assurance rule applies to doubtful performance, not to an outright repudiation.

questions.q: Builder wrongfully refuses to build Owner's commercial structure. Owner makes no effort to hire a replacement, lets the lot sit idle for a year, then sues for a full year's lost rental value. Result?
options: Owner recovers the full year's lost rental value as expectation damages.
Owner recovers only the losses that could not reasonably have been avoided — the avoidable-consequences (mitigation) rule bars the rest.
Owner recovers nothing — failure to mitigate forfeits all damages.
Owner recovers nominal damages only.
questions.explain: The non-breaching party must make reasonable efforts to mitigate; losses that could have been reasonably avoided are not recoverable. But failure to mitigate reduces damages — it does not forfeit the claim entirely.

questions.q: Buyer contracts to buy Seller's one-acre parcel of land. Seller refuses to convey. Buyer sues. The court will most likely:
options: Award damages only — specific performance is never available for breach of contract.
Order specific performance — land is deemed unique, so damages are inadequate.
Order specific performance only if Buyer is a merchant.
Award damages only, because Buyer could buy a different parcel.
questions.explain: Specific performance is available when damages are inadequate — and every parcel of land is treated as unique as a matter of law. The same reasoning covers rare goods and heirlooms.

questions.q: Uncle orally promises Nephew $20,000 toward college tuition. Relying on the promise, Nephew enrolls and incurs $15,000 in non-refundable tuition charges. Uncle reneges. The promise is:
options: Unenforceable — a gratuitous promise lacks consideration.
Enforceable under promissory estoppel to the extent necessary to avoid injustice.
Enforceable — Nephew's enrollment supplied consideration.
Unenforceable — estoppel requires a signed writing.
questions.explain: Restatement section 90: a promise the promisor should reasonably expect to induce definite and substantial reliance, which does induce such reliance, is enforceable to the extent necessary to avoid injustice — even without consideration or a writing.

questions.q: D intends to shoot V dead. D aims at V and fires, misses, and kills W, a bystander. Under the doctrine of transferred intent, D is guilty of:
options: Attempted murder of V only.
Murder of W — the intent to kill V transfers to W.
Involuntary manslaughter of W, because D formed no intent toward W.
Nothing as to W — intent cannot transfer across victims.
questions.explain: Transferred intent: when D intends to kill one person but kills another by mistake, the intent transfers and D is guilty of the completed homicide of the actual victim. Attempt as to V may also lie, but the murder of W is complete.

questions.q: D stabs V, inflicting a wound that proper treatment would have healed. At the hospital, an intoxicated surgeon operates with gross negligence, and V dies from complications of the botched surgery. Under the majority rule on causation, D is:
options: Not liable for the death — the surgeon's negligence was a superseding cause.
Liable for the death — subsequent medical negligence is foreseeable and does not break the chain of causation.
Liable only for attempted murder.
Not liable — the wound was survivable.
questions.explain: Subsequent medical negligence — even gross negligence — is treated as foreseeable and does not supersede the defendant's act as the cause of death. Only truly extraordinary, unforeseeable interventions break the chain.

questions.q: A and B agree to rob a bank; A waits in the getaway car while B goes inside. A bank guard shoots and kills B during the robbery. Under the majority (agency) approach to felony murder, A is guilty of felony murder for B's death?
options: Yes — the death occurred during the robbery.
No — the killing was done by a non-felon, and the agency doctrine limits felony murder to killings committed by felons or their agents.
Yes — under Pinkerton, A is liable for all foreseeable crimes of his co-conspirator.
No — robbery is not an inherently dangerous felony.
questions.explain: The majority agency rule: felony murder covers only killings committed by the felons or their agents in furtherance of the felony — not killings by victims, police, or guards resisting the felony. Pinkerton is a conspiracy doctrine, not a substitute for the agency limit.

questions.q: D writes X a letter asking X to kill V for $5,000. X reads the letter and refuses. D is guilty of:
options: Conspiracy — the two of them discussed the killing.
Solicitation — the crime is complete upon the asking; X's refusal is irrelevant.
Attempted murder — the letter was a substantial step.
Nothing — X refused, so no crime occurred.
questions.explain: Solicitation is complete when the defendant asks, counsels, or commands another to commit a crime — it does not require agreement (that would be conspiracy) or any step toward completion (that would be attempt).

questions.q: A and B conspire to burglarize a warehouse. During the burglary, B — without A's knowledge — assaults a night watchman who surprises them. Under the Pinkerton doctrine, A is liable for the assault:
options: For every crime B commits during the conspiracy, without exception.
Only if the assault was a foreseeable crime committed in furtherance of the conspiracy.
Never — A is liable only for crimes he personally commits or aids.
Only if A specifically agreed to the assault in advance.
questions.explain: Pinkerton liability has two gates: the substantive crime must have been committed in furtherance of the conspiracy AND have been reasonably foreseeable to the defendant. An assault on a watchman during a burglary typically passes both.

questions.q: A hiker lost in a blizzard breaks into an empty mountain cabin, eats stored food, and burns furniture to survive the night. Charged with burglary, the hiker's necessity defense:
options: Fails — property crimes can never be justified by necessity.
Succeeds if the harm avoided (freezing to death) clearly outweighed the harm caused and there was no lawful alternative.
Fails — necessity requires an imminent threat from a human aggressor.
Succeeds only if the cabin owner later consents.
questions.explain: Necessity (choice of evils) justifies the crime when the defendant reasonably believed the criminal act was necessary to avoid a greater imminent harm, with no legal alternative. Saving a life outweighs broken windows and burned chairs.

questions.q: D is attacked with fists in a public park. D could have safely run away, but instead draws a knife and stabs the attacker dead. Under the majority rule on self-defense, D's use of deadly force was:
options: Justified — a person under attack never has a duty to retreat.
Not justified — the majority rule requires retreat before using deadly force when safe retreat is available outside the home.
Justified — the attacker provoked the fight.
Automatically reduced to voluntary manslaughter.
questions.explain: The majority rule: before using deadly force, the defendant must retreat if he can do so safely — except in his own home (castle doctrine) or, in some states, his workplace. Non-deadly force carries no duty to retreat.

questions.q: D becomes voluntarily intoxicated at a party and, in a drunken haze, drives off in V's car, genuinely but unreasonably believing it is his own identical car. Charged with larceny, a specific-intent crime, D's intoxication:
options: Is no defense — voluntary intoxication never negates mens rea.
May negate the specific intent to steal, supporting acquittal on larceny (though a lesser general-intent offense could still lie).
Is irrelevant because D's mistake about the car was unreasonable.
Requires proof that someone spiked D's drink.
questions.explain: Voluntary intoxication is admissible to negate the mens rea of specific-intent crimes: if D was too drunk to form the intent to steal, larceny fails. It is not a defense to general-intent or strict-liability crimes, and it never applies the way involuntary intoxication does.

questions.q: Without entering the home, an officer aims a thermal-imaging device at D's house from the public street and detects unusual heat patterns suggesting an indoor marijuana grow. He gets a warrant based solely on that imaging. At trial D moves to suppress the grow-house evidence, arguing the imaging itself was an unconstitutional search. Result?
options: The evidence stays — no physical trespass occurred, so no search took place.

The warrant is void and the evidence is suppressed — using sense-enhancing technology not in general public use to learn details of the home's interior IS a search, so the warrant's only basis was unconstitutionally obtained.
The imaging is a search but no warrant was needed — heat patterns carry no expectation of privacy.
The imaging is lawful — thermal imagers are in general public use.
questions.explain: Kyllo v. United States: using sense-enhancing technology not in general public use, aimed at the home, to learn details of the home's interior IS a search. The warrant rested solely on unconstitutional fruit, so it is void and the evidence is suppressed.

questions.q: At 11 p.m. in a neighborhood known for drug trafficking, an officer sees a man standing on a corner, briefly speaks with him, and watches the man run when marked police cars approach. The officer chases, stops him, pats him down, and finds drugs in his pocket. Result?
options: Lawful stop and lawful frisk — flight from police is always enough.
Unlawful stop but lawful frisk.
Lawful stop — flight plus high-crime area plus late night gives reasonable suspicion — but the frisk was unlawful: no facts suggested he was armed and dangerous, so the drugs are suppressed.
Unlawful stop and unlawful frisk — a high-crime area can never support reasonable suspicion.
questions.explain: Flight + high-crime area + late night = reasonable suspicion for the STOP (Illinois v. Wardlow); but the FRISK needs its own armed-and-dangerous basis — none here, so the frisk is unlawful and the drugs are suppressed.

questions.q: An officer arrests the driver on an outstanding traffic warrant, handcuffs him, and locks him in the back of the cruiser. She then searches the car's passenger compartment and finds cocaine in the glove box. At the suppression hearing she testifies the search was incident to the arrest. Result?
options: Lawful — a lawful arrest always authorizes searching the car.
Lawful — the automobile exception needs no probable cause.

Unlawful — under Arizona v. Gant, once the arrestee is secured the car may not be searched incident to arrest unless he might still access it or evidence of the crime of arrest might be inside; neither is true here. Suppress the cocaine.
Lawful — a routine inventory search.
questions.explain: Arizona v. Gant: once the arrestee is secured, the car may be searched incident to arrest only if (1) he might still access it or (2) evidence of the crime of arrest might be inside — neither is true for a handcuffed driver held on a traffic warrant. Suppress the cocaine.

questions.q: Officers illegally enter D's home without a warrant and photograph a ledger on the table. Unknown to them, a separate team had already obtained a valid search warrant for the same home and was ten minutes away; they would have photographed the same ledger. At trial the photos are:
options: Suppressed — fruit of the poisonous tree, and no exception applies.
Admitted — inevitable discovery: the warrant team was already on its way and would have found the ledger lawfully.
Admitted — the good-faith exception, because the officers believed the entry was lawful.
Suppressed — attenuation requires the taint to fade over time, and ten minutes is not enough.
questions.explain: Inevitable discovery (Nix v. Williams): the independent lawful team already had a valid warrant and was ten minutes away — they would have photographed the same ledger lawfully.

World-Wide Volkswagen: foreseeability that a product reaches the forum is not purposeful availment — the defendant must have targeted the forum. M did nothing aimed at Oregon. Option 2 is the classic foreseeability trap. Option 3 misstates the law — 'continuous and systematic' was the OLD general-jurisdiction test, retired by Daimler and Goodyear. Option 4 states the general-jurisdiction rule correctly but answers the wrong question: V needs SPECIFIC jurisdiction, which fails at step one (no purposeful availment).
options: Grant the motion — M's mere placement of the pump into the stream of commerce, without targeting Oregon, is not purposeful availment.
Deny the motion — the injury occurred in Oregon, so M should have foreseen being sued there.
Deny the motion — M's national distribution network constitutes continuous and systematic contacts with Oregon.
Grant the motion — a corporation can only be sued where it is incorporated or has its principal place of business.
questions.q: V, an Oregon resident, buys a used industrial pump at an Oregon equipment auction. The pump was made by M, a California manufacturer that sells only through independent national distributors, runs no ads in Oregon, and has no Oregon salespeople. The pump fails and injures V in Oregon. V sues M in Oregon state court. M moves to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. How should the court rule?

questions.explain: General jurisdiction = 'at home' = place of incorporation plus principal place of business (Daimler; Goodyear). Substantial sales are not enough — option 1 is the pre-2011 trap. Option 3 misreads Mallory: consent-by-registration works only where the STATE STATUTE deems registration to be consent (Pennsylvania's scheme); Florida's does not here, and a bare registered agent is not consent. Option 4 is nonsense — the plaintiff's residence is irrelevant to personal jurisdiction over the defendant.
options: Deny — C's substantial Florida sales and registered agent make it 'at home' in Florida.
Grant — C is at home only in Delaware and Texas; doing business alone is not enough, and the registration statute does not create consent.
Deny — under Mallory v. Norfolk Southern, registration to do business is consent to general jurisdiction.
Grant — a Georgia plaintiff cannot sue a Delaware corporation in Florida.
questions.q: C is incorporated in Delaware with its headquarters (nerve center) in Texas. C sells 30% of its products in Florida through independent retailers and maintains a registered agent in Florida as state law requires. P, a Georgia resident, sues C in Florida over a car crash in Nevada. Florida's registration statute does not deem registration to be consent to jurisdiction. C moves to dismiss. Result?

questions.explain: Burnham v. Superior Court: 'tag' jurisdiction — personal service while the defendant is physically present in the forum is a classic basis needing NO contacts analysis, even for unrelated claims. Options 1 and 3 demand contacts where none are required. Option 4 is the common over-reading: the classic bases (presence, domicile, consent, waiver) bypass International Shoe entirely.
options: Grant — D is not domiciled in New York and the claim is unrelated to New York.
Deny — personal service on a defendant physically present in the forum establishes jurisdiction even for unrelated claims.
Grant — a transient layover is too fleeting to satisfy minimum contacts.
Deny — but only if the plaintiff also shows minimum contacts under International Shoe.
questions.q: D, a Nigerian businessman who lives in Lagos, changes planes at JFK Airport in New York on his way to London. While waiting at the gate, he is personally served with a New York lawsuit over a contract dispute that has no connection to New York. D moves to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. How should the court rule?

questions.explain: FRCP 12(h)(1): the personal-jurisdiction defense (12(b)(2)) is waived if not raised in the first response — motion or answer. Option 1 states the SUBJECT-MATTER jurisdiction rule (12(b)(1), never waived) — the exam's favorite swap. Option 3 is backwards: asserting a counterclaim without the PJ defense underscores the waiver. Option 4 reaches the right result for the wrong reason — it is the omission, not the counterclaim, that waives.
options: Grant — personal jurisdiction can be raised at any time, like subject-matter jurisdiction.
Deny — the 12(b)(2) defense was waived by omission from the first response.
Grant — the counterclaim proves D did not intend to waive anything.
Deny — but only because filing a counterclaim submits D to the court's power.
questions.q: P sues D in federal court. D files an answer asserting a counterclaim but raising no jurisdictional defenses. Three months later, D moves to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. P opposes. How should the court rule?

Officers arrest D for armed robbery. The gun is missing. At the scene, before any Miranda warnings, an officer asks, "Where's the gun?" D answers, "In the dumpster behind the store," and the gun is recovered there. D moves to suppress the statement.
options: Suppress it — custody plus interrogation requires warnings first.
Admit it — the public-safety exception: the question was reasonably prompted by concern for public safety.
Admit it — but only because D waived by answering.
Admit it — the gun would inevitably have been found anyway.
questions.explain: New York v. Quarles: a question reasonably prompted by concern for public safety ('Where's the gun?' with the gun missing in a public place) needs no Miranda warnings first, and the answer is admissible. Option 4 misuses inevitable discovery — nothing shows lawful means already in motion.

questions.q: D is in custody at the station, warned, and waives. Midway he says, "Maybe I should talk to a lawyer, I'm not sure." The detective keeps questioning and D confesses.
options: Suppress — any mention of counsel invokes the Edwards shield.
Admit — but suppress on retrial.
Admit — the invocation was ambiguous, so questioning could continue.
Suppress — but only if D proves he subjectively wanted counsel.
questions.explain: Davis v. Washington: invocation of the right to counsel must be UNEQUIVOCAL — 'maybe I should talk to a lawyer' is ambiguous, so questioning may continue and the confession is admissible. 'Maybe' is not an invocation; 'I want' is.

questions.q: A robbery victim gets a good look at the robber's face in a well-lit store, describes him in detail to police, and two days later picks him from a six-photo array — but the detective told her, 'take your time, the suspect's photo is in there.' No charges have been filed yet. D moves to suppress the identification.
options: Admit it — the procedure was suggestive, but the Biggers reliability factors are strong.
Suppress it — no counsel was present at the photo array.
Suppress it — suggestiveness alone requires exclusion.
Suppress it — single-photo procedures require same-day administration.
questions.explain: Manson v. Brathwaite / Neil v. Biggers two-step: suggestiveness is step one, reliability step two. The Biggers factors are all strong here (close well-lit look, detailed accurate description, 48 hours, certain at trial) — reliability saves the identification. No Wade right at photo arrays (Ash), no Sixth Amendment right pre-indictment (Kirby).

questions.q: D is arrested at home. Without Miranda warnings, during a voluntary conversation he says, 'The stolen laptop is in my car trunk.' Police recover it, and the prosecution offers the laptop at trial.
options: Suppress it — fruit of the unwarned statement.
Admit it — Patane: the statement is out, but its physical fruits come in.
Admit it — inevitable discovery.
Suppress it — Elstad requires warnings before any fruits.
questions.explain: United States v. Patane: Miranda is prophylactic — the unwarned-but-voluntary STATEMENT is excluded, but its PHYSICAL FRUITS are admissible. This is the exam's favorite cross-amendment swap: under the Fourth Amendment the laptop would be poisoned fruit; under the Fifth it is clean.

questions.q: D tells V his watch is solid gold worth $5,000. V pays $5,000 cash, intending D to keep the money. The watch is brass worth $50. D's crime is:
options: Larceny by trick — V's consent was induced by fraud.
Embezzlement — D lawfully received the cash, then converted it.
False pretenses — D obtained title to the money by misrepresentation of present fact.
No crime — sales talk is mere puffery.
questions.explain: The title test decides the theft triangle: V intended D to KEEP the money, so title passed by a misrepresentation of present fact → false pretenses. Larceny by trick requires the victim to part with possession only (e.g., 'let me examine it'). Embezzlement requires lawful possession first — here the fraud preceded the transfer. A specific false statement of fact is not puffery.

questions.q: At 2 a.m., D walks through V's front door — left standing wide open — intending to steal the television. Frightened by the dog, he leaves without touching anything. At common law, D is:
options: Not guilty of burglary — entry through an open door is not a breaking.
Guilty of burglary — intent plus entry into a dwelling at night is enough.
Guilty of attempted burglary — he abandoned the theft before completing it.
Not guilty of burglary — nothing was stolen.
questions.explain: Common-law burglary requires a BREAKING — force to gain entry. Walking through an open door is not a breaking, so the completed offense fails despite intent, entry, dwelling, and night. Completion of the target theft is not an element — the intent at entry is the gravamen — but without a breaking there is no burglary. Trespass or attempted larceny may survive.

questions.q: D, a skilled pickpocket, lifts V's wallet from his coat pocket. V never notices; no force beyond the lifting is used. D is guilty of:
options: Robbery — any taking from the person is robbery.
Larceny — the force used did not exceed what the taking required.
Robbery — stealth counts as force against the person.
Embezzlement — D took property already in his control.
questions.explain: Robbery = larceny + force or threat of imminent force BEYOND what the taking requires. An unnoticed lift uses no such force → larceny. 'Any taking from the person is robbery' is the classic trap; stealth is not force. Force used to retain property in immediate flight would make it robbery — not present here.

questions.q: T, a bank teller, lawfully receives cash deposits into her drawer each morning. Three weeks in, she begins pocketing $200 a week, intending to repay it 'when things improve.' T is guilty of:
options: Larceny — she trespassorily took the bank's money.
False pretenses — she obtained the money by misrepresentation.
No crime as to the conversion — she lawfully possessed the cash when she received it.
Embezzlement — fraudulent conversion of property lawfully in her possession; the intent may form after possession began, and intent to repay is no defense.
questions.explain: Embezzlement = fraudulent conversion of property already lawfully in possession (custody). Unlike larceny, the fraudulent intent may form AFTER possession began; intent to repay is no defense. Larceny fails because the original receipt was not trespassory. False pretenses fails because no misrepresentation obtained the money — she was entrusted with it.

questions.q: Congress passes the Safe Schools Act, making it a federal crime to possess a firearm within 1,000 feet of a school. The Act contains no requirement that the firearm have moved in or otherwise affected interstate commerce. The Act is:
options: Constitutional — schools are channels of interstate commerce, which Congress may keep clear of firearms.
Constitutional — gun possession near schools, considered together nationwide, substantially affects interstate commerce.
Unconstitutional — possessing a gun near a school is non-economic activity with no substantial effect on interstate commerce, and the Act lacks a jurisdictional element.
Unconstitutional — the Second Amendment bars Congress from regulating firearms at all.
questions.explain: Lopez: possessing a gun near a school is non-economic activity — Congress cannot aggregate non-economic activity to manufacture a substantial effect, and findings don't save it (Morrison). Without a jurisdictional element the Act falls. Schools are not “channels” of commerce (those are the routes themselves).

questions.q: Congress charters the Federal Broadband Agency, headquartered in Maryland. Maryland enacts a property tax that applies to all commercial buildings in the state, including the Agency's offices. The tax is:
options: Unconstitutional — under McCulloch v. Maryland, a state may not tax a federal instrumentality; the power to tax involves the power to destroy.
Constitutional — states retain concurrent power to tax all property within their borders.
Constitutional — the tax is non-discriminatory and applies equally to private and state buildings.
Unconstitutional — only Congress may tax property used in interstate commerce.
questions.explain: McCulloch, holding 2: a state may not tax a federal instrumentality — “the power to tax involves the power to destroy,” and the Supremacy Clause forbids it. Non-discriminatory form doesn't save it (Maryland's tax was also facially neutral as to the Bank).

questions.q: A state law requires male applicants for state trooper positions to pass a rigorous physical fitness test; female applicants are exempt. A rejected male applicant challenges the law. The court should apply:
options: Strict scrutiny — gender is a suspect classification requiring a compelling interest.
Intermediate scrutiny — the classification must be substantially related to an important government interest.
Rational-basis review — hiring standards are economic regulation.
No review — staffing a police force is a core state police power.
questions.explain: Craig v. Boren: gender classifications get intermediate scrutiny — substantially related to an important interest. Gender is quasi-suspect, NOT suspect; “strict scrutiny for gender” is the classic wrong answer.

questions.q: Congress offers each state 5% of its federal highway funds on condition that the state raise its minimum drinking age to 21. A state challenges the condition. The condition is:
options: Unconstitutional — Congress is commandeering the state legislature.
Constitutional — the condition satisfies South Dakota v. Dole's limits, and 5% is encouragement rather than coercion, under the spending power.
Unconstitutional — the Twenty-first Amendment reserves alcohol regulation exclusively to the states.
Constitutional — a national drinking age substantially affects interstate commerce.
questions.explain: Dole: conditional spending is valid when it serves the general welfare, is unambiguous, is related to the federal interest (highway funds ↔ safe roads ↔ drinking age), and has no independent bar — and 5% is mild encouragement, not NFIB-style coercion. The 21st Amendment doesn't bar conditional spending; commandeering is ordering legislatures, not offering money.

questions.q: Facing a landfill shortage, State X enacts a law barring the import of solid waste generated in other states; waste generated inside State X may still go to the state's landfills. An out-of-state waste hauler challenges the law. The law is:
options: Constitutional — waste disposal is a core exercise of the state's police power over health and safety.
Constitutional — the dormant Commerce Clause applies only where Congress has legislated on the subject.
Unconstitutional — the ban facially discriminates against interstate commerce and is virtually per se invalid.
Constitutional — the court will uphold it if the burden on interstate commerce is not clearly excessive under Pike balancing.
questions.explain: Philadelphia v. New Jersey: facial discrimination against interstate commerce — virtually per se invalid. The police power never saves a discriminatory law; the dormant Clause needs no congressional action; Pike balancing is for evenhanded laws, not discriminatory ones.

questions.q: State Y requires every commercial truck using its highways to install a specific contoured mudguard. The rule applies equally to in-state and out-of-state trucks, but out-of-state carriers must refit their fleets at significant cost. A carrier challenges the rule. The court should apply:
options: Per se invalidity — the rule discriminates against out-of-state carriers.
Pike balancing — the rule stands unless its burden on interstate commerce is clearly excessive relative to local safety benefits.
Strict scrutiny — highway regulation burdens the fundamental right to travel.
No dormant-Clause review — evenhanded highway-safety laws are immune from the dormant Commerce Clause.
questions.explain: The rule is evenhanded, so Pike balancing applies: upheld unless the burden is clearly excessive vs. the local safety benefit (cf. Bibb's mudguards; Clover Leaf). Per-se invalidity is for discriminatory laws; strict scrutiny is rights vocabulary; no immunity exists for evenhanded laws.

questions.q: Federal aviation regulations require pilots to rest at least 8 hours before a flight. State Z requires 10 hours of rest for any flight originating in the state. A pilot challenges the state rule as preempted by federal law. The state rule is:
options: Preempted — a state standard that differs from the federal standard is displaced.
Not preempted — the pilot can obey both by resting 10 hours; impossibility requires that both commands cannot be obeyed.
Preempted — field occupation, since aviation safety is pervasively federally regulated.
Preempted as an obstacle — the state rule frustrates Congress's purpose of uniform rest rules.
questions.explain: Florida Lime: the federal rule is a floor and the state rule a reachable ceiling — obeying both is possible, so no impossibility preemption. Differs-from ≠ preempted; field preemption needs a clear and manifest congressional purpose; nothing shows the state rule frustrating Congress's chosen means.

questions.q: Congress passes the Firearm Background Act, requiring county sheriffs to conduct federal background checks on handgun purchasers. A sheriff challenges the requirement. It is:
options: Constitutional — Congress may regulate firearms under the Commerce Clause.
Constitutional — the Supremacy Clause obliges state officers to enforce federal law.
Unconstitutional — Congress may not commandeer state executive officers to administer a federal program.
Constitutional — background checks are a traditional state police function, so no federalism problem arises.
questions.explain: Printz v. United States: Congress may not compel state executive officers to administer a federal regulatory program. Commerce power does not authorize the commandeering method; the Supremacy Clause binds courts (Testa), not officers; the police-like nature of the task is why commandeering doctrine forbids it.

questions.q: State A makes interracial marriage a crime. A couple married in another state is prosecuted on returning home. Under current law, the statute is:
options: Valid under rational basis — preserving tradition is a legitimate interest.
Valid under intermediate scrutiny — marriage regulation is a state concern.
Invalid — race classifications face strict scrutiny, and no compelling interest supports the ban.
Valid under strict scrutiny — the wartime deference of Korematsu applies.
questions.explain: Loving v. Virginia: race is a suspect class, so strict scrutiny applies and 'racial purity' is not a compelling interest. Rational basis never applies to a race classification; intermediate is for gender/illegitimacy; Korematsu's wartime deference is disavowed and never extends to marriage bans.

questions.q: State B's military academy admits men only. Women are offered a separate leadership institute with fewer resources, no alumni network, and no military tradition. The exclusion is:
options: Valid — gender is a suspect class, but military training is a compelling interest.
Invalid — gender gets intermediate scrutiny, and the state lacks an exceedingly persuasive justification; the substitute is not equal.
Valid under rational basis — states may experiment with single-sex education.
Invalid — gender classifications face strict scrutiny.
questions.explain: United States v. Virginia (VMI): gender is quasi-suspect, so intermediate scrutiny with an 'exceedingly persuasive justification' applies; a separate-but-unequal substitute does not satisfy it. Gender is never a suspect class, so strict scrutiny (and the compelling-interest framing) is the wrong tier.

questions.q: A city requires a special-use permit for a group home for adults with intellectual disabilities, though boarding houses, fraternities, and nursing homes need none. Neighbours' fears are the only reason given. The ordinance is:
options: Invalid — disability is a quasi-suspect class, so intermediate scrutiny applies.
Valid — under rational basis, neighbourhood fears are a legitimate interest.
Invalid — disability is a suspect class, so strict scrutiny applies.
Invalid — under rational basis, because the permit rests on irrational fear, not a legitimate interest; disability is not elevated to a higher tier.
questions.explain: City of Cleburne: the permit fails rational basis because irrational fear is not a legitimate interest — but disability is NOT elevated to a higher tier. Both halves matter: fails rational basis AND class not elevated.

questions.q: After Dobbs, State C bans abortion after 15 weeks, with exceptions for the mother's life and fatal fetal anomalies. A clinic challenges the ban. Under current law, the ban is:
options: Valid if rationally related to a legitimate interest, such as protecting prenatal life or maternal health.
Invalid under Casey's undue-burden test, because 15 weeks burdens women before viability.
Invalid — abortion is a fundamental right, so strict scrutiny applies.
Valid only if the state proves a compelling interest by necessary means.
questions.explain: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization overruled Roe and Casey: no constitutional right to abortion remains, so regulations get rational-basis review. Casey's undue-burden test is dead law for abortion; Lawrence and Obergefell survive for their own rights.

questions.q: A state university hires a lecturer on a one-year contract. The university's written rules award tenure only after five years of service, and no practice suggests otherwise. At the end of the year the university does not renew her contract, giving no reasons and no hearing. She claims due process required a hearing before non-renewal. Is she right?
options: Yes — every public employee is entitled to a hearing before non-renewal.
No — she has no property interest, because she has only a hope of renewal, not a legitimate claim of entitlement.
Yes — because the university is a state actor, due process always requires a hearing.
No — but only because she failed to prove the university acted in bad faith.
questions.explain: Board of Regents v. Roth (1972): a one-year contract with tenure only after five years, and no practice otherwise, gives a hope of renewal, not a legitimate claim of entitlement. No property interest, so no hearing is owed, and the analysis stops at question 1. State action alone never creates a hearing right; bad faith is not the test — entitlement is.

questions.q: The Social Security Administration reviews a disability recipient's medical file, concludes he is no longer disabled, and terminates his benefits. He receives written notice and a full evidentiary hearing afterwards, with retroactive benefits if he prevails, but no evidentiary hearing before termination. He claims due process required a pre-termination evidentiary hearing. Is he right?
options: Yes — under Goldberg, benefits may never be terminated without a prior evidentiary hearing.
Yes — because disability benefits are a property interest, a full trial is always required first.
No — because disability benefits are not property at all.

No — under Mathews, the private interest is softened by back payments, the medical evidence is largely documentary so a live hearing adds little, and the administrative burden is great, so a post-termination hearing suffices.
questions.explain: Mathews v. Eldridge (1976): disability benefits ARE property, so question 1 passes — but question 2 is Mathews balancing, not Goldberg automatic. Back payments soften the private interest, documentary medical evidence means a live pre-termination hearing adds little, and the administrative burden is great. Goldberg's full pre-termination hearing was on welfare/subsistence facts, not a universal rule.

questions.q: Police arrest a man for shoplifting. The charge is dismissed. The police nevertheless circulate a flyer to local merchants naming him, with his photograph, under the heading “active shoplifters”. He loses no job, licence, or legal status as a result. He claims the flyer deprived him of a liberty interest without due process. Is he right?
options: Yes — public defamation by the government is itself a deprivation of liberty.
Yes — because the charge was dismissed, any further government action against him requires a hearing.
No — reputation alone is not a liberty interest; he needs stigma-plus, a tangible loss alongside the stigma.
No — because the police acted in good faith.
questions.explain: Paul v. Davis (1976): the flyer is stigma, but with no job, licence, or legal status lost there is no “plus”. Reputation alone is not a liberty interest; defamation by the government is a state tort matter, not a due process case. Dismissal of the charge does not convert every later government statement into a hearing right, and good faith is not the test — the interest is.

questions.q: A city school board employs a security guard under a state statute providing he may be dismissed only for cause. The board, believing he lied on his application, gives him written notice of the charge and an opportunity to respond in writing, then dismisses him. A full evidentiary hearing follows, at which he may call witnesses. He claims due process required a full evidentiary hearing before dismissal. Is he right?
options: Yes — a for-cause job always requires a full trial before termination.
No — under Loudermill, notice plus an opportunity to respond before termination, followed by a full post-termination hearing, satisfies due process.
No — because a security guard's job is not a property interest.
Yes — because a written response is never an opportunity to be heard.
questions.explain: Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill (1985): a for-cause job IS a property interest, and before termination due process requires only notice of the charges and an opportunity to respond — in person or in writing. A full evidentiary hearing afterwards completes the process. Loudermill expressly rejects a full pre-termination trial, and a written response IS an opportunity to be heard at the pre-termination stage.

missbank.statement: Consequential damages (like lost profits) are recoverable only if the SPECIFIC loss was reasonably foreseeable to the breaching party AT THE TIME OF CONTRACT FORMATION — not just that something was 'urgent.'
missbank.detail: Adaeze told the carrier only 'deliver fast — it's urgent,' never that the mill would sit idle or what the profits were. The carrier could not foresee $30,000 in lost mill profits, so she recovered nothing beyond the shipping charge. Hook: 'urgent' is a feeling; Hadley needs facts.

missbank.statement: Recklessness = CONSCIOUS disregard of a PERCEIVED risk. If the defendant never perceived the risk, he was at most negligent — never reckless.
missbank.detail: D fired into the air believing the yard was empty; it credibly never occurred to him anyone was there. No perceived risk, no conscious disregard — so no recklessness, even though firing a gun near a house looks reckless objectively. The statute punished recklessness only, so D walked. Hook: recklessness lives inside the defendant's head.

missbank.rule: MPC conspiracy is unilateral; common law is bilateral
missbank.statement: Under the MPC (unilateral approach), ONE genuine criminal mind is enough — an agreement with a feigning undercover officer IS conspiracy. At common law (bilateral), two genuine criminal minds are required, so the feigning officer defeats it.
missbank.detail: D agreed with U to rob a bank; U was undercover and never meant it. MPC: D is guilty of conspiracy — D believed he agreed. Common law: no conspiracy, because U never truly agreed. Always ask which rulebook the question names. Hook: 'unilateral = uno = one mind.'

missbank.statement: M'Naghten insanity = the defendant EITHER did not know the nature and quality of his act OR did not know that it was wrong. One prong suffices.
missbank.detail: Daniel knew he was ending a human life (prong one failed) but believed God commanded it, so he did not know it was morally wrong (prong two satisfied) — the classic deific decree. Insane under M'Naghten. Hook: 'knowing the act is not enough — he must also know it's wrong.'

missbank.statement: When the buyer actually covers in good faith and without unreasonable delay: damages = (COVER price − CONTRACT price) × QUANTITY. The market-price measure (section 2-713) applies ONLY when the buyer does NOT cover.
missbank.detail: 1,000 bushels at $5 contract, covered at $6: ($6 − $5) × 1,000 = $1,000. The $750 market differential was the trap — market measure never applies once the buyer covers. Hook: 'cover minus contract, times quantity.'

missbank.rule: Mirror image (common law) vs. battle of the forms (UCC)
missbank.statement: Common law: acceptance must MIRROR the offer exactly — any variance is a counteroffer killing the offer. UCC section 2-207: a definite acceptance CAN form a contract despite additional or different terms.
missbank.detail: Between merchants, additional terms become part of the deal unless the offer limited acceptance to its terms, they materially alter the deal, or objection is made. Conflicting ('different') terms knock each other out and UCC gap-fillers apply. First question on any formation problem: goods or not goods?

missbank.statement: Acceptance is effective on DISPATCH (mailing); revocation is effective only on RECEIPT.
missbank.detail: B mailed acceptance Wednesday; A's revocation reached B Thursday — contract formed Wednesday, revocation too late. This is Adams v. Lindsell, the same dispatch principle from English common law. The MBE loves dispatch-vs-receipt races.

missbank.statement: A merchant's signed writing holding an offer open is irrevocable WITHOUT consideration — but the irrevocable period can NEVER exceed three months, even if the writing says longer.
missbank.detail: Four months stated, revoked at two: the offer was irrevocable, but only for three months. At common law, by contrast, an offer is revocable any time before acceptance unless it is an option supported by consideration.

missbank.rule: Perfect tender and the right to cure
missbank.statement: UCC section 2-601: goods must conform EXACTLY — any non-conformity lets the buyer reject the whole shipment. But section 2-508: the seller may CURE with a conforming delivery within the contract time.
missbank.detail: 95 red + 5 blue bicycles: buyer may reject all (no substantial-performance doctrine for goods), but the seller gets a second chance before the delivery deadline passes. Common law's substantial performance does not cross into goods territory.

missbank.statement: The felony that caused the death CANNOT be the assault that is the homicide itself — the predicate felony must be INDEPENDENT of the killing.
missbank.detail: Beating V to break his legs, V dies: aggravated assault merges, so no felony murder. But all is not lost for the prosecution — intent to inflict serious bodily injury is itself malice (route two), so it is second-degree murder. Hook: merger kills the theory, not the charge.

missbank.statement: Attempt requires SPECIFIC INTENT to commit the target crime — so there is no attempted felony murder, no attempted depraved-heart murder, and no attempted involuntary manslaughter. You cannot 'intend' an unintended killing.
missbank.detail: D fired wildly at pursuing officers to scare them: no attempted felony murder (felony murder needs no intent to kill) — but the completed assault stands on its own. Attempt always asks: did he specifically intend the result?

missbank.rule: Factual impossibility is never a defense to attempt
missbank.statement: If the crime was factually impossible (empty pocket, fake drugs, unloaded gun the defendant thought was loaded), attempt liability still attaches — what matters is intent plus conduct beyond mere preparation.
missbank.detail: Hand in the empty pocket with intent to steal = attempted larceny. Contrast legal impossibility (what he did wasn't actually a crime at all), which mostly survives only at common law. Hook: 'the pocket was empty; the intent was full.'

missbank.statement: There is NO general legal duty to rescue a stranger — moral duty is not legal duty. An omission supplies actus reus only where a legal duty to act exists.
missbank.detail: The expert swimmer who walked past the drowning stranger committed no crime: none of the five duty sources (statute, status relationship, contract, voluntary undertaking, creation of the peril) applied. But-for causation is irrelevant without a duty.

missbank.rule: Strict liability: mistake of fact is no defense
missbank.statement: For a strict-liability element, NO mens rea is required — so even an honest AND reasonable mistake of fact is no defense.
missbank.detail: D reasonably believed V was 18 (fake ID, looked 18): guilty anyway, because the statute made age a strict-liability element. The honest-and-reasonable-mistake defense belongs to malice and general-intent crimes, not strict liability.

Nevada crash, Florida suit against a Delaware/Texas company: specific fails (claim unrelated to Florida contacts) and general fails (not at home in Florida) — Daimler/Goodyear. Always ask first: is the claim connected to the forum? That fork decides which test you run. Hook: 'connected claim = specific; at home = general.'
missbank.rule: Specific vs. general jurisdiction — the fork
missbank.statement: SPECIFIC jurisdiction = the CLAIM arises from the defendant's forum contacts (purposeful availment + relatedness + reasonableness). GENERAL jurisdiction = ANY claim, but only where the defendant is 'at home' (domicile; a corporation's state of incorporation + principal place of business).

missbank.detail: California maker, national distributor, Oregon injury, no Oregon targeting: no jurisdiction (World-Wide Volkswagen). The exam dresses foreseeability up as 'should have known its products end up everywhere' — that sentence is always the trap. Hook: 'foreseeable is not purposeful.'
missbank.statement: Foreseeability that a product or act reaches the forum is NEVER enough — the defendant must have TARGETED the forum (advertising there, designing for its market, establishing distribution channels). Mere stream-of-commerce placement fails.

missbank.detail: Answer with a counterclaim but no PJ defense, then a late 12(b)(2) motion: denied — waived under 12(h)(1). If the same motion had attacked SMJ instead, it could never be too late. Hook: 'PJ is use-it-or-lose-it; SMJ is forever.'
missbank.rule: Personal jurisdiction is waivable; subject-matter jurisdiction is not
missbank.statement: PJ (12(b)(2)) omitted from the defendant's FIRST response = WAIVED, forever. SMJ (12(b)(1)) can never be waived, never be consented into, and can be raised at any time — even on appeal, even by the judge.

missbank.rule: Wardlow: flight + high-crime area = reasonable suspicion for a STOP, never automatically a frisk
missbank.statement: Unprovoked flight in a high-crime area gives reasonable suspicion for the STOP — but the FRISK still needs its own armed-and-dangerous basis. The two-step Terry split.
missbank.detail: Session 15, D2: he marked the stop unlawful; flight plus high-crime area plus late night = specific articulable facts. Bank the line: stop lawful ≠ frisk lawful.

missbank.statement: If lawful means already in motion would have found the evidence anyway, it is ADMITTED — even though the police's own conduct was unlawful.
missbank.detail: Session 15, D4: a separate team with a valid warrant ten minutes away would have photographed the same ledger → photos admitted. He chose suppression, ignoring the antidote.

essays.title: The Widget Deal — Formation Under the UCC
essays.prompt: Acme Corp, a merchant that manufactures industrial widgets, emails Baker Corp, also a merchant: 'We offer 2,000 widgets at $50 each, delivery September 1. This offer remains open for six months.' Baker's purchasing manager immediately replies by email: 'We accept. Please ship C.O.D.' Two months later, the market price of widgets jumps to $80. Acme mails Baker a letter revoking the offer; the letter arrives on a Tuesday. That same Tuesday morning, before the letter arrives, Baker mails its signed purchase order for the 2,000 widgets. Baker's purchase order adds a term requiring Acme to email advance notice of each shipment. Acme refuses to deliver, arguing (1) the offer was revoked before acceptance, (2) no contract exists because the forms do not match, and (3) the email-notice term was never agreed to. Is there an enforceable contract, and on what terms?
issues: UCC vs. common law classification (goods)
Offer and the merchant firm-offer rule (UCC 2-205) with the 3-month cap
Mailbox rule: acceptance on dispatch vs. revocation on receipt
Battle of the forms (UCC 2-207): formation despite additional terms
Whether the additional email-notice term becomes part of the contract between merchants
essays.model: The threshold question on every contract problem is classification: are these goods? Widgets are movable, tangible things, so UCC Article 2 governs formation, performance, and remedies — not the common-law mirror-image rule Acme invokes. Acme's email is an offer: it shows definite commitment (2,000 widgets, $50 each, September 1 delivery) communicated to an identified offeree. An invitation to negotiate would lack such definiteness; this has it. Because Acme is a merchant and the offer is held open in a signed writing — an email satisfies the writing requirement — UCC 2-205 makes it a firm offer: irrevocable without any consideration. But 2-205 caps the irrevocable period at three months even though Acme wrote six, so Acme's revocation at month two was ineffective and the offer remained open. Next comes the timing race. Under the mailbox rule, an acceptance is effective on dispatch while a revocation is effective only on receipt. Baker mailed its signed purchase order Tuesday morning; Acme's revocation letter arrived Tuesday afternoon. Dispatch beat receipt, so a contract formed Tuesday morning before the revocation ever landed. Acme's second argument — no contract because the forms do not match — invokes the common-law mirror-image rule, which the UCC expressly rejects. Under 2-207, a definite and seasonable expression of acceptance forms a contract even though it states additional terms. Baker's purchase order was exactly that. Between merchants, the additional term becomes part of the contract unless (a) the offer expressly limited acceptance to its terms, (b) the term materially alters the deal, or (c) objection has been or is made. None applies: Acme's offer contained no such limitation, a routine email-advance-notice term is not a material alteration, and Acme never objected. Had the term conflicted with Acme's own term it would be a 'different' term subject to the knockout rule, but a purely additional term is governed by the rule above. Conclusion: an enforceable contract for 2,000 widgets at $50 each, delivery September 1, including the email-notice term.
