Acme's refusal to deliver is a breach, and Baker may cover under 2-712 and recover the price difference.

marking.point: Classify as goods → UCC Article 2 governs (not common law)
Valid offer: definite terms communicated
Firm offer under 2-205: merchant + signed writing = irrevocable without consideration
3-month cap on irrevocability despite 'six months' stated
Mailbox rule: acceptance effective on dispatch, revocation only on receipt
Contract formed Tuesday morning before revocation arrived
2-207 rejects mirror-image rule; definite acceptance forms contract despite added term
Additional term between merchants becomes part of deal: not a material alteration, no objection, no limit in offer
Conclusion: enforceable contract on stated terms; Acme in breach
Organization and clarity

essays.title: The Restaurant Sale — Statute of Frauds and Parol Evidence
essays.prompt: In January, Owner orally hires Chef to 'run my restaurant for two years, starting March 1.' In February, Owner sells the restaurant to Buyer. Buyer and Seller sign a detailed written agreement stating: 'This writing is the complete and final agreement of the parties.' Before signing, Seller orally assured Buyer that all kitchen equipment was less than two years old; in fact the ovens are twenty years old. After closing, Chef sues Owner for firing him in April, seeking two years' wages under the oral agreement. Buyer sues Seller for breach of contract, offering testimony about the oral equipment assurance. Seller defends both suits. How should the court rule in each case?
issues: Statute of Frauds Year rule: 2-year term starting in the future cannot be performed within one year
No employment exception to the Statute of Frauds
Complete vs. partial integration; merger clause as evidence of complete integration
Parol evidence rule bars prior oral terms in a breach-of-contract action
Fraud exception: follows the claim — formation attack vs. contract-term enforcement
essays.model: Two lawsuits, two doctrines. Start with Chef v. Owner. The Statute of Frauds (MYLEGS: Marriage, Year, Land, Executor, Suretyship) requires certain contracts to be in writing. The Year rule asks whether the agreement could possibly be fully performed within one year of its making — not whether it likely would be. A fixed two-year term starting March 1 cannot possibly be completed within one year of the January agreement. The classic trap is death: death would terminate the fixed term, not perform it, so it does not take the contract outside the Statute. (Contrast a lifetime-employment contract, which death fully performs and which is therefore outside the Statute.) There is no employment exception to the Statute of Frauds, and part performance does not save an employment contract the way it can save a land contract. The oral agreement is therefore unenforceable, and Chef's wage claim fails. Buyer v. Seller turns on the parol evidence rule. The signed writing states it is the 'complete and final agreement of the parties' — strong, though not irrebuttable, evidence of complete integration, and no facts here rebut it. Where a writing is completely integrated, the parol evidence rule bars prior or contemporaneous extrinsic terms offered to add to or contradict the writing. Buyer's testimony about the oral equipment assurance is exactly such an added term, so it is inadmissible in the breach-of-contract action. The fraud exception is the designed trap: it admits extrinsic evidence when the plaintiff attacks formation itself — for example, pleading fraudulent inducement to rescind the deal or recover in tort. But Buyer sued for breach of contract, trying to enforce the oral promise as a term of the writing, which is precisely what the rule forbids. The exception follows the claim. Had Buyer pleaded fraudulent inducement and sought rescission or tort damages, the testimony would come in. Conclusion: Chef loses under the Statute of Frauds; Buyer loses the breach-of-contract claim on the equipment promise under the parol evidence rule, though a properly pleaded fraudulent-inducement claim could admit the testimony.

marking.point: Year rule: fixed 2-year term starting in future cannot be performed within one year of making
Death terminates but does not perform a fixed-term contract; no employment exception
Chef's oral agreement unenforceable under Statute of Frauds
Merger language evidences complete (not partial) integration
Parol evidence rule bars prior oral terms that add to a completely integrated writing
Fraud exception follows the claim: formation attack admits the evidence; breach-of-contract term-enforcement does not
Buyer loses breach claim on the oral promise but could plead fraudulent inducement
Conclusions for both suits
Organization and clarity

essays.title: The Broken Contract — Remedies Across Two Deals
essays.prompt: MillCo's only conveyor belt snaps. MillCo hires RushCo to rush the broken belt to the factory for a pattern, saying only 'get it there fast — we're in a hurry.' RushCo delays unreasonably for three weeks; the mill stands idle and MillCo loses $60,000 in profits. RushCo never knew the mill could not run without the belt. Separately, GrainCo contracts to buy 5,000 bushels of corn from FarmCo at $4/bushel for July 1 delivery. On June 1 FarmCo unequivocally repudiates. On June 5 GrainCo buys substitute corn in good faith at $4.50/bushel; the market price on June 1 was $4.30. GrainCo's contract with FarmCo also provided: 'If FarmCo fails to deliver, FarmCo pays $200,000.' GrainCo's actual proven losses from the breach are $3,000. Advise MillCo and GrainCo on their recoverable damages.
issues: Hadley v. Baxendale: consequential damages require foreseeability of the specific loss at formation
UCC cover (2-712) vs. market (2-713): cover applies when buyer actually covers in good faith
Anticipatory repudiation: aggrieved party may treat as immediate breach
Liquidated damages vs. penalty: unreasonably large clauses are void; actual damages still recoverable
Mitigation/avoidable consequences
essays.model: MillCo's claim turns on Hadley v. Baxendale. Lost profits are consequential damages, and Hadley permits them only if the specific loss was reasonably foreseeable to the breaching party at the time of contract formation — either because it flows in the ordinary course from such a breach, or because special circumstances were communicated and the defendant tacitly accepted the risk. MillCo told RushCo only that it was 'in a hurry.' Urgency is a feeling, not a fact: RushCo never learned the mill would stand idle or what the profits were, so $60,000 in lost profits was not in the parties' contemplation when the contract was made. The tacit-agreement test fails. MillCo therefore recovers nothing beyond the delivery charge itself. GrainCo stands on firmer ground. FarmCo's unequivocal June 1 statement was an anticipatory repudiation, and the aggrieved party may either await performance or treat the repudiation as an immediate breach — GrainCo properly chose the latter. Because GrainCo actually covered on June 5 in good faith and without unreasonable delay, UCC 2-712 supplies the measure: (cover price minus contract price) times quantity, or ($4.50 − $4.00) × 5,000 = $2,500, plus provable incidental and consequential damages. The market-price measure of 2-713 applies only when the buyer does not cover, so the $4.30 market figure is irrelevant — it is the exam's standard trap. The $200,000 clause is void as a penalty. A liquidated-damages clause is enforceable only if the amount was a reasonable forecast of probable loss judged at formation (when actual damages were difficult to estimate); $200,000 against $3,000 in real losses is unreasonably large, so it falls under Restatement 356 / UCC 2-718. Striking the clause does not forfeit GrainCo's actual damages. Finally, mitigation: GrainCo's prompt cover satisfies the avoidable-consequences rule; had it let losses mount unreasonably, the avoidable portion would be barred, though the claim itself would survive. Conclusion: MillCo recovers the delivery charge only; GrainCo recovers $2,500 in cover damages plus incidentals — not $200,000.

marking.point: Hadley rule: consequential damages need foreseeability of the specific loss at formation
'In a hurry' is not notice of idle-mill profits; MillCo's $60,000 barred
Anticipatory repudiation: GrainCo may treat as immediate breach
2-712 cover applies because GrainCo actually covered in good faith; 2-713 market measure does not
$200,000 clause void as penalty (unreasonably large vs. probable loss at formation)
Penalty falls but actual damages remain recoverable
Mitigation: prompt cover satisfies avoidable-consequences rule
Conclusions for both clients
Organization and clarity

essays.title: Three Deaths — Homicide in All Its Forms
essays.prompt: D1, after a calm ten-minute drive to V1's house with a loaded gun, shoots V1 dead, later explaining he had decided during the drive that V1 'had to go.' D2, furious over a gambling debt, attacks V2 with a tire iron intending only to break V2's arms; V2 dies of head injuries sustained in the beating. D2's lawyer argues the assault 'merges' so no homicide charge can stand. D3, fleeing a burglary he committed, fires his gun wildly down a crowded alley to scare off pursuers; a stray bullet kills a bystander. D3 never intended to kill anyone. For each defendant, identify the proper homicide charge under the common-law approach and explain why the alternatives fail.
issues: Malice aforethought: four routes (intent to kill, intent to inflict SBI, depraved heart, felony murder)
First-degree murder: deliberate + premeditated (premeditation can form in an instant)
Merger doctrine: the assault causing death cannot be the felony-murder predicate
Depraved heart: extreme recklessness manifesting extreme indifference to human life
Felony murder requires intent to commit the felony, not intent to kill; no attempt for unintentional killings
essays.model: Homicide analysis runs in two steps: is it murder at all (malice aforethought?), and if so, which degree? Malice aforethought — which does not mean premeditation — has four routes: (1) intent to kill, (2) intent to inflict serious bodily injury, (3) depraved heart (extreme recklessness manifesting extreme indifference to human life), and (4) felony murder. First-degree murder adds deliberation plus premeditation to intent to kill; premeditation has no minimum thinking time and can form in an instant. D1 is guilty of first-degree murder. He formed intent to kill (malice route one), and the calm ten-minute drive with a loaded gun is deliberation and premeditation — cool reflection beforehand, far beyond the instant-premeditation minimum. D2 is guilty of second-degree murder on the intent-to-inflict-serious-bodily-injury theory. Defense counsel's merger point is half right: the aggravated assault that caused V2's death cannot serve as the predicate felony for felony murder, because the predicate must be independent of the killing itself — the assault merges into the homicide. But merger kills the felony-murder theory, not homicide liability: D2 intended serious bodily injury (broken arms), and death resulting from intended serious bodily injury is malice route two. With no premeditation shown, that is second-degree murder. D3 is guilty of second-degree murder on a depraved-heart theory. Firing wildly down a crowded alley to scatter pursuers is extreme recklessness manifesting extreme indifference to human life — malice route three. That D3 never intended to kill anyone is no defense, because malice aforethought does not require intent to kill; it is also why this is murder rather than involuntary manslaughter, which covers ordinary recklessness or criminal negligence. Felony murder (death during the burglary) is a possible alternative theory for D3, but depraved heart fits the facts most directly. Conclusion: D1 — first-degree murder (premeditated intent to kill); D2 — second-degree murder (intended serious bodily injury; merger defeats only the felony-murder theory); D3 — second-degree murder (depraved heart).

marking.point: Malice aforethought framework: four routes stated
D1: intent to kill + deliberation/premeditation from the drive = first-degree murder
Premeditation needs no minimum duration
D2: merger bars using the death-causing assault as felony-murder predicate
D2: merger kills the theory, not the charge — intended SBI is malice route two = second-degree murder
D3: firing down a crowded alley = extreme recklessness / extreme indifference = depraved heart
Malice does not require intent to kill (answers D3's defense)
Second-degree (not first-degree) for D2 and D3: no premeditation shown
Conclusions for all three defendants
Organization and clarity

essays.title: The Crew — Inchoate Crimes and Accomplice Liability
essays.prompt: Al agrees with Ben, an undercover officer who is only pretending, to rob a jewelry store next month; they take no further step. Separately, Al slips his hand into a stranger's pocket to steal a wallet, but the pocket is empty. Al also lends his van to Carla, knowing she will use it as the getaway vehicle for a burglary she has planned with Dan; Al shares no agreement with them. During the burglary, Dan shoots and kills a security guard who confronts him. Finally, Al writes Ed a letter urging Ed to burn down a rival's warehouse; Ed ignores the letter. Analyze Al's criminal liability for each episode under both the common-law and MPC approaches where they differ.
issues: Attempt: specific intent + beyond mere preparation (CL) / substantial step (MPC); factual impossibility no defense
Conspiracy: agreement + dual intent; bilateral (CL) vs. unilateral (MPC); overt-act requirements
Accomplice liability: aid + dual intent (purpose); CL natural-and-probable-consequences vs. MPC purpose-only scope
Pinkerton: needs conspiracy membership — not available to a mere aider
Solicitation: complete on the asking; merges into conspiracy or completed offense
essays.model: The undercover agreement: conspiracy requires an agreement plus dual intent (intent to agree and intent to achieve the criminal objective). The rulebook decides everything here. At common law the majority bilateral approach requires two genuine criminal minds — Ben the undercover officer never truly agreed, so there is no conspiracy at common law. (The common law requires no overt act, but without a true agreement there is nothing to attach it to.) Under the MPC's unilateral approach, one genuine criminal mind suffices: Al believed he was agreeing, so Al is guilty of conspiracy. The overt-act objection also fails on MPC terms: section 5.03(5) requires no overt act for conspiracy to commit a first- or second-degree felony, and robbery is a second-degree felony under the MPC. The empty pocket: attempted larceny under both rulebooks. Attempt requires specific intent plus conduct beyond mere preparation at common law, or a substantial step strongly corroborative of criminal purpose under MPC 5.01. Al had specific intent to steal and put his hand in the pocket — beyond preparation, a substantial step. Factual impossibility (the empty pocket) is never a defense; what matters is intent plus conduct. It is not completed larceny, which requires an actual taking and carrying away, and not conspiracy, which requires an agreement — Al acted alone. The van: Al is an accomplice to the burglary. Accomplice liability requires actual aid plus dual intent — Al knew of the burglary plan and lent the van with the purpose of facilitating it (mere knowledge without purpose would not suffice). For the guard's killing, the scope rule decides: at common law the accomplice answers for the target crime and its natural and probable consequences, and a killing during a burglary is a foreseeable consequence — so Al is liable for the homicide as well. Under MPC 2.06's narrower purpose-only scope, Al answers only for crimes he had the purpose to facilitate, making the homicide charge weaker. Pinkerton liability — conspirators liable for foreseeable crimes of co-conspirators in furtherance of the conspiracy — does not reach Al at all, because Pinkerton requires conspiracy membership and Al shares no agreement with Carla and Dan; he is an aider, not a co-conspirator. The letter: solicitation, complete the moment Al urged Ed to commit arson. Solicitation needs only the asking — no agreement (conspiracy), no substantial step (attempt), and Ed's refusal is irrelevant. It would merge into a conspiracy or the completed arson had either occurred.

marking.point: Attempt elements: specific intent + beyond mere preparation (CL) / substantial step (MPC)
Factual impossibility (empty pocket) never a defense; not completed larceny, not conspiracy
Conspiracy: agreement + dual intent stated
Bilateral (CL): feigning officer defeats conspiracy; unilateral (MPC): one mind suffices + no overt act needed for serious felonies
Accomplice: actual aid + dual intent (purpose to facilitate); Pinkerton needs conspiracy membership, unavailable here
Scope split: CL natural-and-probable-consequences (homicide foreseeable) vs. MPC purpose-only
Solicitation complete on the asking; Ed's refusal irrelevant; no merger (no agreement, no completed crime)
Conclusions per episode with rulebook switches stated
Organization and clarity

essays.title: The Defenses — Justification and Excuse
essays.prompt: (1) At 2 a.m., homeowner Hal hears glass break and finds a stranger climbing through his kitchen window holding a crowbar; Hal shoots the intruder dead. (2) Ian's business partner puts a gun to Ian's wife's head and orders Ian to drive the getaway car for an armed robbery; Ian complies. (3) Jonah, who suffers from paranoid schizophrenia, kills a stranger because he genuinely believes God commanded it as a holy act; he knew he was ending a life but believed the act was morally commanded. (4) An undercover agent with no prior contact spends two months pressuring Ken, who has no criminal record, to sell drugs, finally offering five times the street price; Ken reluctantly makes one sale. (5) Hiker stranded in a blizzard breaks into an empty cabin and burns furniture to survive. Analyze the best defense for each person.
issues: Self-defense: reasonable fear of imminent death/SBI; deadly force; duty to retreat (majority) vs. castle doctrine
Duress: imminent threat of death/SBI to defendant or close family member; no reasonable escape; limits
Insanity: M'Naghten disjunctive prongs; deific decree
Entrapment: federal subjective test (inducement + predisposition) vs. MPC objective test
Necessity: choice of evils; greater harm avoided; no legal alternative
essays.model: Hal's best defense is self-defense under the castle doctrine. Deadly force is justified against a reasonably perceived imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury; a crowbar-wielding intruder at 2 a.m. supplies it. The majority duty to retreat before using deadly force does not apply inside one's own home. Defense of property alone would not justify deadly force, but this is defense of persons in the home. Ian has duress: an imminent threat of death to a close family member (gun to his wife's head) with no reasonable escape. Duress requires the threat be imminent and of death or serious bodily injury to the defendant or a near relative — satisfied here. (Note the limits: duress never justifies intentional homicide, and it requires no reasonable avenue of escape.) Jonah is insane under M'Naghten. The test's prongs are disjunctive: either he did not know the nature and quality of his act, or he did not know it was wrong. Jonah knew he was killing (prong one fails) but his deific decree — God's command — meant he did not know it was morally wrong (prong two satisfied). One prong suffices. Ken has entrapment under the federal subjective test: the government induced the crime (two months of pressure plus five times the price) and Ken, with no record and evident reluctance, showed no predisposition. Under the MPC's objective test the focus would be on whether the police conduct created a substantial risk the offense would be committed by law-abiding persons — also likely satisfied, but the question asks for the federal test. The hiker has necessity (choice of evils): breaking in and burning furniture was reasonably necessary to avoid the far greater imminent harm of freezing to death, with no lawful alternative available. Conclusion: Hal (castle-doctrine self-defense), Ian (duress), Jonah (M'Naghten insanity), Ken (entrapment, subjective test), hiker (necessity) — each defense fits its facts, and each has boundaries the grader will check.

marking.point: Self-defense framework: reasonable fear of imminent death/SBI; deadly force rules
Castle doctrine: no duty to retreat in the home; deadly force not allowed for property alone
Duress elements: imminent death/SBI threat to defendant or close family member; no reasonable escape
Duress limits noted (never for intentional homicide)
M'Naghten: prongs disjunctive; deific decree satisfies 'did not know it was wrong' though nature of act was known
Entrapment subjective test: government inducement + lack of predisposition (clean record, reluctance, extraordinary pressure/price)
Necessity: greater harm avoided, imminent, no legal alternative
Correct defense matched to each of the five defendants
Organization and clarity

chapters.title: Fourth Amendment: Search & Seizure
key_rules: SESSION 15 — CRIMINAL PROCEDURE I: THE FOURTH AMENDMENT — search & seizure. Phase 1 · Criminal Procedure.

ONE LINE FIRST. We open a new book today: criminal procedure — the rules that govern how the police investigate. And pal, this one is personal: you've done stops, searches, and arrests for twenty years. Today you get the American rulebook for the same work.
THE BIG FRAME — ASK TWO QUESTIONS, IN ORDER. When police act and the defense moves to suppress, run this classify-first habit every time:
1. WAS THERE A SEARCH OR SEIZURE AT ALL? If the Fourth Amendment doesn't even apply, the police needed nothing. If it does —

2. DID THEY HAVE A WARRANT, OR DOES AN EXCEPTION FIT — WITH EVERY ELEMENT MET? The warrant is the default. Every warrantless police action must fit an exception completely. The MBE's favorite wrong answer is the exception with one element missing.
Memorize the shape: search/seizure? → warrant? → exception, element by element.

1. WAS IT A "SEARCH"? — TWO DOORS IN, EITHER ONE SUFFICES. FIRST, WHAT THE WORDS MEAN. A SEARCH is a government intrusion into something you have a right to keep private. A SEIZURE is the government taking or holding you (or your property). "Government" matters — the Fourth Amendment restrains the state, not private people: a store detective acting purely on his own isn't a state actor, but police directing him are.

DOOR ONE — KATZ V. UNITED STATES (1967): THE "REASONABLE EXPECTATION OF PRIVACY" TEST (REP). Two prongs: (a) you subjectively expected privacy, and (b) society recognizes that expectation as objectively reasonable. Katz was making calls from a glass phone booth; the government said "he exposed his voice." The Court said the expectation is what counts — what you seek to preserve as private may be constitutionally protected.

DOOR TWO — UNITED STATES V. JONES (2012): THE TRESPASS REVIVAL. If the police physically intrude on your "persons, houses, papers, or effects" to gather information, that's a search — even if no REP analysis is needed (GPS tracker stuck on a car). Either door makes it a search. The exam loves giving you a fact pattern where one door is shut and the other is open.
THINGS WITH NO REASONABLE EXPECTATION OF PRIVACY (NO SEARCH AT ALL):
What you knowingly expose to the public — your voice in a public place, your face on the street.
TRASH LEFT AT THE CURB for collection — California v. Greenwood (1988). Once it's at the curb, you've abandoned your privacy claim.
OPEN FIELDS beyond the home and its curtilage (the fenced yard right around the house) — Oliver v. United States (1984). "No Trespassing" signs don't create REP in a field.
THINGS WITH REP (THE EXAM'S MODERN EDGE):

127 DAYS OF CELL-SITE LOCATION RECORDS — Carpenter v. United States (2018). Long-term tracking reveals a "comprehensive chronicle" of your life; you have REP in the whole, even if each public sighting alone wouldn't.

DETAILS OF YOUR HOME'S INTERIOR LEARNED WITH SENSE-ENHANCING TECHNOLOGY NOT IN GENERAL PUBLIC USE — Kyllo v. United States (2001): aiming a thermal imager at a house from the street is a search. The home is the apex of REP; the government may not see through its walls.

2. WAS IT A "SEIZURE"?: OF A PERSON: a show of authority that would make a reasonable person feel not free to leave — patrol lights, a physical touch, blocking the path. An ARREST is the full seizure (needs probable cause); an INVESTIGATIVE STOP is the brief one (needs only reasonable suspicion — see §4). A consensual chat ("mind if I ask you a question?") with no show of authority is no seizure at all.
OF PROPERTY: a "meaningful interference" with your possessory interest — taking the suitcase, not merely looking at it.
3. THE WARRANT — THE DEFAULT, AND ITS THREE REQUIREMENTS. WARRANT (define it once, use it forever): a court order authorizing a search or arrest. For a search warrant, all three are mandatory:
1. Issued by a NEUTRAL AND DETACHED MAGISTRATE — a judge, not the officer's own supervisor;
2. Supported by PROBABLE CAUSE (see §4); and
3. PARTICULARLY DESCRIBING the place to be searched and the things to be seized.
The constitutional enemy is the "GENERAL WARRANT" — a blank permission to rummage wherever the officer pleases. Particularity is what killed it.
4. THE THREE BURDENS, IN ASCENDING ORDER. The exam loves asking you to rank or confuse these. Lowest to highest:
1. REASONABLE SUSPICION — specific, articulable facts (more than a hunch) suggesting criminal activity is afoot. Supports a TERRY STOP and nothing more.

2. PROBABLE CAUSE — a fair probability, judged on the totality of the circumstances, that contraband or evidence will be found (search) or that the person committed a crime (arrest). Supports arrests and warrants.
3. PREPONDERANCE OF THE EVIDENCE — more likely than not. This is the civil standard; it appears here only so you never confuse it with probable cause.
Bridge from your training: you know the difference between "intelligence suggests" and "we have enough to charge." Reasonable suspicion is the first; probable cause is the second.

5. STANDING — WHO MAY COMPLAIN?: STANDING means: only the person whose own Fourth Amendment rights were violated may ask the court to suppress evidence. Your rights travel with you, not with the contraband.
An OVERNIGHT GUEST has REP in the host's home and may challenge the search — Minnesota v. Olson (1990).
A MERE PASSENGER in someone else's car usually may not — no possessory interest in the car — Rakas v. Illinois (1978). (The driver/owner can.)
6. THE EXCEPTION CATALOG — WHEN THE POLICE DON'T NEED A WARRANT. Each exception is a checklist. One missing element kills it. This is the section the MBE mines hardest.

A) SEARCH INCIDENT TO A LAWFUL ARREST — CHIMEL V. CALIFORNIA. After a lawful arrest, police may search the arrestee's PERSON and the area within his IMMEDIATE CONTROL (arm's reach — where he might grab a weapon or destroy evidence). For CARS, Arizona v. Gant (2009) narrows it to two surviving doors: the search is lawful only if (1) the arrestee is UNSECURED AND MIGHT REACH the passenger compartment, OR (2) it's reasonable to believe EVIDENCE OF THE CRIME OF ARREST is inside. Arrestee handcuffed and locked in the cruiser on a traffic warrant? Both doors shut — no search. Memorize the two doors.

B) TERRY STOP AND FRISK — TWO STEPS, TWO JUSTIFICATIONS. The STOP (brief detention) needs REASONABLE SUSPICION OF CRIMINAL ACTIVITY — specific facts, like the casing pattern in the worked example below. The FRISK (pat-down) is a separate step needing reasonable suspicion the person is ARMED AND DANGEROUS. Scope: pat the OUTER CLOTHING first; reach inside only if you feel something that is plainly a weapon — PLAIN FEEL (Minnesota v. Dickerson). Stop without frisk-basis = frisk unlawful. This two-step split is the single most-tested Terry point.

C) THE AUTOMOBILE EXCEPTION — CARROLL V. UNITED STATES. PROBABLE CAUSE + A READILY MOBILE VEHICLE → police may search the entire car, including closed containers inside, without a warrant. (Rationale: cars move, and they're pervasively regulated, so privacy expectations are lower.) Note the "plus": probable cause alone isn't the exception — mobility is the second element.

D) EXIGENT CIRCUMSTANCES. No warrant needed for HOT PURSUIT of a fleeing suspect, IMMINENT DESTRUCTION OF EVIDENCE, or EMERGENCY AID to someone believed inside and in danger. Scope is limited to the emergency — once it ends, so does the exception.

E) CONSENT. A search is reasonable if the person VOLUNTARILY consents — no claim of lawful authority, no coercion of custody. A third party with COMMON AUTHORITY (a roommate, over shared spaces) can consent — BUT a physically present co-occupant who OBJECTS defeats the consent (Georgia v. Randolph, 2006). If the objector has been lawfully removed (arrested and taken away), the remaining occupant's consent stands (Fernandez v. California, 2014). The one-liner: PRESENCE DECIDES.

F) PLAIN VIEW. The officer is LAWFULLY PRESENT at the vantage point, the contraband is IMMEDIATELY APPARENT as such, and he has lawful access to it. Seeing it isn't a search; seizing it is the exception.

G) INVENTORY SEARCH. A car LAWFULLY IMPOUNDED, searched under STANDARDIZED, NON-PRETEXTUAL PROCEDURES → the inventory is reasonable. (No standardized procedures = no exception — an on-scene rummage isn't an inventory.)

7. THE EXCLUSIONARY RULE — AND WHERE IT DOES NOT REACH. The EXCLUSIONARY RULE: evidence obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment is EXCLUDED AT TRIAL. It is a DETERRENT aimed at police misconduct — not a personal right of the defendant. Because of that purpose:
Mapp v. Ohio (1961) made the rule binding on the STATES (it already bound federal courts).
It does NOT apply in GRAND-JURY PROCEEDINGS, CIVIL CASES, or PAROLE-REVOCATION HEARINGS — no jury deciding guilt, no deterrence payoff.
Illegally obtained statements MAY still be used to IMPEACH the defendant's own testimony — Harris v. New York (1971). (You can't use the violation as a sword to lie on the stand.)
FRUIT OF THE POISONOUS TREE: evidence derived from the violation is excluded too — unless one of the three antidotes saves it:
1. INDEPENDENT SOURCE — the police got it separately through a lawful path.
2. INEVITABLE DISCOVERY — they would have found it anyway through lawful means already in motion (Nix v. Williams: the second search team was already on its way).

3. ATTENUATION — the taint faded, judged by three factors: time passed, intervening circumstances, and the flagrancy of the misconduct (Utah v. Strieff: an outstanding arrest warrant discovered during an unlawful stop broke the chain).

Plus one more safety valve: GOOD FAITH — United States v. Leon (1984). Officers REASONABLY RELIED ON A WARRANT that later turns out defective (magistrate's error, not theirs) → the evidence stays. No deterrence purpose in punishing an honest mistake.

8. WORKED EXAMPLE — TERRY, THE MBE'S FAVORITE POLICE FACT PATTERN. Officer Cole, patrolling at 2 a.m., watches Kelechi pace past a closed jewelry store six times, peering into the window, conferring with a second man, then walking away and returning. Cole approaches, asks for ID; Kelechi mumbles and reaches into his jacket pocket. Cole pats down the jacket's outer surface, feels a hard object shaped like a pistol grip, reaches in, and seizes a gun. The DA wants the gun admitted.

STEP 1 — WAS THERE A SEARCH/SEIZURE AT ALL? Yes. The stop is a seizure of the person (Kelechi isn't free to leave); the pat-down is a search. So the Fourth Amendment applies, a warrant is normally required, and we need an exception with every element met.

STEP 2 — THE EXCEPTION'S ELEMENTS. Terry v. Ohio: (a) the STOP needs REASONABLE SUSPICION of criminal activity — specific, articulable facts, more than a hunch (the pacing/peering/conferring is the classic casing pattern); (b) the FRISK is a separate step needing reasonable suspicion the person is ARMED AND DANGEROUS (late-night burglary-in-progress context + the pocket reach); (c) scope: pat the OUTER CLOTHING first, reach inside only on the PLAIN FEEL of a weapon.

STEP 3 — APPLY. Specific facts → reasonable suspicion → lawful stop. Armed-and-dangerous suspicion → lawful frisk. Pistol-grip shape through the fabric → plain feel → reach-in lawful. THE GUN IS ADMITTED.

STEP 4 — THE CONTRASTS THAT LOCK IT (the MBE moves one fact at a time): stop him only because it's a "high-crime area," with no specific facts → no reasonable suspicion → unlawful stop → gun excluded. Pat him down with no armed-and-dangerous basis → frisk exceeds Terry → excluded. Reach straight into the pockets without feeling a weapon first → exceeds scope → excluded. And if Cole had probable cause to arrest first, the exception switches to SEARCH INCIDENT TO ARREST — the label changes because the justification did.
PRACTICE — This session's drill questions live in the Drills tab, with full explanations for every answer. Attempt each one there before reading its analysis, then send your letters in chat.

YOUR INVESTIGATOR TRANSFER (ONE QUESTION FOR YOU). In your SIB years, you ran operations with stops, vehicle searches, and premises entries. Under this American rulebook: WHICH OF YOUR SEARCHES WOULD HAVE NEEDED A WARRANT, AND WHICH EXCEPTIONS WOULD HAVE COVERED YOU? And where did you draw the line in practice between a stop, a frisk, and an arrest? The labels are new; the police work is old — I'd like to hear where your line was.
SPACED REVIEW — SESSION 14 (DEFENSES), IN 60 SECONDS. Try to say each one from memory before reading the line.

JUSTIFICATION VS. EXCUSE: justification = the act was right (self-defense, defense of others/property, necessity); excuse = the actor isn't blameworthy (duress, insanity, infancy, intoxication, entrapment). State the family first in the essay.

SELF-DEFENSE: reasonable belief + imminent unlawful threat + proportional response. DEADLY FORCE only on reasonable belief of imminent death or SBI. RETREAT: majority — no duty; minority — retreat if safely possible; CASTLE DOCTRINE — never retreat in your own home. IMPERFECT SELF-DEFENSE (honest but unreasonable belief) reduces murder → voluntary manslaughter.
DEFENSE OF PROPERTY: non-deadly force fine; DEADLY FORCE NEVER SOLELY FOR PROPERTY; mechanical devices — no doing indirectly what you couldn't do directly (Katko v. Briney).

NECESSITY: six elements (imminent greater harm, no legal alternative, causal link, didn't create the peril, proportionality, no legislative choice). NEVER A DEFENSE TO INTENTIONAL MURDER (Dudley & Stephens); economic necessity never.
DURESS: imminent death/SBI threat from a human, to self or close family, no escape, no fault. NEVER A DEFENSE TO INTENTIONAL HOMICIDE.
ENTRAPMENT: government inducement only. Subjective (majority/federal): inducement + NO PREDISPOSITION. MPC objective: police conduct — would it tempt a law-abiding person?

INSANITY LADDER: M'Naghten (cognitive: didn't know nature/quality OR didn't know it was wrong — EITHER/OR — banked: knowing the act is not enough; he must also know it's wrong) → irresistible impulse (knew wrong, couldn't control) → MPC §4.01 (lacked substantial capacity to appreciate criminality OR conform conduct — broadest) → Durham product test (dead).
INFANCY: under 7 conclusive incapacity; 7–14 rebuttable; 14+ adult.

THE PERMANENT MISS BANK, STILL STANDING: common law needs two guilty minds, the MPC needs one · cover minus contract, times quantity · Hadley foreseeability judged at formation · recklessness is subjective · M'Naghten is either/or.
Next: SESSION 16 — Criminal Procedure II: the Fifth Amendment (self-incrimination, *Miranda warnings) and the Sixth Amendment (right to counsel, lineups and identifications).*

The two-step, every time. (1) Does the forum's long-arm statute reach this defendant and this conduct? (2) If yes, does exercising jurisdiction satisfy Due Process under the 14th Amendment? If the long arm goes all the way to the constitutional limit, the whole fight is step two. In federal court (diversity), use the forum STATE's long arm plus the 14th Amendment.

Due process for personal jurisdiction has two halves: a proper BASIS over the defendant, and proper NOTICE — notice reasonably calculated to apprise the defendant, with an opportunity to be heard (Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank, 1950). Win the contacts fight and lose on notice, and you still lose.

Notice that fails in the mail is not the end: if mailed notice comes back unclaimed, the state must take additional reasonable steps to notify (Jones v. Flowers, 2006). 'We mailed it once' is not always enough.

The classic bases — no contacts analysis needed: (1) personal service on the defendant while physically present in the forum — 'tag' jurisdiction (Burnham v. Superior Court, 1990), even if the claim is unrelated; (2) domicile in the forum; (3) consent — a forum-selection clause or appointing an agent; (4) waiver.

Bank this first: PERSONAL jurisdiction is waivable; SUBJECT-MATTER jurisdiction is never waivable and can never be created by consent. The exam's favorite swap. A defendant who answers without raising PJ loses it (FRCP 12(h)(1)); SMJ can be raised at any time, even on appeal, even by the court itself.

Raising it: the plaintiff bears the burden of establishing PJ. The defendant challenges by pre-answer motion under FRCP 12(b)(2) or in the answer — but it must be in the FIRST response, or it is waived. 12(b)(2) is personal jurisdiction; 12(b)(1) is subject-matter. Don't cross the streams.

International Shoe (1945): where no classic basis exists, due process demands 'minimum contacts' with the forum — contacts such that the suit does not offend 'traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice.' Everything below hangs on this sentence.

SPECIFIC jurisdiction (the claim is connected to the forum) needs all three: (1) purposeful availment — the defendant purposefully directed activities at the forum, invoking its benefits and protections (Burger King v. Rudzewicz, 1985 — a 20-year franchise deliberately reaching into Florida); (2) the claim arises out of or RELATES TO those contacts — Ford Motor Co. v. Montana (2021): no strict causal link required, 'relates to' is enough; (3) exercising jurisdiction is REASONABLE — the Asahi fairness factors: burden on the defendant, the forum's interest, the plaintiff's interest in convenient relief, the interstate system's interest in efficiency, and the shared substantive interests of the states.

GENERAL jurisdiction (any claim, even unrelated) needs only one thing, and it is a high wall: the defendant must be 'at home' in the forum (Goodyear, 2011). A person is at home where domiciled. A corporation is at home in its state of incorporation and its principal place of business — the 'nerve center' where officers direct and control (Daimler v. Bauman, 2014; Hertz v. Friend, 2010). Merely doing business, or having big sales, in the forum is NOT enough.

The stream-of-commerce trap: merely placing a product into the stream of commerce, knowing it MIGHT end up in the forum, is not purposeful availment (World-Wide Volkswagen v. Woodson, 1980 — car sold in New York, crash in Oklahoma: no Oklahoma jurisdiction). Foreseeability that the product arrives is never enough; the defendant must have TARGETED the forum — advertising there, designing for its market, establishing distribution channels (the Asahi debate). If the facts show only 'it was foreseeable,' the answer is no jurisdiction.

Websites: the Zippo sliding scale. A passive site that just posts information does not create jurisdiction; an interactive site doing business with forum residents does. The middle — interactive but not clearly commercial — is judged by how much business is actually conducted with forum residents.

The 2023 twist — consent by registration: Mallory v. Norfolk Southern Railway Co., 600 U.S. 122 (2023). A state may require an out-of-state corporation to consent to GENERAL personal jurisdiction as the price of registering to do business there (Pennsylvania's scheme). This is CONSENT, not contacts — the International Shoe analysis is bypassed entirely. But note the limit: this works only where the state's statute actually deems registration to be consent — an ordinary registered agent, by itself, is not consent.

Service of process (FRCP 4): individuals — personal delivery, leaving copies at the dwelling with a person of suitable age and discretion, or delivery to an authorized agent; corporations — an officer or managing/general agent; waiver of service by mail (Rule 4(d)) — the defendant gets extra time to respond and the plaintiff saves costs. Serve within 90 days of filing (Rule 4(m)). State courts have their own service rules — on the MEE, name the method the facts used.

The long-arm categories to recognize: transacting business in the state; committing a tortious act within the state (or outside the state causing injury inside, usually with additional contacts); owning, using, or possessing real property in the state. If the long arm does not cover the conduct, stop — there is no jurisdiction even if due process would allow it.

Foreign-lawyer traps, collected: (a) Do not import Commonwealth 'service out of the jurisdiction' gateways — run the US two-step instead. (b) Corporate 'citizenship' for diversity (SMJ) says nothing about personal jurisdiction — the exam baits you into mixing them. (c) Tag jurisdiction still lives: being served while physically present is enough, claim related or not — much broader than most Commonwealth rules. (d) On an essay, structure it: long-arm first, then constitutional basis, then notice — one IRAC per issue, conclude each.

One-line exam checklist: long-arm? → classic basis? → if not, specific (purposeful + related + reasonable) or general (at home)? → notice adequate? → waived? Run it in that order and the PJ question solves itself.

Fifth & Sixth Amendments: Self-Incrimination, Miranda, Counsel & Identifications
key_rules: SESSION 16 — CRIMINAL PROCEDURE II: FIFTH & SIXTH AMENDMENTS — self-incrimination, Miranda, counsel & identifications. Phase 1 · Criminal Procedure.

ONE LINE FIRST. The drill loop is fully closed — every session through 15 is graded and banked. Criminal liability is done, the Fourth Amendment is done. Today we finish criminal procedure: the rules for INTERROGATIONS, CONFESSIONS, LAWYERS, AND LINEUPS. And pal, if the Fourth Amendment was your patrol work under the American rulebook, this session is your INTERVIEW ROOM under it — the Judges' Rules caution you grew up with in the Commonwealth has an American cousin named Miranda, and you already know the family business.

THE BIG FRAME — TWO AMENDMENTS, ONE QUESTION EACH: FIFTH AMENDMENT: was the defendant's own mouth used against him — and if so, was he fairly warned first? The privilege against self-incrimination + Miranda.
SIXTH AMENDMENT: did he have his lawyer when the machinery turned adversarial — and were the identifications clean? Right to counsel + lineups + confrontation.

Run every question through this order: FIFTH (DID HE TALK? WAS IT PROTECTED?) → MIRANDA (CUSTODY + INTERROGATION? WARNED? INVOKED?) → SIXTH (HAD PROCEEDINGS BEGUN? WAS COUNSEL THERE?). The exam mixes them in one fact pattern on purpose.

PART ONE — THE FIFTH AMENDMENT: THE PRIVILEGE AGAINST SELF-INCRIMINATION. THE TEXT: "No person ... shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself." Five words do the work: COMPELLED, CRIMINAL CASE, WITNESS AGAINST HIMSELF.
1. THE FOUR GATES — TESTIMONIAL, COMPELLED, SELF-INCRIMINATING, PERSONAL. The privilege opens only if ALL FOUR are true. The MBE tests each gate separately.
GATE 1 — TESTIMONIAL. The privilege protects testimony — facts drawn from the contents of your mind. It does NOT protect your body as physical evidence:

NOT TESTIMONIAL (NO PRIVILEGE): blood draws (Schmerber v. California, 1966), fingerprints, voice exemplars ("say 'give me the money' into this recorder"), handwriting samples, standing in a lineup, DNA swabs. The government can compel these.
TESTIMONIAL (PRIVILEGE APPLIES): answering questions about what you did, knew, or saw.
GATE 2 — COMPELLED. The pressure must come from the GOVERNMENT. Your wife urging you to confess is not compulsion; a detective threatening you is.
GATE 3 — SELF-INCRIMINATING. The answer must create a real, reasonable danger of criminal liability — not a fanciful one. (Fear of embarrassment or civil liability isn't enough.)
GATE 4 — PERSONAL. The privilege belongs to NATURAL PERSONS ONLY:

CORPORATIONS, PARTNERSHIPS, AND UNIONS HAVE NO FIFTH AMENDMENT PRIVILEGE — the collective-entity doctrine (Braswell v. United States, 1988). The custodian of corporate records must produce them even if they incriminate him personally.
You can't claim it for someone else. Your lawyer can't invoke it on your behalf.

Bridge from your world: in your years taking statements, the suspect's words about what happened were the prize — that is exactly what this privilege walls off. His blood sample after a crash? No wall. The distinction is mind vs. body.

2. WHERE IT APPLIES — AND HOW YOU CLAIM IT: The privilege applies IN ANY PROCEEDING where the answer could expose you to criminal liability — not just a criminal trial: grand-jury hearings, civil depositions, legislative inquiries. (The "criminal case" is where the exposure lies, not where you sit.)
YOU MUST GENERALLY CLAIM IT — it is not self-executing. Sit silent without invoking and a later court may say you never asserted it.

ONCE PROPERLY CLAIMED: the government may not punish the silence — and at trial, the prosecutor MAY NOT COMMENT ON THE DEFENDANT'S DECISION NOT TO TESTIFY, and the judge may not instruct the jury to treat it as evidence of guilt (Griffin v. California, 1965). Silence is not a confession.

3. IMMUNITY — HOW THE GOVERNMENT GETS THE TESTIMONY ANYWAY. Kastigar v. United States (1972): the government may COMPEL TESTIMONY BY GRANTING IMMUNITY — but the immunity must be USE-AND-DERIVATIVE-USE IMMUNITY: the government may not use the compelled testimony OR ANYTHING DERIVED FROM IT against the witness. That is enough; TRANSACTIONAL IMMUNITY (a promise never to prosecute for the whole transaction) is NOT required. After valid immunity is granted, refusal to testify = contempt of court.

REQUIRED-RECORDS DOCTRINE: records you are required by law to keep under a valid regulatory scheme (tax records, licensing records) are NOT privileged — you assumed the record-keeping duty when you entered the regulated activity.

THE GARRITY RULE (your police world, American version): if a public employee is ORDERED TO ANSWER QUESTIONS ON PAIN OF LOSING HIS JOB, those compelled answers CANNOT BE USED AGAINST HIM IN A CRIMINAL PROSECUTION (Garrity v. New Jersey, 1967). He can be fired for refusing to answer — but the state can't have both the answers and the prosecution.

PART TWO — MIRANDA: THE AMERICAN CAUTION. Miranda v. Arizona (1966): the Supreme Court's answer to custodial interrogation — because the station-house interview room is inherently coercive, warnings are required before the privilege can be meaningfully waived.

YOUR BRIDGE: you know the JUDGES' RULES CAUTION — "You are not obliged to say anything unless you wish to do so, but whatever you say will be taken down in writing and may be given in evidence." Miranda is the American cousin: same family (protect the suspect from his own pressured mouth), stricter household rules.
1. THE TRIGGER — CUSTODY + INTERROGATION (BOTH REQUIRED). No custody, no Miranda. No interrogation, no Miranda. The MBE's favorite wrong answer supplies only one.

CUSTODY — the OBJECTIVE test: would a reasonable person in the suspect's position feel FREE TO TERMINATE THE ENCOUNTER AND LEAVE? (Not what the officer intended, not what the suspect secretly felt — the reasonable person.)
STATION-HOUSE INTERROGATION = custody.
A ROUTINE TRAFFIC STOP = NOT CUSTODY (Berkemer v. McCarty, 1984) — brief, public, one or two officers. (So the driver's roadside admissions come in without warnings.)
Formal arrest always = custody, but custody doesn't require formal arrest — the question is restraint on freedom of movement to the degree of arrest.
INTERROGATION — express questioning OR ITS FUNCTIONAL EQUIVALENT: words or conduct the police SHOULD KNOW ARE REASONABLY LIKELY TO ELICIT AN INCRIMINATING RESPONSE (Rhode Island v. Innis, 1980).

A detective telling the suspect "think of the poor victim's family, they deserve closure" while driving him to the station = the functional equivalent of interrogation (this is close to the actual Innis facts — the "Christian burial speech").
A suspect who VOLUNTEERS a confession unprompted ("I did it, I can't live with it") = NOT interrogation — no warnings were needed, and it comes in.
2. THE FOUR WARNINGS: 1. You have the right to remain silent;
2. Anything you say CAN AND WILL BE USED AGAINST YOU in court;
3. You have the right to consult an attorney BEFORE AND DURING questioning;
4. If you cannot afford one, an attorney will be APPOINTED for you.

3. WAIVER — KNOWING, INTELLIGENT, AND VOLUNTARY. The government bears the burden of proving a valid waiver, judged on the TOTALITY OF THE CIRCUMSTANCES. A signed written waiver is strong evidence but not conclusive — coercion (length, deprivation, threats, trickery that overbears the will) kills it.
4. INVOKING THE RIGHTS — TWO RIGHTS, TWO DIFFERENT RULES. This is the most-tested Miranda ground. Memorize the split.

RIGHT TO SILENCE — INVOKED → POLICE MUST "SCRUPULOUSLY HONOR" IT (Michigan v. Mosley, 1975). They MAY re-approach later if: significant time has passed, FRESH WARNINGS are given, a DIFFERENT OFFICER questions, and it's about a DIFFERENT CRIME. Cut one corner and the re-questioning is tainted.

RIGHT TO COUNSEL — INVOKED → THE EDWARDS SHIELD (Edwards v. Arizona, 1981): ALL police-initiated interrogation must STOP until counsel is present OR THE SUSPECT HIMSELF REINITIATES contact. Stronger than the silence rule — no "try again tomorrow with a different detective."

THE SHIELD'S LIMIT — Maryland v. Shatzer (2010): a 14-DAY BREAK IN CUSTODY (suspect released back to the general prison population) ends Edwards protection; police may then re-approach with fresh warnings.
INVOCATION MUST BE UNEQUIVOCAL (Davis v. Washington, 1994):
"Maybe I should talk to a lawyer" / "I think I want a lawyer" = AMBIGUOUS → questioning may continue.
"I want a lawyer" / "I'm not saying anything until I see my lawyer" = CLEAR → questioning must stop.
The one-liner: "MAYBE" IS NOT AN INVOCATION; "I WANT" IS.

5. THE TWO EXCEPTIONS: PUBLIC SAFETY (New York v. Quarles, 1984): a question REASONABLY PROMPTED BY CONCERN FOR PUBLIC SAFETY needs no warnings first — "Where's the gun?" asked of a suspect just arrested in a supermarket, with the gun missing. The statement comes in.
ROUTINE BOOKING (Pennsylvania v. Muniz, 1990): name, date of birth, address — asked at booking, these are NOT INTERROGATION, so no warnings are needed for them.

6. THE REMEDIES — NARROWER THAN THE FOURTH AMENDMENT. This is where students bleed points by importing Fourth Amendment instincts. Miranda is PROPHYLACTIC — a violation is not itself a constitutional violation. So:
The UNWARNED STATEMENT IS EXCLUDED from the prosecution's case-in-chief.

But PHYSICAL FRUITS OF THE UNWARNED STATEMENT ARE ADMISSIBLE (United States v. Patane, 2004): the suspect, unwarned but speaking voluntarily, says "the gun is in my bedroom" — the GUN COMES IN. Contrast with the Fourth Amendment, where the gun would be fruit of the poisonous tree. This contrast is an MBE favorite.
An unwarned but VOLUNTARY statement may still be used to IMPEACH THE DEFENDANT'S OWN TRIAL TESTIMONY (Harris v. New York; Oregon v. Hass): he can't take the stand and lie, shielded by Miranda.

TWO-STEP SEQUENCING (Oregon v. Elstad, 1985): unwarned voluntary statement, then PROPER WARNINGS + VALID WAIVER, then the suspect repeats the statement → the SECOND STATEMENT IS ADMISSIBLE. The warnings cured it.

BUT THE DELIBERATE TWO-STEP (Missouri v. Seibert, 2004): police INTENTIONALLY interrogate first, warn, then re-ask to launder the confession → the SECOND STATEMENT IS SUPPRESSED. (Justice Kennedy's controlling concurrence: if police take curative measures — a real break, a clear statement that the first answers can't be used — the second may survive. Deliberate end-run with no cure = out.)

7. ONE LINE ON THE SIXTH AMENDMENT'S INTERROGATION RULE. Once adversarial proceedings have BEGUN (indictment and beyond), Massiah v. United States (1964) adds a Sixth Amendment layer: the government may NOT DELIBERATELY ELICIT statements from the charged defendant WITHOUT HIS COUNSEL PRESENT — even with Miranda warnings. Miranda is pre-indictment; Massiah is post-indictment. Same interview room, different amendment guarding the door.

PART THREE — THE SIXTH AMENDMENT: COUNSEL, IDENTIFICATIONS, AND THE TRIAL RIGHTS. THE CATALOG (define once): the Sixth Amendment guarantees a SPEEDY AND PUBLIC TRIAL, trial by an IMPARTIAL JURY, NOTICE of the charges, CONFRONTATION of adverse witnesses, COMPULSORY PROCESS for favorable witnesses, and the ASSISTANCE OF COUNSEL. The exam tests counsel and identifications hardest; the rest get one line each at the end.

1. WHEN THE RIGHT TO COUNSEL ATTACHES — THE STARTING LINE. The right attaches AT OR AFTER THE INITIATION OF ADVERSARIAL JUDICIAL PROCEEDINGS — indictment, information, preliminary hearing, or formal arraignment (Rothgery v. Gillespie County, 2008: even the initial appearance before a magistrate counts).
BEFORE THAT LINE: no Sixth Amendment right to counsel — a PRE-INDICTMENT LINEUP may proceed without defense counsel present (Kirby v. Illinois, 1972).
AFTER THAT LINE: counsel is required at every CRITICAL STAGE — a stage where the defendant's rights could be lost or the trial's fairness affected.
2. THE CRITICAL STAGES (MEMORIZE THE LIST): POST-INDICTMENT LINEUP (United States v. Wade, 1967) — counsel must be present. (Pre-indictment lineup: no right — Kirby.)
PRELIMINARY HEARING (Coleman v. Alabama).
ARRAIGNMENT where a plea is entered.
PLEA BARGAINING — counsel's bad advice here can undo the plea (Lafler v. Lee, 2012).
SENTENCING and the FIRST APPEAL AS OF RIGHT (Douglas v. California).
3. WHO GETS COUNSEL — THE GIDEON LINE: Gideon v. Wainwright (1963): the state must appoint counsel for indigent defendants in FELONY cases.
Argersinger v. Hamlin (1972): extended to any MISDEMEANOR THAT ACTUALLY RESULTS IN IMPRISONMENT.
Scott v. Illinois (1979): the line is ACTUAL IMPRISONMENT — charged with a jailable offense but only fined? No right to appointed counsel.
Alabama v. Shelton (2002): a SUSPENDED sentence still triggers the right (the imprisonment hangs over you).
4. INEFFECTIVE ASSISTANCE — THE STRICKLAND TWO-PRONG TEST. Strickland v. Washington (1984). BOTH prongs required:
1. DEFICIENT PERFORMANCE — the lawyer's work fell below an objective standard of reasonableness (with a strong presumption the lawyer was competent).
2. PREJUDICE — a reasonable probability the outcome would have differed but for the errors.
The trap: a bad outcome plus bad lawyering is NOT enough — you need the CAUSAL LINK. Lose either prong and the claim fails.

5. SELF-REPRESENTATION AND CONFLICTS: Faretta v. California (1975): a competent defendant may KNOWINGLY AND INTELLIGENTLY WAIVE COUNSEL AND REPRESENT HIMSELF — the court can't force a lawyer on him (but may appoint standby counsel over his objection). And he can't later complain his own representation was ineffective.

Conflicts: joint representation of co-defendants requires each defendant's informed consent — Cuyler v. Sullivan: to overturn for a conflict, show the lawyer actively represented conflicting interests and it adversely affected performance.
6. IDENTIFICATIONS — THE TWO DOCTRINES (THE MOST-TESTED LINEUP GROUND). Keep them apart:

SIXTH AMENDMENT RIGHT TO COUNSEL — applies at POST-INDICTMENT LINEUPS AND SHOWUPS (United States v. Wade, 1967). NEVER at photo arrays (United States v. Ash, 1973). NEVER PRE-INDICTMENT (Kirby v. Illinois, 1972). Remedy for violation: per se exclusion, subject to an independent-source hearing.

DUE-PROCESS FAIRNESS — applies ANY TIME (Manson v. Thwaites, Neil v. Biggers). Two steps: (1) was the procedure UNNECESSARILY SUGGESTIVE? (2) if so, was the identification nevertheless RELIABLE? Run the five Biggers reliability factors — the witness's opportunity to view, degree of attention, accuracy of the prior description, level of certainty, and the time between the crime and the identification. SUGGESTIVENESS ALONE NEVER EXCLUDES — strong reliability saves the identification.

7. CONFRONTATION AND THE TRIAL RIGHTS: Crawford v. Washington (2004): TESTIMONIAL statements (made for use at trial — affidavits, station-house interrogations) require the witness to be UNAVAILABLE PLUS A PRIOR OPPORTUNITY TO CROSS-EXAMINE. (Non-testimonial excited utterances go through the old reliability test.)
Bruton rule: in a JOINT TRIAL, a non-testifying co-defendant's confession implicating you can't be cured with a limiting instruction — sever or exclude.
Speedy trial: Barker v. Wingo's four factors — length of delay, reason, whether the defendant asserted the right, prejudice.

Jury: the right attaches to offenses punishable by MORE THAN SIX MONTHS (Baldwin); guilty verdicts must be UNANIMOUS (Ramos v. Louisiana); any fact increasing the maximum sentence must be found by the jury beyond a reasonable doubt (Blakely v. Washington).
PRACTICE — This session's drill questions live in the Drills tab, with full explanations for every answer. Attempt each one there before reading its analysis, then send your letters in chat.

SPACED REVIEW — SESSION 15 (FOURTH AMENDMENT) IN 60 SECONDS: SEARCH? Katz REP or Jones trespass — either door. No REP in trash at the curb (Greenwood) or open fields (Oliver). REP in 127 days of CSLI (Carpenter) and thermal imaging of the home (Kyllo).
SEIZURE? Show of authority; not free to leave.
Warrant needs a NEUTRAL MAGISTRATE, PROBABLE CAUSE, and PARTICULARITY. Standing: only the person whose own rights were violated may suppress.

Exceptions: search incident to arrest — Chimel's arm's reach; Gant's two doors for cars (unsecured arrestee who might reach in, or evidence of the crime of arrest inside). Terry: stop needs REASONABLE SUSPICION OF CRIME; frisk needs its OWN ARMED-AND-DANGEROUS BASIS; outer clothing first; plain feel (Dickerson). Automobile: Carroll — PC + readily mobile car. Exigent circumstances: hot pursuit, imminent destruction, emergency aid. Consent: voluntary; present objector defeats (Randolph), absent objector doesn't (Fernandez). Plain view: lawful vantage + immediately apparent. Inventory: impounded + standardized procedures.

Exclusionary rule = deterrent, not a personal right. Not in grand-jury, civil, or parole-revocation proceedings. Impeachment use allowed (Harris v. New York). Fruit of the poisonous tree — three antidotes: independent source, inevitable discovery (Nix v. Williams), attenuation (Strieff: time, intervening circumstances, flagrancy). Good faith: Leon — reasonable reliance on a defective warrant.

PERMANENT MISS BANK (NOW 7): common law needs two guilty minds, the MPC needs one · cover minus contract, times quantity · Hadley foreseeability judged at formation · recklessness is subjective · M'Naghten is either/or · Wardlow flight + high-crime area = reasonable suspicion for a stop, never automatically a frisk · inevitable discovery — lawful means already in motion that would have found the evidence.
Tomorrow: Session 17 — Criminal Law's last mile: the specific crimes. Theft/larceny, robbery, burglary, arson, kidnapping, sex offenses. The four-element frame pays off there.

chapters.title: Specific Crimes: Theft, Robbery, Burglary, Arson, Kidnapping, Sex Offenses
key_rules: SESSION 17 — CRIMINAL LAW V: SPECIFIC CRIMES — theft, robbery, burglary, arson, kidnapping, sex offenses. Phase 1 · Criminal Law arc closes.

ONE LINE FIRST. The drill loop is fully closed — every session through 16 is graded and banked, and your Session 16 sweep (4/4) closed the Criminal Procedure arc with the inevitable-discovery miss repaired. Today is the LAST MILE OF CRIMINAL LAW: the specific crimes. Homicide was Session 12; everything that isn't homicide lives here — the theft family, robbery, burglary, arson, kidnapping, and the sex offenses. And pal, you investigated every one of these in Nigeria. The shapes are old friends; only the American element-recipes are new. TOMORROW, CONSTITUTIONAL LAW BEGINS — a whole new subject, and a fresh subject means a fresh summit.

THE BIG FRAME — NAME THE CRIME BY THE ELEMENTS, NOT BY THE HEADLINE. Sessions 11–14 built the machine: ACTUS REUS → MENS REA → CONCURRENCE → CAUSATION. The specific crimes are that machine running with extra attachments — each crime is a RECIPE, and missing one ingredient means the named crime FAILS (a lesser one may still stand). The exam's favorite trick is a fact pattern that smells like robbery but is missing the force, or smells like burglary but is missing the breaking.
Two habits, carried forward:
1. RUN THE FOUR-ELEMENT FRAME FIRST, then the crime's own recipe. The recipe never replaces the frame.
2. COMMON LAW FIRST, THEN THE MODERN/MPC VARIATION. State labels differ wildly (New York calls most of this "larceny" by statute) — the examiners grade ELEMENTS, not labels.

Bridge from your world: Nigeria's Criminal Code criminalizes all of these — stealing, robbery, burglary and housebreaking, arson, kidnapping, sexual offences. You know what these crimes are. What the exam wants is the COMMON-LAW ELEMENT CHECKLIST and where the American rulebook's version diverges from the Nigerian one.

PART ONE — THE THEFT FAMILY (THE EXAM'S FAVORITE PLAYGROUND). Three crimes, one umbrella idea — STEALING — distinguished by HOW THE THIEF GOT CONTROL OF THE PROPERTY. This is the single most-tested distinction in criminal law on the MBE. The entire trick is one question: WHAT DID THE OWNER INTEND TO PART WITH, AND WHEN DID THE THIEF'S BAD INTENT FORM?
1. LARCENY (COMMON LAW) — THE TRESPASSORY TAKING. THE RECIPE — FOUR INGREDIENTS:

1. TRESPASSORY TAKING AND CARRYING AWAY — a taking WITHOUT THE OWNER'S CONSENT ("trespassory" is the criminal-law cousin of the tort word you learned in Session 3), PLUS ASPORTATION, the carrying away. Asportation needs only the SLIGHTEST MOVEMENT — the classic: shifting a purse six inches on a counter is enough. Lifting it counts; the thief need not get away.

2. OF PERSONAL PROPERTY OF ANOTHER — tangible personal property (money, goods, the family jewels). At common law, not real estate, not services (modern statutes reach both — another label-vs.-element trap).

3. WITH SPECIFIC INTENT TO PERMANENTLY DEPRIVE — and here is the timing rule that runs the whole theft family: THE INTENT MUST EXIST AT THE TIME OF THE TAKING (concurrence, Session 11). Steal a car intending to return it after the weekend = not larceny at common law (modern statutes add JOYRIDING as the lesser crime for exactly this gap).
4. THE TAKING MUST BE TRESPASSORY — consent obtained by trick is NOT REAL CONSENT (see larceny by trick below).

THE CONTINUING-TRESPASS DOCTRINE — the exam's favorite concurrence rescue: a trespassory taking is treated as CONTINUING for as long as the thief keeps the property. So a joyrider who takes the car for the weekend and LATER DECIDES TO KEEP IT OR STRIP IT commits larceny — the original trespass was still running when the felonious intent formed, so concurrence is satisfied. The trick the exam loves: "He took it meaning to return it, then changed his mind — larceny?" YES — BY CONTINUING TRESPASS.

LARCENY BY TRICK: the owner is INDUCED BY FRAUD TO HAND OVER POSSESSION ONLY — "let me examine your watch," then the thief sprints. This is still LARCENY: the trick voids the consent, the taking stays trespassory, and TITLE NEVER PASSED. The watch-owner intended the thief to hold it, not keep it.
2. EMBEZZLEMENT — THE INSIDE JOB. THE RECIPE: FRAUDULENT CONVERSION of property ALREADY LAWFULLY IN THE DEFENDANT'S POSSESSION.

The timing twist — THE EXACT OPPOSITE OF LARCENY'S RULE: in embezzlement, the fraudulent intent MAY FORM AFTER POSSESSION BEGAN. The bank teller lawfully receives the cash drawer on Monday and decides on Friday to pocket $2,000 — embezzlement, even though the taking (the possession) was innocent. Concurrence is satisfied differently here because the crime is the conversion, not the acquisition.
Two fine points the exam probes:

CUSTODY, NOT MERE ACCESS. The defendant must have been ENTRUSTED WITH POSSESSION — the clerk with the register, the valet with the car keys. The janitor who merely has a key to the room has access, not custody — his taking is larceny, not embezzlement. CUSTODY VS. ACCESS is a whole MBE question by itself.
INTENT TO REPAY IS NO DEFENSE. "I was going to put it back" does not save the embezzler.
3. FALSE PRETENSES — WHEN TITLE PASSES BY FRAUD. THE RECIPE: OBTAINING TITLE (not just possession) by a MISREPRESENTATION OF PAST OR PRESENT FACT, with intent to defraud.

The fraud must be about PAST OR PRESENT FACT — "this watch is solid gold" (it is brass). A lie about the FUTURE — "I'll pay you back Tuesday" — is NOT false pretenses at common law. A lie about tomorrow is just a lie about tomorrow.

THE TITLE TEST — this is what separates it from larceny by trick: did the owner intend the thief to KEEP it (title passes → FALSE PRETENSES) or only HOLD it (possession only → LARCENY BY TRICK)? The con artist who sells you brass as gold for $5,000 cash: you intended him to keep the money → FALSE PRETENSES. The "buyer" who asks to examine your watch and runs: you intended him to hand it back → LARCENY BY TRICK.
THE MBE THEFT TRIANGLE — ONE QUESTION DECIDES IT. When the stem smells like stealing, ask "DID TITLE PASS?":
NO — TRICK GOT ONLY POSSESSION → LARCENY BY TRICK (title never passed; the trick voids consent).
YES — FRAUD GOT TITLE → FALSE PRETENSES (misrepresentation of past/present fact).
LAWFUL POSSESSION FIRST, FRAUDULENT CONVERSION LATER → EMBEZZLEMENT (intent may form after possession began).

THE MPC CONSOLIDATION. The Model Penal Code collapses the whole family into one crime — THEFT (MPC §§223.2–223.6) — with MODES: theft by unlawful taking, theft by deception, theft by extortion, receiving stolen property. So when the stem says "UNDER THE MODEL PENAL CODE": call it THEFT, then name the mode. The elements don't change — only the label does.
4. ROBBERY — LARCENY PLUS FORCE. THE RECIPE: LARCENY + FORCE OR THREAT OF IMMINENT FORCE AGAINST A PERSON, used TO OBTAIN OR RETAIN the property.
The taking must be FROM THE PERSON OR IN THEIR PRESENCE — the wallet from the pocket, the cash from the register while the clerk watches.

The force must be MORE THAN WHAT THE TAKING REQUIRES. The unnoticed pickpocket = LARCENY (no force). The snatch where the victim notices, grabs back, and the thief yanks it away = ROBBERY. FORCE USED TO RETAIN THE PROPERTY IN IMMEDIATE FLIGHT COUNTS — the exam loves the purse-snatch that turns into a tug-of-war.
THREAT OF IMMINENT FORCE suffices — the gun, the raised fist, "your money or your life." Imminent is the key word (see extortion below).
AGGRAVATED ROBBERY — most jurisdictions add aggravators: deadly weapon, infliction of serious bodily injury, an accomplice present. The grading varies; the base recipe doesn't.

5. EXTORTION (BLACKMAIL) — THE FUTURE-THREAT COUSIN. THE RECIPE: obtaining property by THREAT OF FUTURE HARM — "pay me $10,000 by Friday or your affair goes public," "nice shop, shame if it burned down."

THE TIMELINE TEST is the whole distinction: IMMINENT THREAT = ROBBERY; FUTURE THREAT = EXTORTION. The fist in your face is robbery; the letter promising ruin next week is extortion. (Bridge: Nigeria's Criminal Code has the same shape — the American exam just insists on the timeline.)
PART TWO — BURGLARY & ARSON:
6. BURGLARY (COMMON LAW) — SIX ELEMENTS, AND THE BREAKING IS THE TRIPWIRE. THE RECIPE — ALL SIX:

1. BREAKING — FORCE TO GAIN ENTRY, HOWEVER SLIGHT. Pushing open a CLOSED door counts. Lifting a closed window counts. WALKING THROUGH A DOOR LEFT STANDING OPEN IS NOT A BREAKING — this is the classic MBE trap: night + dwelling + felonious intent + open door = NO COMMON-LAW BURGLARY.
2. ENTERING — any part of the body. A hand through the window is an entry.
3. THE DWELLING — a residence (not a warehouse at common law).
4. OF ANOTHER — you cannot burglarize your own home.
5. AT NIGHTTIME — a common-law element (modern statutes drop it).

6. WITH INTENT TO COMMIT A FELONY OR THEFT THEREIN — and here is the gravamen: THE INTENT AT THE TIME OF ENTRY IS THE CRIME. The burglar need not complete the target crime inside — enter at night intending to steal, get scared, leave empty-handed: STILL BURGLARY. The intent was there when the threshold was crossed.

MODERN/MPC VARIATION (MPC §221.1): any BUILDING OR OCCUPIED STRUCTURE (not just dwellings), ANY HOUR, and REMAINING inside with criminal intent counts as entry. Grading turns on dwelling/night/weapon. On the MBE, apply the common-law six unless the stem signals a statute.
7. ARSON (COMMON LAW) — MALICE, BURNING, DWELLING OF ANOTHER. THE RECIPE: MALICIOUS + BURNING + OF THE DWELLING + OF ANOTHER.

MALICE = INTENT OR RECKLESS DISREGARD — mere negligence is not enough. The careless smoker who drops a cigarette is not an arsonist at common law (modern reckless-burning statutes may still catch him).
BURNING = ACTUAL CHARRING OF WOOD. Scorching or blackening without charring = NOT ARSON — the charring rule. (Yes, the exam really does test whether the wood charred.)
OF ANOTHER'S DWELLING — at common law. Modern statutes reach YOUR OWN PROPERTY (the insurance-fraud arson — burning your own failing business for the payout) and any structure, with degrees.
ATTEMPT — the lit match that fizzles out in the rain = ATTEMPTED ARSON.
PART THREE — KIDNAPPING, FALSE IMPRISONMENT, SEX OFFENSES:

8. KIDNAPPING — CONFINEMENT + MOVEMENT + PURPOSE. THE RECIPE: (1) UNLAWFUL CONFINEMENT OR RESTRAINT + (2) ASPORTATION (MOVEMENT) OR CONCEALMENT + (3) FOR A NEFARIOUS PURPOSE — ransom, facilitating a felony, terrorizing the victim, interfering with a governmental or political function.

THE MOVEMENT DEBATE — the one the exam tests: at COMMON LAW, ANY MOVEMENT SUFFICES (dragging the victim across the room). MODERN STATUTES AND THE MPC (§212.1) REQUIRE SUBSTANTIAL MOVEMENT — "from his place of residence, business, or a substantial distance." Read the stem for which rulebook it's using.
AGGRAVATED KIDNAPPING — ransom, child victim, infliction of serious bodily injury (grading varies).

FALSE IMPRISONMENT — the lesser included offense: unlawful confinement WITHOUT the movement or the nefarious purpose. (Bridge: the tort you learned in Session 2 — same name, and the criminal version is the same confinement idea wearing handcuffs.)
9. RAPE AND THE SEX OFFENSES. COMMON-LAW RECIPE: UNLAWFUL SEXUAL INTERCOURSE WITH A WOMAN, BY FORCE OR THREAT OF FORCE, WITHOUT CONSENT.
The modern law keeps the skeleton and changes the flesh:
GENDER-NEUTRAL STATUTES — most states now say "person," not "woman."

THE MARITAL EXEMPTION IS ABOLISHED IN MOST STATES — the common-law rule that a husband could not rape his wife is THE CLASSIC TRAP ANSWER. Under the MPC (§213.1) and modern statutes, marriage is no defense. If the stem's wrong answer says "not guilty — she was his wife," it is testing whether you know the exemption is dead.
THE FORCE STANDARD — jurisdictions split between EXTRINSIC FORCE (force beyond the act itself) and lesser standards; know the split exists.

FRAUD IN THE FACTUM VS. FRAUD IN THE INDUCEMENT — impersonating the victim's spouse in the dark = FRAUD IN THE FACTUM (she consented to a different act) → VITIATES CONSENT. Lying about wealth, marriage prospects, or fame to obtain consent = FRAUD IN THE INDUCEMENT (she consented to the act, misled about the motive) → DOES NOT VITIATE CONSENT. The exam loves this pair.

STATUTORY RAPE = STRICT LIABILITY AS TO AGE. Session 11's rule returns in full armor: MISTAKE OF AGE, EVEN A REASONABLE ONE, IS NO DEFENSE. The "she showed me a convincing fake ID" answer is always wrong.

MISTAKE AS TO CONSENT — an HONEST AND REASONABLE mistake that the victim consented can negate the mens rea in some jurisdictions (DPP v. Morgan — the minority rule; know it exists). The MPC requires RECKLESSNESS AS TO NON-CONSENT (§213.1). Where the stem gives no jurisdiction, argue both.

GRADING — modern statutes grade these (first/second/third degree; "sexual assault" terminology in many states). The exam tests ELEMENTS; state the common-law recipe, note the statutory variation, move on.
THE MEE ANGLE (ESSAY WRITING). When a specific-crimes question appears as an essay — and the theft triangle is an MEE perennial:
1. LIST EVERY ELEMENT of the charged crime, numbered. The grader's point sheet is an element checklist; an element you never name is a point you never earn.
2. STATE THE COMMON-LAW RULE, THEN THE MODERN/MPC VARIATION in one line each — that two-line move is worth points on its own.
3. RUN THE TRIANGLE EXPLICITLY when the facts smell like stealing: "Title did not pass — the victim parted with possession only — so this is larceny by trick, not false pretenses."

4. NAME THE LESSER INCLUDED OFFENSE when the charged crime fails an element — open-door entry defeats burglary, but trespass and attempted larceny survive; the unnoticed pickpocket defeats robbery, but larceny stands.

INVESTIGATOR TRANSFER QUESTION. From your own docket, pal: a fraud suspect takes a victim's phone saying "let me make a quick call," then sprints down the street with it. LARCENY BY TRICK OR FALSE PRETENSES — AND WHICH FACT DECIDES IT? (Answer: larceny by trick — the victim parted with POSSESSION ONLY, expecting the phone back; title never passed. Move one fact — the victim sold him the phone for cash that turned out to be counterfeit — and it becomes false pretenses.)
PRACTICE — This session's drill questions live in the Drills tab, with full explanations for every answer. Attempt each one there before reading its analysis, then send your letters in chat.

⏪ SPACED REVIEW — SESSION 16 IN 60 SECONDS. THE TRIGGER: Miranda needs CUSTODY + INTERROGATION, both. Station house = custody; traffic stop = no (Berkemer). Express questioning or its functional equivalent = interrogation (Innis). INVOCATION SPLIT: silence → "scrupulously honored" (Mosley); counsel → the Edwards shield (no police-initiated interrogation until counsel arrives or the suspect reinitiates; a 14-day break ends it — Shatzer). "MAYBE I SHOULD GET A LAWYER" ≠ INVOCATION (Davis — it must be unequivocal). REMEDIES ARE NARROWER THAN THE FOURTH: the unwarned statement is out, but its PHYSICAL FRUITS COME IN (Patane — the favorite cross-amendment swap; under the Fourth the laptop would be poisoned fruit, under the Fifth it is clean). IDENTIFICATIONS RUN TWO DOCTRINES: Sixth Amendment counsel at POST-INDICTMENT LINEUPS ONLY (Wade; no photo arrays — Ash; no pre-indictment — Kirby), plus the due-process two-step — SUGGESTIVENESS, THEN BIGGERS RELIABILITY (suggestiveness alone never excludes).

THE PERMANENT MISS BANK — SEVEN ENTRIES, STILL STANDING: (1) common law needs two guilty minds, the MPC needs one · (2) cover minus contract, times quantity · (3) Hadley foreseeability judged AT FORMATION · (4) recklessness is SUBJECTIVE · (5) M'Naghten is either/or · (6) WARDLOW — flight plus high-crime area gives reasonable suspicion for the STOP, never automatically the FRISK · (7) INEVITABLE DISCOVERY — a lawful team already en route with a valid warrant means the evidence comes IN.

NEXT — SESSION 18. CONSTITUTIONAL LAW BEGINS. New subject, new summit: judicial review and the structure of American government — Marbury v. Madison, the federal legislative powers, and the master key (the tiers of scrutiny) that unlocks half the subject. Bring the classify-first habit; Con Law rewards it more than any subject so far.
How confident do you feel on the specific-crimes recipes — 1 to 5, alongside your four drill letters? That's the third confidence capture; the trend line is part of the training.

chapters.title: Constitutional Law I: Judicial Review, Federal Powers & Tiers of Scrutiny
key_rules: SESSION 18 — CONSTITUTIONAL LAW I: THE MAP — Judicial Review, Federal Powers & Tiers of Scrutiny. Phase 1 · Constitutional Law begins.

ONE LINE FIRST — The Criminal Law arc is fully closed — teaching and drills, Sessions 9 through 17, and your Session 17 sweep (4/4, including the false-pretenses title test you half-expected to miss) means the whole subject now sits in the bank. Note the calibration: you keep scoring above your confidence. Trust the preparation.

Today a new summit: Constitutional Law, the fourth MBE subject — and the one most foreign-trained lawyers find strangest, because it is not about what people DID, it is about WHO IS ALLOWED TO DO WHAT. This session is the map of the entire subject: judicial review, who holds what power, and the master key — tiers of scrutiny — that unlocks half the questions you will ever see here.
THE MAP — THREE PILLARS. All of Constitutional Law is three questions:
1. WHO DECIDES? — Judicial review: the courts' power to strike down unconstitutional acts. (Marbury — today.)
2. WHO HOLDS THE POWER? — Structure: federalism (federal government vs. the states) and separation of powers (Congress vs. President vs. courts). (Today and Sessions 19–20.)

3. WHOSE RIGHTS? — Individual rights: when the government sorts people into groups or burdens their liberties, how hard does the court look? (Tiers of scrutiny — today; the rights themselves in Sessions 21–23.)

THE CLASSIFY-FIRST HABIT, UPGRADED. In criminal law you classified the CRIME; here you classify the ACTOR and the QUESTION TYPE before touching the doctrine: Is Congress acting, or a state, or the President? Is this a POWER question (may the government do this at all?) or a RIGHTS question (may it do it THIS WAY, to THESE PEOPLE)? Get that classification right and the answer is usually one step away.

BRIDGE FROM YOUR WORLD: Nigeria's 1999 Constitution does all of this too — section 1 makes the Constitution supreme, section 4 divides legislative power (the Exclusive and Concurrent lists are Nigeria's version of 'enumerated vs. reserved'), section 6 gives the courts judicial power. You know the architecture. The American exam tests the MACHINERY inside it: how far each power reaches, and the three calibrated lenses (the tiers) the courts use instead of Nigeria's single 'reasonably justifiable in a democratic society' test (section 45). New lenses, familiar building.
PART ONE — JUDICIAL REVIEW: Marbury v. Madison (1803)

THE STORY (story first, always). The presidential election of 1800: John Adams, the Federalist president, loses to Thomas Jefferson, the Democratic-Republican. In his final weeks in office, Adams and his Federalist Congress do something petty and brilliant — they pack the judiciary, creating new judgeships and appointing loyal Federalists to fill them, working late into the night before Jefferson's inauguration. History calls them the 'midnight judges.' One appointee: William Marbury, named a justice of the peace for the District of Columbia.
