His commission is signed and sealed — but in the rush, it is never DELIVERED.

Jefferson takes office. His Secretary of State, James Madison, finds the undelivered commissions and — on Jefferson's orders — refuses to deliver them. The Federalists are to be frozen out. Marbury does what any of us would do: he sues. And he sues DIRECTLY in the Supreme Court, asking it for a writ of mandamus — a court order commanding a public official to perform a legal duty — against Madison. His legal hook: Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789, which appeared to authorize the Supreme Court to issue mandamus orders directly.

The Chief Justice who hears the case is John Marshall — himself an Adams appointee, a Federalist, and the man who had been Adams's Secretary of State when the commissions were signed. He is judging a case about his OWN paperwork. Awkward — and he turns it into the most important decision in American law.
MARSHALL'S THREE QUESTIONS (memorize this sequence — the exam loves it):
1. DOES MARBURY HAVE A RIGHT TO THE COMMISSION? Yes. The appointment was complete when the commission was signed and sealed; delivery was a mere formality. A legal right was violated.

2. DO THE LAWS OF THE COUNTRY AFFORD HIM A REMEDY? Yes. 'The very essence of civil liberty certainly consists in the right of every individual to claim the protection of the laws, whenever he receives an injury.' A right without a remedy is no right at all.

3. IS A MANDAMUS ISSUING FROM THIS COURT THE PROPER REMEDY? No — and here is the thunderbolt. Section 13 of the Judiciary Act purported to give the Supreme Court ORIGINAL JURISDICTION (the power to hear a case first, as a trial court) to issue mandamus. But Article III, Section 2 of the Constitution lists the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction exhaustively: 'Cases affecting Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, and those in which a State shall be Party.' A mandamus suit by Marbury against Madison is none of those. CONGRESS CANNOT EXPAND THE COURT'S ORIGINAL JURISDICTION BY STATUTE. Section 13 is therefore unconstitutional — and void.

And then the sentence that built the American legal order: 'It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.' When a statute conflicts with the Constitution, the Constitution — the supreme law — controls, and the court must follow it and disregard the statute.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THE EXAM — Point 1: JUDICIAL REVIEW ESTABLISHED. Courts may void acts of Congress and the President that violate the Constitution. Note what the Constitution never says in so many words — no clause reads 'courts may strike down statutes.' Marshall REASONED it from the nature of a written constitution and the judge's duty to decide cases. (The transfer question at the end of this chapter goes here.)

Point 2: THE POLITICAL GENIUS. Marshall asserted the Court's greatest power while ruling AGAINST his own party's petitioner — he gave Jefferson nothing to defy. There was no order for the President to disobey, so the power survived its birth.

Point 3: IT BINDS THE STATES TOO. Cooper v. Aaron (1958) — after Brown v. Board of Education desegregated schools, Arkansas resisted; the Court held its interpretation of the Constitution is the supreme law of the land, binding on the states. State officials are not free to nullify it.

Point 4: BRIDGE. A Nigerian judge voiding an inconsistent statute cites section 1(3) — 'this Constitution shall prevail, and that other law shall to the extent of the inconsistency be void.' Marbury is the American section 1(3): same supremacy, but the Americans had to INVENT the judicial role because their text doesn't hand it over as plainly as yours does.

DEFINITIONS. JUDICIAL REVIEW: the power of courts to declare acts of the legislature or executive unconstitutional and refuse to enforce them. ORIGINAL JURISDICTION: a court's power to hear a case first (as the trial court), versus APPELLATE JURISDICTION (reviewing a lower court's decision). WRIT OF MANDAMUS: a court order commanding a public official to perform a clear legal duty.
PART TWO — THE STRUCTURE: WHO HOLDS WHAT POWER

FEDERALISM: ENUMERATED POWERS AND THE TENTH AMENDMENT. The federal government is a government of ENUMERATED (listed) POWERS. Article I, Section 8 lists what Congress may do — tax, borrow, regulate interstate commerce, declare war, and so on. If a power is not in the list (and not fairly implied by it), Congress does not have it. The Tenth Amendment says the rest is 'reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.'

The states, in turn, hold the POLICE POWER — the general power to legislate for the health, safety, welfare, and morals of their people. (Definition: POLICE POWER has nothing to do with the police force — it is the state's broad regulatory authority. Do not confuse it with law enforcement.)

When federal and state law collide, the SUPREMACY CLAUSE (Article VI, Clause 2) resolves it: the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties are 'the supreme Law of the Land' — valid federal law displaces conflicting state law. (Preemption — the machinery of HOW — is Session 19.)

BRIDGE: Nigeria's Second Schedule does the same job with the Exclusive Legislative List (federal only), the Concurrent List (both), and the residual matters left to the states. The American version is just shorter: one federal list, one reservation sentence.

SEPARATION OF POWERS: THREE ARTICLES, THREE JOBS. Article I — the LEGISLATIVE power, vested in Congress. Article II — the EXECUTIVE power, vested in the President. Article III — the JUDICIAL power, vested in the federal courts.

Each branch's fights with the others (Can Congress veto executive action? Can the President impound funds? — the exam's separation-of-powers questions) come in Session 20. For today, bank the frame: POWER QUESTIONS ASK WHETHER THE ACTOR IS INSIDE ITS OWN ARTICLE.
PART THREE — CONGRESS'S BIG THREE POWERS. On the MBE, when Congress acts, the question is almost always one of these three. Learn them as a set.

1. THE COMMERCE CLAUSE (Article I, Section 8, Clause 3). THE TEXT: Congress may 'regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes.' Sixteen words that built the modern federal government.

THE STORY — Gibbons v. Ogden (1824): New York granted a steamboat monopoly on its waters; a competing operator (Gibbons) held a federal coastal license. Chief Justice Marshall — him again — struck down the monopoly: 'commerce' is not just buying and selling, it is 'INTERCOURSE' — all commercial interaction — and 'among the several States' means INTERMINGLED WITH, not merely crossing a state line. Federal commerce power is 'complete in itself.'
THE THREE CATEGORIES (from United States v. Lopez, 1995 — memorize these; the exam recites them): Congress may regulate —
Category 1: THE CHANNELS OF INTERSTATE COMMERCE — the highways, airways, waterways, the internet, telephone networks. Congress can keep them free of harmful things.
Category 2: THE INSTRUMENTALITIES OF INTERSTATE COMMERCE, AND PERSONS OR THINGS IN INTERSTATE COMMERCE — the trucks, the planes, the goods and people moving across state lines.
Category 3: ACTIVITIES THAT SUBSTANTIALLY AFFECT INTERSTATE COMMERCE — and this is where all the fighting happens.

THE EXPANSION — Wickard v. Filburn (1942): A farmer grew wheat for his own family's consumption, exceeding his federal quota. He argued: my wheat never enters commerce. The Court upheld the quota anyway — because even if HIS wheat was trivial, wheat grown for home use NATIONWIDE, IN THE AGGREGATE, substantially affects the interstate wheat market. This is the AGGREGATION PRINCIPLE: Congress may regulate purely local, individual conduct if the CLASS OF ACTIVITY, taken together, substantially affects interstate commerce.

THE MODERN LIMIT — United States v. Lopez (1995) and United States v. Morrison (2000): Congress made it a federal crime to possess a gun near a school (Lopez), and created a federal civil remedy for gender-motivated violence (Morrison). Both struck down. Why? The regulated activity was NON-ECONOMIC — possessing a gun, committing violence — and Congress cannot pile non-economic activity into an 'aggregate' to manufacture a substantial effect. Congressional FINDINGS about economic effects do not save it (Morrison rejected pages of findings). THE LINE THE EXAM DRAWS: economic activity → aggregate → Congress wins. Non-economic activity → Congress needs a JURISDICTIONAL ELEMENT (e.g., 'a firearm that has moved in interstate commerce') or the law falls.

THE COUNTERWEIGHT — Gonzales v. Raich (2005): Home-grown marijuana for personal medical use — Congress CAN regulate it, because marijuana is a COMMODITY WITH AN ESTABLISHED INTERSTATE MARKET; growing it is ECONOMIC activity in the Wickard sense, and exempting home-grown supply would undercut the federal scheme. WICKARD SURVIVES; LOPEZ LIMITS.
THE EXAM FORMULA, ONE LINE: Is the activity economic in nature? Yes → aggregate it → valid. No → look for a jurisdictional element tying it to interstate commerce; without one → invalid.
2. THE TAXING AND SPENDING POWER (Article I, Section 8, Clause 1). Congress may 'lay and collect Taxes... to pay the Debts and provide for the... GENERAL WELFARE.' Two doctrines, both heavily tested:

CONDITIONAL SPENDING — South Dakota v. Dole (1987): Congress told states: raise your drinking age to 21 or lose 5% of your federal highway funds. Upheld. Congress may attach CONDITIONS to federal money if four limits are met — memorize as four gates:
Gate 1: The spending must pursue the GENERAL WELFARE.
Gate 2: The conditions must be UNAMBIGUOUS (states must know what they are accepting).
Gate 3: The conditions must be RELATED to the federal interest in the funded program (highway funds ↔ safe highways ↔ drinking age — related).
Gate 4: No INDEPENDENT CONSTITUTIONAL BAR (the condition can't require the state to do something the Constitution forbids).

Plus the fifth, unwritten gate: the pressure must not become COERCION — 5% was 'relatively mild encouragement.' In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), Congress threatened states with the loss of ALL their existing Medicaid funds unless they expanded Medicaid — the Court called that 'a gun to the head' and struck the condition down (while severing it, so the expansion survived as optional).

PLAIN-WORDS NOTE — SEVERING: when a court 'severs' an unconstitutional piece, it cuts that piece out and leaves the rest of the law standing. In NFIB, the coercive condition was cut out; the Medicaid expansion itself survived, as an option the states could choose or refuse.

TAX VS. PENALTY — NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), the other half: the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate (buy insurance or pay) could NOT be sustained under the Commerce Clause — Congress cannot compel INACTIVE commerce ('the power to regulate commerce does not include the power to compel it'). But the payment WAS sustained as a TAX — courts look at function, not labels: it raised revenue, was collected by the IRS, and wasn't so heavy as to be purely punitive. THE EXAM TRAP: Congress's label doesn't decide — the Court asks what the exaction DOES.

3. THE NECESSARY AND PROPER CLAUSE (Article I, Section 8, Clause 18) — McCulloch v. Maryland (1819). THE STORY: Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States. Nothing in Article I says 'Congress may charter a bank.' Maryland, hostile to the Bank, taxed its Baltimore branch. Two questions reached the Court.

HOLDING 1 — IMPLIED POWERS: The Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress choose any APPROPRIATE MEANS to carry out its enumerated powers. 'Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the constitution, and ALL MEANS WHICH ARE APPROPRIATE, WHICH ARE PLAINLY ADAPTED TO THAT END, which are not prohibited, but consist with the letter and spirit of the constitution, ARE CONSTITUTIONAL.' The Bank stands. (Definition: IMPLIED POWERS — powers not listed but reasonably adapted to carrying out listed ones. Note: 'necessary' here means USEFUL/CONDUCIVE, not ABSOLUTELY INDISPENSABLE — the exam's favorite misreading.)

HOLDING 2 — FEDERAL SUPREMACY OVER THE STATES: Maryland's tax is void. 'THE POWER TO TAX INVOLVES THE POWER TO DESTROY' — if a state could tax a federal instrumentality, it could tax it out of existence, making the state supreme over the nation. The Supremacy Clause forbids it.
THE LIMIT TO BANK: Necessary and Proper is NOT A STANDALONE POWER — it must be hitched to an enumerated one. Congress cannot use it to invent entirely new fields of authority.

PART FOUR — THE MASTER KEY: TIERS OF SCRUTINY. When the government CLASSIFIES people (treats groups differently) or BURDENS a right, the court doesn't just ask 'is this reasonable?' — it picks one of three lenses first. THE LENS USUALLY DECIDES THE CASE. This is the single highest-yield framework in Constitutional Law.
THE THREE TIERS:
1. STRICT SCRUTINY — THE GOVERNMENT ALMOST ALWAYS LOSES. The test: the law must be NECESSARY (narrowly tailored — no less restrictive way to do it) to achieve a COMPELLING government interest.

Strict scrutiny is triggered by: SUSPECT CLASSIFICATIONS — race, national origin, and (for state laws) alienage; and burdens on FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS (voting, interstate travel, privacy — Sessions 21–22).

'Strict in theory, fatal in fact': the government nearly always loses. (One exam-era footnote: race-conscious admissions in higher education were struck down under this test in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023) — strict scrutiny doing its fatal work.)
2. INTERMEDIATE SCRUTINY — THE REAL FIGHT. The test: the law must be SUBSTANTIALLY RELATED to an IMPORTANT government interest.

Intermediate scrutiny is triggered by: GENDER (Craig v. Boren, 1976 — the exam's favorite), ILLEGITIMACY (classifications based on nonmarital birth), and COMMERCIAL SPEECH. Note the vocabulary: gender is QUASI-SUSPECT, not suspect — calling it 'suspect' (strict scrutiny) is the classic wrong answer.
Here the government sometimes wins and sometimes loses — which is why the exam lives here.
3. RATIONAL-BASIS REVIEW — THE GOVERNMENT ALMOST ALWAYS WINS. The test: the law must be RATIONALLY RELATED to a LEGITIMATE government interest.
Rational-basis review is triggered by: EVERYTHING ELSE — age, disability, wealth, economic regulation (Williamson v. Lee Optical, 1955).
The challenger must negate EVERY CONCEIVABLE rational basis — even ones the government never stated. The court will invent justifications for the government. Almost never fatal.

THE MNEMONIC (alphabetical, both halves): STRICT — Compelling interest, Necessary (narrowly tailored) fit. INTERMEDIATE — Important interest, Substantially related fit. RATIONAL BASIS — Legitimate interest, Rationally related fit. (S-C-N · I-I-S · R-L-R.)

TWO TRAPS TO BANK NOW — Trap 1: ALIENAGE SPLITS BY WHO CLASSIFIES. STATE laws discriminating against noncitizens → STRICT SCRUTINY (Graham v. Richardson). FEDERAL alienage classifications → RATIONAL BASIS (immigration is a plenary federal power). And a state's exclusion of aliens from core governmental functions (police, voting, teaching) drops to rational basis. The exam asks 'state or federal?' before it asks anything else.

PLAIN-WORDS NOTE — PLENARY POWER: 'plenary' means complete and full. A plenary power is one handed over wholesale — here, the federal power over immigration — so the courts step back and barely question how it is used.

Trap 2: BRIDGE. Nigeria's section 45 asks whether a rights restriction is 'reasonably justifiable in a democratic society' — one test for all rights. The American system replaces that single test with three calibrated tiers. When you feel the urge to apply one reasonableness test to everything, stop: PICK THE TIER FIRST.
THE CLASSIFY-FIRST HABIT FOR CON LAW MBE QUESTIONS:

Step 1: WHO IS ACTING? Congress → which enumerated power (Commerce? Taxing/Spending? Necessary & Proper hitched to what?). State → police power, but check federal limits (Supremacy, dormant Commerce — Session 19). President → Article II (Session 20).
Step 2: POWER QUESTION OR RIGHTS QUESTION? 'May the government do this AT ALL?' → Parts Two–Three. 'May it do it TO THESE PEOPLE / IN THIS WAY?' → Part Four: pick the tier.
Step 3: APPLY THE TEST MECHANICALLY. The exam rewards the checklist, not the essay.

PRACTICE: This session's 4 drills — the Lopez gun-near-school problem, the McCulloch federal-tax problem, the gender-scrutiny problem, and the Dole drinking-age conditions problem — live in the Drills tab, with answer keys and explanations. Attempt them there before checking the answers.

PRACTITIONER TRANSFER QUESTION: You spent 20 years under a written constitution in Nigeria: when a Nigerian court voids an inconsistent statute, it cites section 1(3) — the text hands the judge the power. WHAT DID MARSHALL HAVE TO INVENT IN MARBURY THAT YOUR JUDGES GET FOR FREE IN THE TEXT? (One sentence. The answer is the whole point of Part One.)

SPACED REVIEW — SESSION 17 IN 60 SECONDS. THE THEFT TRIANGLE — ONE QUESTION DECIDES IT: DID TITLE PASS? Trick got only POSSESSION → LARCENY BY TRICK (title never passes; the trick voids consent). Fraud got TITLE → FALSE PRETENSES (misrepresentation of PAST OR PRESENT fact — never future promises). LAWFUL POSSESSION FIRST, CONVERSION LATER → EMBEZZLEMENT (intent may form AFTER possession began; intent to repay is no defense).
ROBBERY = larceny + force/threat of IMMINENT force BEYOND what the taking requires (the unnoticed pickpocket is larceny — stealth is not force); EXTORTION = threat of FUTURE harm.

BURGLARY (common law) = breaking + entering + dwelling + of another + nighttime + intent to commit a felony/theft therein — the BREAKING is the tripwire (open door = no breaking), and the INTENT AT ENTRY is the gravamen (gravamen = the essential heart of the charge). ARSON (common law) = malicious + burning (actual CHARRING) + dwelling + of another.

KIDNAPPING = confinement + asportation/concealment + nefarious purpose (common law: any movement; modern/MPC: substantial movement). STATUTORY RAPE = STRICT LIABILITY AS TO AGE — even reasonable mistake is no defense.

THE PERMANENT MISS BANK — 7 ENTRIES, STILL STANDING: (1) common law needs TWO guilty minds, the MPC needs ONE; (2) COVER MINUS CONTRACT, times quantity; (3) HADLEY foreseeability judged AT FORMATION; (4) recklessness is SUBJECTIVE; (5) M'NAGHTEN is EITHER/OR; (6) WARDLOW — flight + high-crime area = reasonable suspicion for the STOP, never automatically the FRISK; (7) INEVITABLE DISCOVERY — a lawful team already en route with a valid warrant means the evidence comes in.

NEXT — SESSION 19: Federalism's limits: the DORMANT COMMERCE CLAUSE (when Congress is silent, states still can't discriminate against interstate commerce), PREEMPTION (how the Supremacy Clause actually displaces state law — express, field, and conflict), and ANTI-COMMANDEERING (Congress can't order state legislatures or officers around). The other half of the structure.

chapters.title: Constitutional Law II: Dormant Commerce, Preemption & Anti-Commandeering
key_rules: SESSION 19 — CONSTITUTIONAL LAW II: THE NEGATIVE CONSTITUTION — Dormant Commerce, Preemption & Anti-Commandeering. Phase 1 · Constitutional Law.

ONE LINE FIRST. Session 18 closed with a clean sweep — 4/4, the third straight perfect set on a brand-new domain — and your calibration note stands: you keep scoring above your confidence. Trust the preparation, pal.

Session 18 was Congress's affirmative commerce power — when Washington may act. Today is the flip side: THREE WAYS WASHINGTON AND THE STATES FIGHT OVER THE SAME GROUND. When a state regulates commerce (the dormant Commerce Clause), when federal and state law collide (preemption), and when Congress tries to boss the states around (anti-commandeering). Call it the negative constitution: the session is about what the structure forbids.

THE CLASSIFY-FIRST HABIT, CON LAW EDITION: every question today starts with one fork — who is acting? A STATE law affecting commerce → dormant Commerce Clause. A FEDERAL law meeting a STATE law → preemption (Supremacy Clause). A FEDERAL law ordering a STATE GOVERNMENT to do something → anti-commandeering. Get the actor right and the doctrine picks itself.

BRIDGE FROM YOUR WORLD: Nigeria's Second Schedule does this same work with the Exclusive and Concurrent Legislative Lists — and section 4(5) of the 1999 Constitution is preemption in plain text: where a state law is inconsistent with a National Assembly law, the federal law prevails. You have lived these doctrines. Today you learn their American names.
PART ONE — THE DORMANT COMMERCE CLAUSE: WHAT STATES MAY NOT DO TO INTERSTATE COMMERCE:

WHY "DORMANT"? THE STORY (STORY FIRST, ALWAYS). The phrase sounds odd. It means: the Commerce Clause grants Congress power over interstate commerce — and even when Congress has said nothing at all, that grant has a "DORMANT" (SLEEPING, NEGATIVE) SIDE that limits what states may do to interstate commerce.

The history is the reason. Under the ARTICLES OF CONFEDERATION (America's first, failed constitution, before 1789), the states behaved like rival countries: New York taxed firewood and produce coming in from New Jersey and Connecticut at its docks; states slapped duties on each other's goods. The young republic was strangling its own trade. The Framers wrote the Commerce Clause largely to KILL THAT ECONOMIC BALKANIZATION — Justice Cardozo's phrase — so that America would be one national market, not thirteen customs houses. The dormant Commerce Clause is the Court enforcing that original bargain: states may not rebuild the tariff walls the Constitution tore down.

DEFINITION — DORMANT (OR "NEGATIVE") COMMERCE CLAUSE: the principle that the Commerce Clause's grant of power to Congress implicitly limits state regulation of interstate commerce, even absent any federal legislation. It limits STATES (and their cities/counties), never Congress.
THE TWO-QUESTION TEST (MEMORIZE THIS — THE EXAM'S SORTING MACHINE). Every dormant-Commerce-Clause question is answered by asking two questions, in order:
QUESTION 1: DOES THE STATE LAW DISCRIMINATE AGAINST INTERSTATE COMMERCE?
"Discriminate" here means the law treats OUT-OF-STATE economic interests worse than IN-STATE ones — on its face ("no waste from other states"), in its purpose, or in its practical effect.

IF YES → VIRTUALLY PER SE INVALID. The law survives only if the state proves BOTH: (a) it serves an IMPORTANT, LEGITIMATE, NON-PROTECTIONIST purpose (public health or safety — not shielding local businesses from competition); AND (b) there is NO REASONABLE NON-DISCRIMINATORY ALTERNATIVE. The state almost always loses. Think of it as strict scrutiny's cousin — and say so on an essay.
IF NO (THE LAW IS EVENHANDED) → GO TO QUESTION 2.

QUESTION 2: UNDER PIKE BALANCING, IS THE BURDEN ON INTERSTATE COMMERCE "CLEARLY EXCESSIVE" RELATIVE TO THE LOCAL BENEFITS? (Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc., 1970.) The court weighs the burden against the local payoff. The challenger usually loses — but a lopsided burden still falls.

THE DISCRIMINATION CASES (STORIES FIRST). PHILADELPHIA V. NEW JERSEY (1978) — the signature case. New Jersey, running out of landfill space, passed a law BANNING THE IMPORT OF SOLID WASTE FROM OTHER STATES — while New Jersey's own garbage flowed freely to its landfills. The Court struck the law 7–2: "Whatever New Jersey's ultimate purpose, it may not be accomplished by discriminating against articles of commerce coming from outside the State unless there is some reason, apart from their origin, to treat them differently." Note the exam point: the law's purpose was legitimate (protecting the environment, conserving landfill space) — but purpose doesn't save FACIAL DISCRIMINATION. Origin alone is never a reason.

DEAN MILK CO. V. CITY OF MADISON (1951). Madison, Wisconsin required all milk sold in the city to be PASTEURIZED WITHIN FIVE MILES OF THE CITY CENTER. On its face it applied to everyone — but in practice it shut out Illinois milk producers while protecting local dairies. Struck down: a reasonable non-discriminatory alternative existed (the city could inspect distant plants or rely on their home-state inspections). The trap the exam recycles endlessly: "the city could achieve its health goal without the five-mile wall" — that sentence is the alternative prong doing its work.

HUGHES V. OKLAHOMA (1979). Oklahoma banned the EXPORT OF MINNOWS caught in state waters. Facial discrimination against interstate commerce — struck. (Yes, the Supreme Court decided a case about minnows. The doctrine doesn't care about the cargo.)

MAINE V. TAYLOR (1986) — the rare case the STATE WINS the discrimination test, and the exam's favorite trap answer. Maine banned importing live baitfish to protect its waters from parasites no test could reliably detect. The Court upheld the ban: the purpose was legitimate (ecological survival, not economics), and — critically — NO ADEQUATE NON-DISCRIMINATORY ALTERNATIVE EXISTED (testing couldn't catch the parasites). When you see an answer choice claiming a discriminatory law is valid, check Maine v. Taylor's two prongs: legitimate purpose plus no alternative. Both must be true.

DISCRIMINATION IN EFFECT counts too: HUNT V. WASHINGTON STATE APPLE ADVERTISING COMMISSION (1977). North Carolina required all apples sold in the state to carry the USDA grade or none at all — wiping out Washington's superior state grading system and stripping Washington apples of their competitive advantage. Facially neutral, discriminatorily effective — struck. And the oldest formulation, BALDWIN V. G.A.F. SEELIG (1935): New York set minimum milk prices that Vermont producers had to meet — struck as the very "economic Balkanization" the Clause forbids.

THE EVENHANDED CASES — PIKE BALANCING. PIKE V. BRUCE CHURCH, INC. (1970) — the balancing test's name case. Arizona required cantaloupes grown in Arizona to be PACKED IN ARIZONA before shipment. Bruce Church, an Arizona grower, packed across the line in California. The law was evenhanded (it applied to all Arizona cantaloupes) — but its burden on interstate commerce was clearly excessive relative to Arizona's claimed interest in the melons' reputation. Struck.

MINNESOTA V. CLOVER LEAF CREAMERY (1981) — the state wins the balancing. Minnesota banned plastic nonreturnable milk containers (cardboard only), for environmental reasons. The burden on interstate commerce (out-of-state plastics makers) was real but not "clearly excessive" next to the environmental benefit. UPHELD. The exam pair to bank: Pike (burden wins) vs. Clover Leaf (benefit wins) — same test, opposite outcomes, and the facts decide.

MBE HABIT FOR PIKE: the scale almost always tips to the state unless the facts scream disproportion — a tiny local payoff against a massive interstate burden. If the question gives you an evenhanded safety or environmental law with modest compliance costs, expect "upheld."

THE THREE OUTS (EXCEPTIONS — THE EXAM'S FAVORITE WRONG ANSWERS): 1. THE MARKET-PARTICIPANT EXCEPTION. When the state acts as a BUYER OR SELLER IN THE MARKET — not as a regulator — the dormant Clause doesn't apply. REEVES, INC. V. STAKE (1980): South Dakota owned a cement plant and, during a shortage, sold first to South Dakotans. Upheld — a private cement company could do the same. HUGHES V. ALEXANDRIA SCRAP CORP. (1976): Maryland paid bounties for junk cars titled in Maryland — the state was spending its own money. Upheld. THE LIMIT: SOUTH-CENTRAL TIMBER DEVELOPMENT V. WEYERHAEUSER (1984) — Alaska sold state-owned timber on condition buyers process it in Alaska. That condition regulated the downstream private market; the state had stepped out of the participant role and back into the regulator's chair. STRUCK. Exam fork: selling its own stuff on its own terms (exception applies) vs. telling private buyers what to do after the sale (exception lost).

2. CONGRESSIONAL CONSENT. Congress can authorize what the dormant Clause would otherwise forbid — because the limit exists to protect Congress's domain, and Congress may waive the protection. The classic: the MCCARRAN-FERGUSON ACT, letting states regulate the business of insurance. If the facts say "Congress has expressly permitted the states to do this," the dormant-Clause challenge dies.

3. QUARANTINE AND THE NO-ALTERNATIVE WIN — really Maine v. Taylor again, filed here for the test-taker: a discriminatory law survives only on legitimate purpose + no alternative. Don't invent a freestanding "health exception."

Two one-liners for completeness: the dormant Clause binds states and localities only — NEVER CONGRESS (Congress's own commerce regulation is judged under Session 18's affirmative-power rules, not this test). And in FOREIGN commerce the Court applies more searching scrutiny than in interstate commerce — Congress's power over foreign commerce is exclusive (Japan Line v. County of Los Angeles).

BRIDGE: your investigator's nose already knows discrimination — a checkpoint that waves through local trucks but searches every out-of-state one is discrimination in effect. The American court asks the same question about the statute: does it sort by origin?
PART TWO — PREEMPTION: WHEN FEDERAL LAW AND STATE LAW COLLIDE:

THE IDEA IN ONE PARAGRAPH. The SUPREMACY CLAUSE (Article VI) says valid federal law is supreme. PREEMPTION is the machinery: when Congress has spoken, conflicting state law gives way. The whole doctrine is a question of CONGRESSIONAL INTENT — did Congress mean to displace the state law? The exam tests whether you can name the type of preemption the facts describe.

DEFINITION — PREEMPTION: the invalidation of state law because it conflicts with, or Congress intended it to yield to, federal law. Bridge: Nigeria's SECTION 4(5) — "if any law enacted by a House of Assembly is inconsistent with any law validly made by the National Assembly, the law made by the National Assembly shall prevail, and that other law shall to the extent of the inconsistency be void." Same machine, American name.

THE THREE TYPES (WITH THE PRESUMPTION THAT GOVERNS THEM). 1. EXPRESS PREEMPTION. The statute says so: "No State shall establish..." Read the text; if Congress spoke plainly, the analysis ends. Watch for SAVINGS CLAUSES — express carve-outs where Congress says state law is not preempted (ERISA's insurance savings clause is the famous one). The exam loves pairing them: an express preemption clause with a savings clause, and the question turns on which one the facts fall under.

2. FIELD PREEMPTION (IMPLIED). The federal scheme is so PERVASIVE that Congress must have meant to occupy the whole field, leaving no room for the states — or the federal interest is so DOMINANT (foreign affairs, immigration) that state law is inherently displaced.

HINES V. DAVIDOWITZ (1941) — the name case. Pennsylvania required aliens to register with the state; Congress had enacted a comprehensive federal Alien Registration Act. The Court struck Pennsylvania's law: the federal scheme was complete, and in immigration the federal interest is dominant. Pair it with RICE V. SANTA FE ELEVATOR CORP. (1947): preemption requires a "CLEAR AND MANIFEST PURPOSE" of Congress — and here is the governing PRESUMPTION: in fields the states have traditionally occupied (health, safety, welfare — the police power), courts PRESUME AGAINST preemption unless Congress's intent is clear. In fields of dominant federal interest (Hines), the presumption flips. MBE habit: name the presumption before the outcome.
3. CONFLICT PREEMPTION (IMPLIED) — two sub-types, and the exam tests the distinction:

(A) IMPOSSIBILITY: it is physically impossible to obey both laws. The trap is FLORIDA LIME & AVOCADO GROWERS V. PAUL (1963): California required avocados to contain at least 8% OIL; federal regulations set the floor at 7%. The growers cried preemption — but a grower could satisfy both by meeting the higher California standard. NO IMPOSSIBILITY, NO PREEMPTION. Exam rule: a stricter state standard that includes compliance with the federal one is not impossibility — impossibility means the two commands genuinely cannot both be obeyed (one says "do X," the other says "do not do X").

(B) OBSTACLE: the state law STANDS AS AN OBSTACLE to the full purposes and objectives of Congress — even though obeying both is technically possible. CROSBY V. NATIONAL FOREIGN TRADE COUNCIL (2000): Massachusetts barred state contracts with companies doing business in Burma; Congress had enacted its own calibrated Burma sanctions giving the President discretion. The state law undercut Congress's chosen means — PREEMPTED AS AN OBSTACLE. GEIER V. AMERICAN HONDA (2000): federal safety standards gave carmakers a choice among passive restraints (airbags or automatic belts, phased in); a state tort suit demanding airbags specifically would have erased the federal choice — OBSTACLE PREEMPTION.

MBE SORTING HABIT: Impossibility ≠ obstacle. When the facts show two commands that can both be met (Florida Lime), refuse the preemption answer. When the facts show the state undoing Congress's chosen means (Crosby, Geier), pick obstacle — even where no express clause exists.
PART THREE — ANTI-COMMANDEERING: CONGRESS MAY NOT CONSCRIPT THE STATES:

THE IDEA IN ONE SENTENCE. Congress may regulate PRIVATE PEOPLE directly — but it may NOT COMMAND THE STATES' LEGISLATURES OR OFFICERS to do its work for it. The states are not Congress's field offices. (Tenth Amendment territory.)

THE STORIES. NEW YORK V. UNITED STATES (1992) — the founding case. Congress's Low-Level Radioactive Waste Policy Amendments gave states a supposed "choice" for disposing of nuclear waste — and one option was that the state "TAKE TITLE" to the waste, assuming all liability for it. The Court struck the take-title provision: Congress may encourage states (with money — Session 18's Dole), and Congress may preempt state law entirely and regulate the field itself — but it may not COMPEL A STATE TO ENACT OR ADMINISTER A FEDERAL REGULATORY PROGRAM. The permitted toolbox instead: CONDITIONAL SPENDING (Dole), CONDITIONAL PREEMPTION ("regulate to our standards or we take over"), and DIRECT REGULATION OF PRIVATE PARTIES.

PRINTZ V. UNITED STATES (1997) — the executive-branch twin. The Brady Act's interim provision ordered local CHIEF LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS to run background checks on handgun buyers. Struck: the federal government "MAY NOT COMPEL THE STATES TO ENACT OR ADMINISTER A FEDERAL REGULATORY PROGRAM" — and that includes conscripting state officers, not just legislatures.

BRIDGE — THIS ONE IS PERSONAL: twenty years you carried a badge in a state command. Printz says Washington could not have ordered your command to run federal background checks — your officers answer to the state, and the federal government must hire its own. When the exam asks whether Congress can require state police to enforce a federal scheme, your SIB years already know the answer: no.

MURPHY V. NCAA (2018) — commandeering by prohibition. The federal PASPA law didn't order states to do anything; it barred them from "AUTHORIZING" sports gambling. New Jersey repealed its ban anyway. The Court struck PASPA's provision: dictating what laws a state may not enact is "A MORE DIRECT AFFRONT TO STATE SOVEREIGNTY" — commandeering in reverse. Exam fork: Congress ordering a state to legislate (New York) and Congress forbidding a state to legislate (Murphy) are the SAME violation.

TESTA V. KATT (1947) — the contrast the exam uses as a trap. A Rhode Island court refused to hear a federal price-control claim; the Supreme Court held state courts of general jurisdiction MUST hear federal claims when they hear analogous state claims. That is NOT commandeering — it is the Supremacy Clause binding judges, who have always been bound to apply supreme federal law. Exam habit: ordering legislatures or executive officers = commandeering (forbidden); requiring courts to apply federal law = Testa (required).

RENO V. CONDON (2000) — the one-liner that closes the trap set. The Driver's Privacy Protection Act restricted how states disclose drivers' personal data. Upheld — because it regulated the states AS OWNERS OF DATABASES, the way it regulated private parties: generally applicable, no sovereign command. Regulating states like everyone else ≠ commandeering them.
THE SESSION'S UNIFIED FIELD (BANK THIS). All three parts are one idea wearing three coats — FEDERALISM AS A LIMIT:

Who acts — Doctrine — Question; STATE regulates commerce — Dormant Commerce Clause — Discriminatory? → per se test. Evenhanded? → Pike balancing.; FEDERAL + STATE law meet — Preemption — Express? Field? Conflict (impossibility vs. obstacle)?; FEDERAL orders the STATE GOVERNMENT — Anti-commandeering — Commanding legislature/officers (New York, Printz, Murphy)? Or regulating/binding courts (Condon, Testa)?

The exam's favorite crossover: a federal law that looks like preemption but is really commandeering — or a spending condition (Session 18, Dole) dressed up as a command. Classify the actor first; the column picks itself.
1. DORMANT COMMERCE CLAUSE = the Commerce Clause's negative side; limits STATES (never Congress) even with no federal statute. History: killing the Articles-of-Confederation tariff wars.

2. TWO-QUESTION TEST: (1) Discriminatory (face/purpose/effect)? → VIRTUALLY PER SE INVALID unless the state proves legitimate non-protectionist purpose AND no reasonable non-discriminatory alternative (Philadelphia v. New Jersey, Dean Milk, Hughes v. Oklahoma; the rare state win: Maine v. Taylor). (2) Evenhanded? → PIKE BALANCING: burden "clearly excessive" vs. local benefits (Pike struck; Clover Leaf upheld).
3. OUTS: market participant (Reeves; limit: South-Central Timber — no downstream regulation); congressional consent (McCarran-Ferguson); quarantine/no-alternative (Maine v. Taylor).

4. PREEMPTION = congressional intent. EXPRESS (read the text; watch savings clauses). FIELD (Hines; presumption against preemption in traditional state fields — Rice). CONFLICT: impossibility (both commands obeyable = no preemption — Florida Lime's 8%-vs.-7% trap) vs. obstacle (state undoes Congress's means — Crosby, Geier).

5. ANTI-COMMANDEERING: Congress can't compel states to enact/administer federal programs — legislatures (New York v. United States take-title), officers (Printz Brady checks), or by forbidding state law (Murphy v. NCAA PASPA). Alternatives: Dole spending, conditional preemption, direct regulation. Not commandeering: Testa (courts must apply federal law), Condon (generally applicable regulation).
6. NIGERIA BRIDGES: s.4(5) = preemption; the Exclusive/Concurrent lists = the federalism map; your command years = Printz's answer.

SPACED REVIEW — SESSION 18 IN 60 SECONDS: MARBURY (1803): courts void acts of Congress/President that violate the Constitution ("it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is"); Congress can't expand the Court's original jurisdiction by statute. Cooper v. Aaron: the Court's reading binds the states.
FEDERALISM: enumerated powers (Art. I §8); Tenth Amendment reservation; state police power (health/safety/welfare/morals); Supremacy Clause.

COMMERCE (SESSION 18): Lopez's three categories (channels / instrumentalities-persons-things / substantial effects); economic activity aggregates (Wickard, Raich); non-economic needs a jurisdictional element (Lopez, Morrison).
MCCULLOCH: Necessary & Proper = appropriate means to enumerated ends ("necessary" means conducive); states can't tax federal instrumentalities.
SPENDING: Dole's four gates (general welfare, unambiguous, relatedness, no independent bar) + non-coercion (NFIB's "gun to the head"); mandate penalty upheld as a tax (function over label).

TIERS MNEMONIC: S-C-N / I-I-S / R-L-R — Strict = Compelling + Necessary (race, national origin, fundamental rights); Intermediate = Important + Substantially related (gender, illegitimacy, commercial speech); Rational basis = Legitimate + Rationally related (everything else). Gender is quasi-suspect, never "suspect." Alienage: state → strict; federal → rational basis.

MISS BANK STILL STANDING (19 entries): Hadley at formation · recklessness subjective · MPC conspiracy unilateral / CL bilateral · M'Naghten either-or · UCC cover = cover − K · mirror image (CL) vs. battle of the forms (UCC) · mailbox rule · firm-offer 3-month cap · perfect tender + cure · felony-murder merger · no attempt for unintentional crimes · factual impossibility never a defense · no duty to rescue · strict liability: mistake no defense · specific vs. general jurisdiction · purposeful availment · PJ waivable / SMJ not · Wardlow stop ≠ frisk · inevitable discovery.
PRACTICE — This session's drill questions live in the Drills tab, with full explanations for every answer. Attempt each one there before reading its analysis, then send your letters in chat.

NEXT — SESSION 20: EQUAL PROTECTION & DUE PROCESS (INDIVIDUAL RIGHTS BEGIN). Structure closes; rights open. EQUAL PROTECTION (classifications, the tiers in action, suspect/quasi-suspect classes, affirmative action) and DUE PROCESS — procedural (what process is due) and substantive (the fundamental rights: privacy, marriage, family, Roe/Casey/Dobbs through Obergefell). The tiers of scrutiny you banked in Session 18 become the working tool of every question.

chapters.title: Constitutional Law III: Equal Protection & Due Process
key_rules: SESSION 20 — CONSTITUTIONAL LAW III: EQUAL PROTECTION & DUE PROCESS — redo, story first: every case with its story, every term defined in plain words on first use.
Sessions 18 and 19 were about governments against each other. From here, the fight is a person against a government. The claim is simple: "My right was trampled."
The machine from Session 18 still runs everything. First, classify. Then pick the suspicion level. Then apply it. But two new questions arrive. Which right? And which government act?
WORDS FIRST, PLAINLY DEFINED
Equal protection means the government must treat like cases alike. It may not sort people by unjustified lines.
Due process means the government may not take away life, liberty, or property except by fair means and for fair reasons.

Both promises live in the Fourteenth Amendment, passed in 1868, which binds the states. Its words are: "No State shall…" Against the federal government, the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause does the same work. The Court also reads equal protection into the Fifth Amendment for federal cases about race. Here is that story now, so it is never a bare citation again.

Bolling v. Sharpe (1954). Story: Black schoolchildren in Washington, DC, challenged segregated schools. But DC is not a state, so the Fourteenth Amendment did not reach it. Rule: The Court used the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause, which binds the federal government, and read equal protection into it. Segregation in DC schools fell on the same day as Brown.

A classification is a law that sorts people. It may sort by race, by sex, by age, or by wealth. Or it may burden a right unequally, so that one group enjoys it less. No sorting, no equal-protection claim.
A tier, also called a level of scrutiny, is how hard the Court looks at the law. There are three.

Strict scrutiny is the hardest look. The government must show a compelling interest. That means an extremely strong reason, like national survival. And the law must be necessary to serve it. Almost nothing survives strict scrutiny. Lawyers say it is "strict in theory, fatal in fact."
Intermediate scrutiny is the middle look. The government must show an important interest, and the law must be substantially related to it. That means a real, close fit, not loose statistics.

Rational basis is the lightest look. The government must show a legitimate interest, and the law must be rationally related to it. Under this test, the Court accepts any conceivable legitimate reason, even if the lawmakers never said it out loud.

A suspect class is a group the Court watches with the hardest look, because of a history of discrimination. Race is the classic example. A quasi-suspect class gets the middle look. Gender is the classic example.
A fundamental right is a right so basic that any unequal burden on it draws strict scrutiny, even when no suspect class is involved. Voting, travel, marriage, and access to the courts are examples.
State action means action by a government. The Fourteenth Amendment binds governments, not private people. A private person acting alone cannot violate it.

Incorporation is how the Bill of Rights reaches the states. The Bill of Rights was first written against the federal government only. The Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause carries most of those rights to the states, one right at a time. That is called selective incorporation.

A penumbra is a shadow. In Griswold, the Court said the written guarantees of the Bill of Rights cast shadows, and privacy lives in those shadows. The word matters for one case only, and its story comes later in this lesson.

Undue burden was the test for abortion laws from 1992 to 2022. A law was invalid if it put a substantial obstacle in the path of a woman seeking an abortion before viability. It is dead law for abortion today, after Dobbs. But exam questions still mention it, so know what it meant.
Congruent and proportional is the leash on Congress. When Congress enforces the Fourteenth Amendment, its remedy must match the violation in size and shape. Not bigger. Not a redefinition.
Exceedingly persuasive justification is the strong form of intermediate scrutiny for gender. The state needs a really convincing reason, not just a plausible one.

Wartime national-security claim is the argument that won Korematsu, and only Korematsu. It says: in wartime, the military judges a security risk, and courts should defer to that military judgment, even when the order sorts people by race. The modern Court disowns it. Its story comes later in this lesson.
1. THE GATEWAY: IS A GOVERNMENT ACTING AT ALL?
Ask this before anything else. If no government is acting, the Fourteenth Amendment does not apply, and the claim ends.

The Civil Rights Cases (1883). Story: Private hotels, theatres, and trains refused service to Black customers. The customers sued under a federal civil-rights law. Rule: No claim. The Fourteenth Amendment binds governments, not private people. A private hotel refusing a guest on its own is private conduct, and the Constitution does not reach it.
But the exam loves three doors where private conduct becomes state action. Learn them as doors.

Door one: public function. Marsh v. Alabama (1946). Story: A company owned an entire town in Alabama. Streets, sidewalks, shops, everything. A Jehovah's Witness named Grace Marsh stood on a street corner handing out religious leaflets. The company told her to stop, and she was arrested for trespassing. Rule: The town was a public function. Running a town is a job only government does. So the First Amendment applied, and Marsh could leaflet. Plain meaning: when a private body does a job that belongs to government alone, it acts as the government.

Door two: entanglement, also called nexus. Lugar v. Edmonds Oil (1982). Story: A creditor wanted a debtor's property. A court clerk helped the creditor seize it without any hearing. Rule: The clerk's hand made it state action. Plain meaning: when government is so involved in the private act that the act is really the state's, the Constitution applies. Nexus means the link between the government and the private act.

Door three: courts enforcing private discrimination. Shelley v. Kraemer (1948). Story: Neighbours signed a private agreement, a covenant, saying no Black family could buy a house on their street. A Black family bought anyway. The neighbours asked a court to enforce the covenant. Rule: The covenant itself was private paper. But a court order enforcing it was state action, and it fell. Plain meaning: a judge's order is the government's act, even when the paper before the judge is private.
One more gateway line. Bank it. Congress's power to enforce these rights comes from section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment. That power means enforce, not redefine.

City of Boerne v. Flores (1997). Story: A Catholic church in Boerne, Texas, wanted to expand its building. A local historic-preservation law blocked the expansion. Congress had passed a law, the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, giving religious claims more protection than the Supreme Court said the Constitution gives. The church relied on it. Rule: Congress went too far. It may enforce the Court's reading of the Constitution. It may not redefine the right to be bigger. Its remedy must be congruent and proportional to the violation it targets. That means matching in size and shape, not larger.
2. EQUAL PROTECTION: THE FRAMEWORK
Three steps, every time.
Step one: is there a classification? Does the law sort people, or burden a right unequally? No classification, no claim.
But a law that merely hits one group harder is not a classification by itself. The exam tests this with purpose. A discriminatory purpose must be shown. Impact alone is not enough.

Washington v. Davis (1976). Story: Washington, DC used a written test for police recruits. More Black applicants failed it than white applicants. The failed applicants sued, saying the test violated equal protection. Rule: No classification. A test that hits one group harder is not sorting by race unless a discriminatory purpose is shown. The city adopted the test to measure job skills, not to exclude Black recruits. So the claim failed at step one. Plain meaning: unequal results do not prove unequal sorting. Purpose must be shown.

Step two: which tier? Use the Session 18 machine. Suspect class, strict scrutiny. Quasi-suspect class, intermediate scrutiny. Everything else, rational basis. Or a fundamental right burdened unequally, which draws strict scrutiny on its own.
Step three: apply the tier. The government must meet what the tier demands.

Two tracks run through the doctrine. Track one: suspect and quasi-suspect classes. Track two: fundamental rights burdened unequally, even with no suspect class. Voting, travel, marriage, and court access live on track two.
3. THE CLASSES
Race: strict scrutiny.

Loving v. Virginia (1967). Story: Mildred and Richard Loving married in Washington, DC, where interracial marriage was legal. They returned home to Virginia, where it was a crime. Virginia arrested them. Rule: The ban fell. Race classifications need a compelling interest. "Racial purity" is not one. Exam move: a marriage ban aimed at one race is both an equal-protection violation and a due-process violation. Both doors open.

Brown v. Board of Education (1954). Story: Linda Brown was a Black schoolgirl in Topeka, Kansas. She had to walk past the white school near her home to reach the Black school farther away. Her father and other parents sued, backed by the NAACP (the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People — the American civil-rights organisation, founded in 1909, that fought racial segregation in court; "Colored People" is the historic term from that era for Black Americans), argued by Thurgood Marshall. Rule: The Supreme Court, unanimous under Chief Justice Earl Warren, held that segregated public schools are unconstitutional. "Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal." The decision overruled Plessy v. Ferguson (1896). In Plessy, Louisiana required separate railway carriages for Black and white passengers, and the Court had allowed it under "separate but equal." Brown ended that. Plain meaning: separation in schools is itself the inequality. No separate school can be equal.

Korematsu v. United States (1944). Story: After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941, President Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066. The military then ordered every person of Japanese ancestry on the West Coast, about 120,000 people, most of them American citizens, into internment camps. Fred Korematsu, a Japanese-American man, refused to report. He was convicted. Rule: The Court upheld his conviction, six to three. It applied strict scrutiny in words, and let the government win in fact. The reason was the wartime national-security claim. The military said the whole group posed a security risk, and the Court deferred to that military judgment in wartime. Exam point: this is the one place the government has ever won under strict scrutiny with a wartime national-security claim. And the modern Court disowns it.

Trump v. Hawaii (2018). Story: President Trump restricted entry into the United States from several mostly Muslim-majority countries. Challengers said the ban targeted Muslims. Rule: The Court upheld the ban, five to four, again deferring to the president's national-security judgment over immigration. But in the same opinion, Chief Justice Roberts wrote that Korematsu "was gravely wrong the day it was decided." He formally overruled it. Exam point: Korematsu is dead law. Nobody can cite it as good authority today.
National origin: strict scrutiny. Same family as race. A law sorting by national origin faces the hardest look.

Alienage: the split by classifier. This is the Session 18 trap, now applied. The tier depends on who is doing the sorting. A state sorting by alienage faces strict scrutiny. The federal government sorting by alienage faces only rational basis.

Graham v. Richardson (1971). Story: Arizona and Pennsylvania denied welfare benefits to resident aliens, people living lawfully in the United States but not yet citizens. The aliens sued. Rule: The states lost. State alienage is strict scrutiny. A state may not fence resident aliens out of basic benefits.

Mathews v. Diaz (1976). Story: A federal law gave Medicare benefits only to aliens who had lived in the United States for five years or more. Aliens resident for a shorter time sued. Rule: The federal government won. Federal alienage is rational basis. Immigration is Congress's job, and the Court defers to Congress there. Exam move: same sorting, different sorter, different tier. Always ask who is classifying.
Gender: intermediate scrutiny, with teeth.

Gender was settled in Session 18. Craig v. Boren (1976). Story, briefly again: Oklahoma sold weak beer to women at 18 but to men only at 21, claiming young men drink and drive more. Rule: Loose statistics about young men's drinking were not a substantial relation to traffic safety. Gender gets intermediate scrutiny. Gender is quasi-suspect, never suspect.

United States v. Virginia (1996), the Virginia Military Institute case. Story: Virginia ran an all-male military academy, the Virginia Military Institute, famous for its harsh training, its alumni network, and its military tradition. Women were offered a separate leadership program at another college, with fewer resources, no alumni network, and no military tradition. Rule: The exclusion fell. The Court demanded an exceedingly persuasive justification, a really convincing reason, and Virginia had none. Separate was not equal here. The women's program was not the equal of the Institute. Slot: intermediate scrutiny, with teeth.
Children born outside marriage: intermediate scrutiny.

Clark v. Jeter (1988). Story: Pennsylvania gave a child born outside marriage only a few years to sue for child support, while a child born to married parents had much longer. Rule: Struck. The short time limit was not substantially related to an important interest. Exam care: the class is quasi-suspect, so the test is intermediate, not strict. Do not upgrade it.
Everything else: rational basis.

Massachusetts Board of Retirement v. Murgia (1976). Story: Massachusetts forced state police officers to retire at age 50. An officer challenged the rule. Rule: Upheld. Age is not a suspect class. The state only needed a rational reason, and it had one.
Wealth is not suspect either. Economic regulation is the classic rational-basis case.

Williamson v. Lee Optical (1955). Story: Oklahoma passed a law saying an optician could fit glasses only after the customer got a prescription from an eye doctor. Opticians sued, saying the real motive was protecting eye doctors from competition. Rule: Upheld. Under rational basis, the Court asks only whether some conceivable legitimate reason exists. It does not ask whether that reason was the real one. Protecting eye health was conceivable, and that was enough.

The bite: City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center (1985). Story: A city demanded a special permit for a group home for people with intellectual disabilities. Boarding houses, fraternities, and nursing homes needed no such permit. The only reason given was the neighbours' fear. Rule: The permit requirement fell, under rational basis. Irrational fear is not a legitimate interest. But here is the trap. The Court refused to call disability a quasi-suspect class. So Cleburne is rational basis that bites. It is not a new tier. Bank it in these words: "Fails rational basis, class not elevated."
4. FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS UNDER EQUAL PROTECTION
No suspect class is needed here. When a law burdens a fundamental right unequally, strict scrutiny applies on the right alone.

Voting. Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections (1966). Story: Virginia charged every voter a poll tax of one dollar and fifty cents. Poor voters who could not pay could not vote. Rule: The poll tax fell. Voting is fundamental, so a wealth-based exclusion gets strict scrutiny. Saving money, or anything less than compelling, cannot justify it.

Reynolds v. Sims (1964). Story: Alabama's voting districts were wildly unequal in population. One district had far more people than another, yet each elected one representative. So some votes counted for much less than others. Rule: "One person, one vote." Each person's vote must count equally.

Travel. Shapiro v. Thompson (1969). Story: Several states required newcomers to live in the state for one full year before receiving welfare benefits. New arrivals sued. Rule: The waits fell. The right to travel is fundamental. Saving money is not a compelling reason to fence newcomers out.

Saenz v. Roe (1999). Story: California paid new residents only what their old state would have paid in benefits, for their first year. A newcomer from another state sued. Rule: Struck. Newly arrived citizens are equal citizens. A state may not give newcomers a second-class welcome.

Courts. Griffin v. Illinois (1956). Story: A poor prisoner wanted to appeal his conviction, but an appeal required a written transcript of the trial, and he could not afford one. The state refused a free copy. Rule: Equal protection forbids making an appeal turn on wealth. The state had to provide the transcript.
Marriage and family. Loving, above, belongs here too. Two more:

Zablocki v. Redhail (1978). Story: Wisconsin barred marriage for parents who were behind on child-support payments, unless a court gave permission. A father behind on support wanted to marry. Rule: Struck. Marriage is fundamental, and the bar was not narrowly tailored to collecting support.

Skinner v. Oklahoma (1942). Story: Oklahoma ordered the sterilization of "habitual criminals," people convicted of three felonies. A man convicted of stealing chickens and of robbing with a gun challenged the order. Rule: Struck. Procreation is fundamental. The state could not cut off a basic human right this way.
5. SUBSTANTIVE DUE PROCESS: THE RIGHT ITSELF

Due process has two halves. Procedural due process asks how the government must act. That is Session 21. Substantive due process asks what the government may not do at all, even with perfect procedure. That is today's half.

Incorporation first. The Bill of Rights was written against the federal government only. The Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause carries most of those rights to the states, one right at a time. That is selective incorporation.

Gitlow v. New York (1925). Story: New York convicted Benjamin Gitlow, a socialist, for urging the overthrow of government. He argued that free speech protected him against the state, not only against the federal government. Rule: Gitlow lost his case, but he won the bridge. The Court said, for the first time, that free speech applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment. That was the first step of incorporation.

McDonald v. Chicago (2010). Story: Chicago banned handguns. Otis McDonald, an elderly man living in a high-crime neighbourhood, wanted a handgun to defend his home. He sued. Rule: The ban fell. The Second Amendment now applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.

Timbs v. Indiana (2019). Story: Indiana seized Tyson Timbs's Land Rover, worth about forty-two thousand dollars, after a drug offence. Timbs said the seizure was an excessive fine. Rule: The ban on excessive fines now applies to the states too. The seizure was grossly out of proportion to the offence.

Nearly all of the Bill of Rights is incorporated now. The famous holdouts are grand-jury indictment and civil jury trial. Exam move: when a state violates speech, religion, or guns, the case runs through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause. That clause is the bridge.
Economic liberty: dead doctrine, living trap.

Lochner v. New York (1905). Story: New York capped bakery workers at sixty hours a week, to protect their health. A bakery owner was fined for letting a worker go over the limit. He argued the law violated his "liberty of contract," the freedom to make work agreements without government interference. Rule: The Court agreed and struck the law. For thirty years, courts used this idea to strike worker-protection laws.

West Coast Hotel v. Parrish (1937). Story: Washington State set a minimum wage for women. A hotel challenged it, relying on Lochner. Rule: The Court upheld the minimum wage. The Lochner era ended. Economic regulation gets rational basis, full stop. Lee Optical, above, finished the job.
Exam trap: if a fact pattern invites you to strike a business regulation for violating economic liberty, refuse. That is Lochner, and Lochner lost.
Privacy and autonomy: the arc. Follow the arc in order. Each case builds on the one before.

Griswold v. Connecticut (1965). Story: Connecticut banned contraceptives, even for married couples. Estelle Griswold, who ran a Planned Parenthood clinic, was fined for giving a married couple contraceptive advice. Rule: The ban fell. The Bill of Rights has penumbras, shadows cast by its written guarantees, like free association, and no quartering of soldiers, and no unreasonable searches. Privacy lives in those shadows. Plain meaning: no single sentence says "privacy," but several guarantees together create a zone of privacy.

Eisenstadt v. Baird (1972). Story: William Baird gave a contraceptive foam to an unmarried woman after a lecture, and was arrested, because Massachusetts allowed contraceptives only for married people. Rule: Struck. Equal protection joined the arc. If married people have the right, unmarried people cannot be denied it.

Roe v. Wade (1973). Story: Texas banned abortion except to save the mother's life. A pregnant woman, called "Jane Roe" in the case, challenged the ban. Rule: The Court found a privacy right covering abortion, and set a trimester frame. In the early months, the choice belonged to the woman and her doctor.

Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992). Story: Pennsylvania restricted abortion with a twenty-four-hour waiting period, informed-consent rules, and a spousal-notice rule for married women. Clinics challenged the law. Rule: The Court kept the core right from Roe, but replaced the trimester frame with the undue-burden test. A law is invalid if it puts a substantial obstacle in the path of a woman seeking an abortion before viability. The spousal notice fell as an undue burden. The other rules stood.

Lawrence v. Texas (2003). Story: Texas police entered a home and found two men in private intimate conduct. The men were arrested under a law banning same-sex intimate conduct. Rule: The ban fell. Liberty protects private choices between consenting adults.

Obergefell v. Hodges (2015). Story: Jim Obergefell married John Arthur in Maryland, where same-sex marriage was legal. When Arthur died, Ohio refused to recognise Obergefell as the spouse on the death certificate. Rule: State bans on same-sex marriage fell, under both due process and equal protection. Marriage equality is the law.

Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022). Story: Mississippi banned abortion after fifteen weeks. The Jackson Women's Health Organization, the state's only abortion clinic, challenged the ban. Rule: The Court overruled Roe and Casey outright. The Constitution contains no right to abortion. So abortion regulations return to rational-basis review. A legitimate interest, like protecting prenatal life or maternal health, rationally served, is enough.

Exam point, stated plainly. Know the arc, but apply today's law. Dobbs is the current rule for abortion. Do not answer a post-Dobbs question with Casey's undue-burden test. That test is dead law for abortion. Lawrence and Obergefell still stand for the autonomy rights they decided.
Family. Parents direct their children's upbringing. These are fundamental liberty interests, so burdens on them get strict scrutiny.

Meyer v. Nebraska (1923). Story: Nebraska banned teaching German to schoolchildren, during the anti-German feeling after the First World War. A teacher, Robert Meyer, was convicted for teaching German to a ten-year-old. Rule: Struck. Parents have a liberty interest in directing their children's education.

Pierce v. Society of Sisters (1925). Story: Oregon required every child to attend a public school. The Society of Sisters, which ran Catholic schools, challenged the law. Rule: Struck. Parents may choose private schooling for their children.

Troxel v. Granville (2000). Story: Grandparents sought a court order for visits with their grandchildren, over the objection of the children's mother, Tommie Granville, a fit parent. Rule: The Court sided with the mother. A fit parent's decision about visits gets presumptive weight. A court may not override it lightly.
6. THE EXAM MOVE: EQUAL PROTECTION VERSUS SUBSTANTIVE DUE PROCESS

Same facts, two questions. Equal protection asks: "Did the government sort people unfairly?" That means classification, then tier. Substantive due process asks: "Did the government invade a liberty at all?" That means is the right fundamental, then tier.
A marriage ban aimed at one race is both. That is Loving. A marriage ban aimed at everyone is substantive due process only. That is the due-process half of Obergefell.
On essays, run both when the facts allow. On multiple choice, the question's wording tells you which door. "Classifies by…" is equal protection. "Prohibits everyone from…" is substantive due process.

Nigeria bridge. Nigeria's Constitution, section 42, freedom from discrimination, is equal protection's cousin. Section 36, fair hearing, is procedural due process's cousin. The ideas are old friends. Only the tier machinery is new. That machinery, classify, pick the tier, apply it, is the one new skill this session teaches.
PRACTICE — This session's drill questions live in the Drills tab, with full explanations for every answer. Attempt each one there before reading its explanation.
NEXT — SESSION 21: PROCEDURAL DUE PROCESS. When the government must give notice and a hearing, and how much process is due, under the Mathews balancing test.

chapters.title: Procedural Due Process
key_rules: SESSION 21 — CONSTITUTIONAL LAW IV: PROCEDURAL DUE PROCESS — how the government takes something from you: gateway first, then Mathews balancing.

*How* the government takes something from you — not *whether* it may. The companion to Session 20: there we asked whether the government's sorting or its reason was fair. Here we ask whether its *procedure* was fair.
THE LESSON
THE GATEWAY, AND THE TWO QUESTIONS IN ORDER

Procedural due process lives in two clauses that say the same thing to two different governments. The Fifth Amendment says the *federal* government may not deprive any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law. The Fourteenth Amendment says the same to the *states*. So the gateway from Session 20 still applies: no state action, no due process claim at all. A private employer firing you is not a due process case, however unfair it feels.
Once you are through the gateway, ask two questions, in this order, and never in reverse:

1. Is there a life, liberty, or property interest at stake? If the answer is no, stop. No interest, no process owed — the case ends here, and this is where the exam most often ends it.
2. If yes, what process is due, and when? Only now do you talk about hearings, notice, and timing.
Most students rush to question 2. The examiner's favourite trap is a beautiful hearing analysis for a person who had no interest in the first place.
QUESTION 1: WHAT COUNTS AS PROPERTY? AN ENTITLEMENT, NOT A HOPE

Property here does not mean only land and cars. It means any legitimate claim of entitlement — something the law, a rule, or a settled mutual understanding has promised you, so that you have more than a mere hope or a one-sided expectation of keeping it. The Constitution does not create these entitlements; state law, a statute, a contract, or an institution's own rules create them. The Constitution only says: once an entitlement exists, the government cannot take it without fair process.

Story first — *Board of Regents v. Roth* (1972). David Roth was hired as an assistant professor at Wisconsin State University–Oshkosh for one year. The university's rules gave tenure only after four years of service. At the end of his one year, Roth was not rehired, with no reasons given and no hearing. He sued, saying the refusal violated due process. The Supreme Court said no. Roth had no property interest, because nothing — no statute, no rule, no promise — entitled him to a second year. He had a hope of rehire, and a hope is not property. *Rule: a unilateral expectation is not an entitlement; without a legitimate claim of entitlement, there is no property interest and no hearing is owed.*

Story first — *Perry v. Sindermann* (1972), the contrast that proves the rule. Robert Sindermann taught at Odessa College in Texas for ten years under a series of one-year contracts, just like Roth. But Odessa's faculty guide said a teacher had a form of tenure after enough years of service, and the college had in practice treated long-serving teachers as tenured. The Court sent his case back for a hearing on the facts: if the guide and the practice together created a mutual understanding that he would keep his job unless cause was shown, then he *did* have a property interest, and a hearing was owed. *Rule: entitlement can grow out of rules plus settled practice — a "de facto tenure" system — not only out of a formal contract. The exam tests Roth and Sindermann as a pair: same one-year contracts, opposite answers, because only one man had something to point to.*

The usual entitlements on the exam: welfare benefits created by statute, a public job that by law can only be lost "for cause", a government licence, and Social Security disability benefits. In each, ask: "What rule, statute, or settled understanding promised this person they could keep it?" If you cannot point to one, the answer is Roth — stop.

And one hard limit, from story first — *Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill* (1985), which returns below: a legislature that creates an entitlement cannot also dictate a lesser procedure and call it part of the deal. The state creates the property; the Constitution defines the process. The "bitter with the sweet" argument — take the job with the weak procedure attached — was rejected.
QUESTION 1, CONTINUED: WHAT COUNTS AS LIBERTY? FREEDOM FROM RESTRAINT — AND REPUTATION IS NOT ENOUGH ALONE
Liberty's core is freedom from physical restraint: being locked up, committed, or otherwise confined by the government. That is a liberty interest, full stop.

But liberty is also where students over-claim. Story first — *Paul v. Davis* (1976). Edward Davis was arrested for shoplifting in Louisville, Kentucky. The charge was later dismissed. But the police had already circulated a flyer to local shopkeepers naming him, with his photograph, under the heading "active shoplifters". Davis sued, saying the flyer deprived him of liberty without a hearing. The Supreme Court said no. Reputation alone, however badly damaged, is not a liberty interest. Defamation by the government is a matter for state tort law (the ordinary law of defamation), not a constitutional case. *Rule: reputation alone fails. You need "stigma-plus" — the government's false public statement PLUS the loss of some tangible interest, such as a job, a licence, or a legal status. Stigma alone is a dead end; stigma-plus opens the door to a hearing.*

So the liberty checklist is short: (a) physical restraint or confinement — yes; (b) public stigma *plus* a tangible loss — yes, a hearing is owed on the stigma; (c) reputation alone, a bad reference, a lost expectation — no.
QUESTION 2: WHAT PROCESS IS DUE? NOTICE, A HEARING, AND AN IMPARTIAL JUDGE — SIZED BY BALANCING

Due process has no fixed checklist that fits every case. Its core, in every case, is two things: notice — warning reasonably calculated to tell you what is happening and why — and an opportunity to be heard — a real chance to tell your side, at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner, before an impartial decision-maker.

Story first — *Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co.* (1950), on notice. A New York bank managed a common trust fund for many beneficiaries, some of whose names and addresses it knew. When it asked a court to settle its accounts, it gave notice only by publishing a small advertisement in a local newspaper. The Supreme Court said that was not enough for the beneficiaries it could have reached by mail. *Rule: notice must be reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties. A newspaper advertisement is fine for people you cannot find; it is not notice to people whose addresses you hold in your own files.*

On impartiality, one story: a judge paid from the fines he imposes is not impartial. In *Tumey v. Ohio* (1927), the mayor of a small Ohio village also sat as judge in liquor cases, and his pay came out of the fines he collected. The Supreme Court struck the scheme down: a decision-maker with a direct financial interest in the outcome denies due process. *Rule: the decision-maker must not have a personal stake in the result — financial interest is the classic disqualification.*

Beyond that core, *how much* process is due is decided by balancing. Story first — *Mathews v. Eldridge* (1976), the master test for this whole session. George Eldridge received Social Security disability benefits. The government reviewed his file, decided he was no longer disabled, and cut his benefits off without giving him an evidentiary hearing first — a hearing where he could appear, testify, and cross-examine witnesses. He got a full hearing afterwards, with back payments if he won. He sued, saying the Constitution required the full hearing *before* the cutoff. The Supreme Court said no. *Rule: the Mathews balancing test weighs three factors: (1) the private interest affected by the government's action; (2) the risk of an erroneous deprivation under the procedures used, and the probable value of additional safeguards; and (3) the government's interest, including the fiscal and administrative burdens of extra procedure. No factor alone decides; the court weighs all three.*

Mathews is the test you run whenever the question asks "was this procedure enough?" — and the exam's favourite move is to run it twice on similar facts and get opposite answers. That is the next pair.
THE PAIR THE EXAM LOVES: GOLDBERG AGAINST MATHEWS

Story first — *Goldberg v. Kelly* (1970). New York City welfare recipients had their benefits cut off without any prior hearing at all — no notice of the reasons, no chance to respond, no confrontation of the witnesses against them. The Supreme Court held that welfare benefits are a statutory entitlement — property — and that cutting them off without a prior hearing violated due process. Because welfare is, for its recipients, the means of subsistence itself, an erroneous cutoff could mean hunger while the recipient waited for a later hearing. So the Court required, *before* termination: timely and adequate notice of the reasons, an opportunity for an oral hearing, a chance to confront and cross-examine adverse witnesses, an impartial decision-maker, a decision based solely on the evidence presented, and a statement of the reasons and evidence relied on. *Rule: where the private interest is subsistence and the risk of error is real, due process demands a full evidentiary hearing before the deprivation.*

Now put Goldberg beside Mathews. Same shape — government benefits, cutoff, a hearing demanded before the cutoff — opposite result. Why? Run the three Mathews factors. (1) Private interest: disability benefits matter greatly, but unlike welfare they are not the recipient's only means of subsistence; other resources and later back payments soften the blow. (2) Risk of error: disability turns largely on written medical evidence, which a paper review handles fairly well; a live hearing adds little, because doctors rarely change their written opinions under cross-examination. (3) Government interest: full pre-termination hearings for every disability review would cost a great deal and slow the whole system. Weighed together: no pre-termination evidentiary hearing required; the post-termination hearing, with retroactive benefits if the recipient wins, is enough.

*Exam move: when you see a benefits case, name the pair, run all three factors, and say which way each one points. A student who writes "Goldberg says a hearing is always required" has missed the session. Goldberg says a hearing was required on Goldberg's facts. Mathews says the factors decide.*
THE LOUDERMILL SHAPE: A SMALL HEARING FIRST, A FULL HEARING AFTER

Story first — *Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill* (1985), in full. James Loudermill was a security guard for the Cleveland school board. Ohio law said he could be dismissed only for cause — that made his job a property interest. He was fired for lying on his job application, and he said the lie was an honest mistake. He got no chance to respond before the firing, though he got a full hearing afterwards. The Supreme Court held that due process required, *before* termination, notice of the charges and an opportunity to respond — in person or in writing — to tell his side. It did *not* require a full evidentiary trial before the firing, because the full post-termination hearing would follow. *Rule: for a public employee with a for-cause job, the pre-termination hearing is a modest one — notice plus a chance to respond — and it is satisfied even without witnesses or cross-examination, so long as a full hearing comes after. Loudermill is the middle shape between Goldberg's full pre-hearing and Mathews' post-hearing only, and the exam asks you to place each new fact pattern on that line.*
QUESTION 2, CONTINUED: WHEN — BEFORE, OR AFTER?

The general rule is that the hearing comes *before* the deprivation, because a hearing after you have lost your home, your job, or your benefits is often too late to matter. But there are two well-marked exceptions.

First, genuine emergency.
