chapters.title: Formation: Offer, Acceptance & Consideration
key_rules: SESSION 7 — CONTRACTS I: FORMATION — Offer, Acceptance & Consideration, with the Session 8 enrichment: UCC vs. Common Law & Products Liability. Phase 1 · Contracts opens.

PART TWO — CONTRACTS I: HOW A CONTRACT IS FORMED. Welcome to Contracts. Ground zero, first principles: A CONTRACT IS A PROMISE (OR SET OF PROMISES) THAT THE LAW WILL ENFORCE. Formation answers one question — did these two people actually make a deal the law recognizes? Three ingredients: OFFER, ACCEPTANCE, AND CONSIDERATION. Miss any one, and there is no contract.

1. OFFER — "I INTEND TO BE BOUND, AND HERE ARE THE TERMS". An offer is a MANIFESTATION OF WILLINGNESS TO ENTER A BARGAIN that justifies the other person in understanding that assent will conclude the deal. Two things matter:

OBJECTIVE STANDARD. We don't ask what the speaker secretly meant — we ask what a REASONABLE PERSON hearing the words would understand. "I'll sell you my car for $5,000" is an offer; "I might sell my car someday" is not.
DEFINITE ENOUGH TO ENFORCE. The offer must identify the parties, the subject matter, and the key terms (quantity, price). A court must be able to tell what the deal was.
COMMUNICATED. The offeree must actually receive the offer. You can't accept an offer you never knew about — this decides the reward cases in today's drills.

WHAT IS NOT AN OFFER: advertisements, catalogs, and price lists are generally INVITATIONS TO MAKE AN OFFER, not offers — unless the ad is specific and promises something to specific persons ("first come, first served," rewards). Auction bids are offers; the auctioneer's call is the invitation. Preliminary negotiations ("let's talk about a deal") are not offers.

AN OFFER DIES WHEN: (a) its time lapses; (b) the offeror REVOKES it (effective only when the offeree RECEIVES the revocation); (c) the offeree REJECTS it or makes a COUNTEROFFER — at common law, any variation is a counteroffer and it KILLS the original offer; (d) the offeror dies or becomes incapacitated; (e) the deal becomes illegal. Special cases you'll meet later: the OPTION CONTRACT and the UCC FIRM OFFER make offers irrevocable for a time.

2. ACCEPTANCE — "I AGREE, ON EXACTLY YOUR TERMS": MIRROR-IMAGE RULE (COMMON LAW). The acceptance must match the offer exactly. "I'll take it for $4,500" in response to a $5,000 offer is not an acceptance — it's a COUNTEROFFER, and the original offer is dead. (The UCC softens this for goods — battle of the forms — coming later.)

BILATERAL VS. UNILATERAL. A BILATERAL offer asks for a promise in return ("I promise to pay you $500 if you promise to paint my house") — accept by promising. A UNILATERAL offer asks for PERFORMANCE ("$500 to whoever finds my dog") — accept by doing it. Reward posters are unilateral offers.
SILENCE IS NOT ACCEPTANCE. With narrow exceptions (prior course of dealing, or the offeree takes the benefit of offered services knowing payment is expected), doing nothing is not agreeing.

THE MAILBOX RULE — AN MBE FAVORITE. If acceptance by mail is authorized, the acceptance is effective WHEN DISPATCHED (dropped in the mailbox), even if it never arrives. Revocations, rejections, and counteroffers work the opposite way: effective only WHEN RECEIVED. So a mailed acceptance beats a phoned-in revocation that comes later.

3. CONSIDERATION — "WHAT DID EACH SIDE GIVE UP?". Consideration is a BARGAINED-FOR EXCHANGE: each party gives something (a promise, an act, or forbearance) IN EXCHANGE FOR what the other gives. It is the legal difference between a deal and a gift.

COURTS DON'T WEIGH ADEQUACY. A peppercorn can be consideration. If it was truly bargained for, the court won't ask whether it was a fair price — gross unfairness is a different doctrine (unconscionability, later).

PAST CONSIDERATION IS NO CONSIDERATION. If the act was already done before the promise, it wasn't bargained for. A promise to pay for something already completed is a gift promise — unenforceable. (Today's Q3.)
PRE-EXISTING DUTY RULE. Promising to do what you are already legally obligated to do is not consideration. (A police officer can't charge extra for doing his duty.)
ILLUSORY PROMISES. "I'll buy from you if I feel like it" — a promise conditioned entirely on the promisor's whim binds him to nothing, so it's not consideration.

MORAL OBLIGATION. A promise made out of gratitude or conscience is generally unenforceable — with classic exceptions: a promise to pay a debt BARRED BY THE STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS, a debt DISCHARGED IN BANKRUPTCY, or a VOIDABLE OBLIGATION (e.g., made as a minor) that is reaffirmed as an adult.
FORBEARANCE COUNTS. Giving up a legal right (agreeing not to sue a claim you honestly believe is valid) is consideration.

THE SUBSTITUTE: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL (§90). When there is no consideration but the promisor REASONABLY SHOULD HAVE FORESEEN that the promisee would RELY on the promise, the promisee DID RELY, and INJUSTICE can only be avoided by enforcement — the court enforces it anyway. Think of it as consideration's safety net.

PRACTICE — PICK ONE LETTER PER QUESTION, THEN READ THE ANALYSIS. Q1. Leo loses his watch and posts flyers: "$200 reward for its return." Mia finds the watch on the sidewalk and returns it to Leo, having never seen the flyers and knowing nothing of the reward. Mia now demands $200. Leo: A. Must pay — she performed exactly what the reward asked for. B. Must pay under promissory estoppel. C. Owes nothing — acceptance requires knowledge of the offer. D. Owes nothing — reward offers are never enforceable.

Q2. Owen says to Paula: "I'll sell you my pickup truck for $6,000." Paula replies: "I'll take it for $5,500." Owen says nothing. The next day Paula says: "Fine — $6,000, we have a deal." The result is: A. A contract — Paula accepted Owen's offer. B. No contract — Paula's counteroffer terminated the original offer. C. A contract — Owen's silence was acceptance of the $5,500. D. No contract — the offer lapsed overnight.

Q3. After Ada graduates from law school, her uncle tells her: "I'm so proud of you — I'll give you $10,000." He later refuses to pay, and Ada sues. She will likely: A. Win — the promise was definite and communicated. B. Win — her graduation is consideration for the promise. C. Lose — past consideration is no consideration; the graduation was complete and was not bargained for. D. Lose — promises between relatives are never enforceable.

Q4. On Monday, Owen mails Paula an offer: "I'll buy your piano for $1,000 — reply by mail." On Tuesday, Paula mails her acceptance. On Wednesday, Owen phones Paula and says: "I revoke the offer." The result is: A. No contract — the revocation reached Paula before she received confirmation of acceptance. B. A contract was formed on Tuesday — an acceptance sent by an authorized means is effective on dispatch. C. No contract — an offer remains revocable until the acceptance is received. D. A contract was formed on Wednesday — Owen's call confirmed the deal.
(Attempt each before reading on.)

ANALYSES. Q1 — C. The flyer is a UNILATERAL OFFER (reward = performance requested). Accepting a unilateral offer requires performance WITH KNOWLEDGE OF THE OFFER — you can't accept an offer you never knew existed. A is the trap: performance alone isn't acceptance without knowledge. B fails — Mia didn't rely on any promise. D is wrong — reward offers are enforceable; knowledge is the missing piece.

Q2 — B. Classic MIRROR-IMAGE RULE. At common law, any variation from the offer is a COUNTEROFFER, and a counteroffer TERMINATES the original offer. Paula's "$5,500" killed Owen's $6,000 offer; her later "fine, $6,000" is a new offer Owen never accepted. C misstates the silence rule (silence is not acceptance), and D is wrong — the offer didn't lapse; it was killed.

Q3 — C. The textbook PAST CONSIDERATION problem. Ada's graduation was already complete when the promise was made — it was not given IN EXCHANGE FOR the promise, so it wasn't bargained for. A gift promise, unenforceable. A and B miss the bargain element; D states a rule that doesn't exist.

Q4 — B. The MAILBOX RULE: an acceptance sent by an authorized medium is effective ON DISPATCH — the contract was formed Tuesday when Paula mailed it. Revocations are effective only ON RECEIPT, so Wednesday's phone call came too late. A and C state the rule backwards; D invents a confirmation requirement.

THE NEXT SESSION. CONTRACTS II — ENFORCEABILITY: the Statute of Frauds (which contracts must be in writing), defenses to formation (fraud, duress, undue influence, mistake, unconscionability), and the parol evidence rule.

CORRECTION TO SESSION 8 WORKED EXAMPLE. The example said "a car sale on the MBE is common-law territory." That was wrong. A car is a movable tangible good. UCC ARTICLE 2 GOVERNS TRANSACTIONS IN GOODS (§§2-102, 2-105) — and cars are goods. The no-contract conclusion still holds (Bisi's "$5,500" was a counteroffer killing the offer; his next-day "$6,000, deal" was a new offer; Amina refused), but the governing law is the UCC, analyzed through §2-207's battle-of-the-forms lens, not the common-law mirror-image rule.
PART A — THE UCC VS. COMMON LAW DICHOTOMY:
STEP 0 — CLASSIFY FIRST (THRESHOLD QUESTION): UCC ARTICLE 2 = sale of GOODS (movable, tangible things: cars, drills, brake
kits, inventory, crops).
COMMON LAW = everything else: services, real estate, employment, intangibles.
MIXED CONTRACTS (goods + services): the PREDOMINANT-PURPOSE TEST — what is
the heart of the deal? Buying a car with a service warranty → goods predominate → UCC. Hiring a plumber who happens to supply pipes → service predominates → common law.
Commonwealth bridge: Nigeria's Sale of Goods Act 1893 is the ancestor of UCC
Article 2 — same DNA (implied terms of quality and fitness). The American twist is vocabulary and the MBE's formation battles, not the concept.
FORMATION — WHERE THE MBE SETS ITS TRAPS: 1. ACCEPTANCE — MIRROR IMAGE VS. BATTLE OF THE FORMS
Common law: MIRROR-IMAGE RULE — the acceptance must match the offer
exactly. Any variance = counteroffer = kills the original offer.
UCC §2-207: a "definite and seasonable expression of acceptance" CAN form a

contract even with additional or different terms. Between MERCHANTS, additional terms become part of the deal UNLESS (a) the offer expressly limits acceptance to its terms, (b) they materially alter the deal, or (c) objection was made or is made within a reasonable time. DIFFERENT (conflicting) terms → the KNOCKOUT RULE: they cancel each other and UCC gap-fillers apply. Between non-merchants, additional terms are mere proposals.
2. FIRM OFFER (IRREVOCABILITY)
Common law: an offer is revocable any time before acceptance — UNLESS it
is an OPTION SUPPORTED BY CONSIDERATION.
UCC §2-205: a MERCHANT'S SIGNED WRITING holding an offer open =
irrevocable up to 3 MONTHS, NO consideration needed.
3. MODIFICATION
Common law: needs new consideration (pre-existing duty rule).
UCC §2-209: a good-faith modification needs NO consideration.
4. MAILBOX RULE: same in both — acceptance effective on DISPATCH;
revocation effective only on RECEIPT. (Your Adams v Lindsell.)
PERFORMANCE: Common law: SUBSTANTIAL PERFORMANCE — minor imperfections are breach
with damages, but don't blow up the whole deal.
UCC §2-601: PERFECT TENDER RULE — goods must conform exactly; any
non-conformity lets the buyer reject. BUT §2-508 gives the seller a right to CURE within the contract time.
STATUTE OF FRAUDS (MUST BE IN WRITING): Common law (MYLEGS): Marriage consideration, Year (cannot be performed
within one year), Land, Executor/administrator, Suretyship (answering for another's debt). Plus UCC's own:
UCC §2-201: sale of goods for $500 OR MORE must be in writing.
Exceptions: specially manufactured goods, admission in pleading or testimony, part performance (payment accepted, or goods received and accepted).
WARRANTIES (UCC ONLY — HIGH YIELD): §2-313 EXPRESS WARRANTY: affirmation of fact, promise, description, or
sample that becomes part of the basis of the bargain.
§2-314 IMPLIED WARRANTY OF MERCHANTABILITY: merchant seller; goods fit
for their ORDINARY purposes.
§2-315 IMPLIED WARRANTY OF FITNESS FOR PARTICULAR PURPOSE: seller knows
the buyer's PARTICULAR purpose AND knows the buyer is relying on the seller's judgment.
REMEDIES SNAPSHOT: UCC buyer on rejection (§§2-711–2-715): COVER (buy substitute, recover
difference) or market-price damages, plus CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES if foreseeable (§2-715).
Common law: expectation damages (put the plaintiff where performance would
have) — foreseeability limit from Hadley v Baxendale.
PART B — PRODUCTS LIABILITY DEEP DIVE:
THREE THEORIES (THREE DOORS TO THE SAME COURTROOM): 1. STRICT LIABILITY IN TORT — Restatement (Second) §402A: a COMMERCIAL

seller of a DEFECTIVE product that is UNREASONABLY DANGEROUS is liable even if ALL POSSIBLE CARE was taken. NO PRIVITY NEEDED. CARE IS IRRELEVANT. (This is the "careful defendant" trap: his carefulness doesn't matter.)
2. NEGLIGENCE — MacPherson v. Buick: the manufacturer owes a duty to
foreseeable users; PRIVITY ABOLISHED. Here care MATTERS — breach means falling below the reasonable manufacturer.
3. WARRANTY (UCC) — express (§2-313), merchantability (§2-314), fitness
(§2-315). Contract-based; privity mostly dead for personal-injury cases (Henningsen).
THREE DEFECTS (CLASSIFY THE DEFECT BEFORE CHOOSING THE THEORY): 1. MANUFACTURING DEFECT — ONE unit deviates from its own design. The
misaligned chuck. The cracked brake pad. The brake-kit batch that left the factory wrong. Proof technique: compare the bad unit against the intended design.
2. DESIGN DEFECT — the WHOLE LINE is dangerous as designed. Two tests:
(a) CONSUMER-EXPECTATION — more dangerous than an ordinary consumer would expect; or (b) RISK-UTILITY — the plaintiff shows a FEASIBLE SAFER ALTERNATIVE DESIGN existed.
3. FAILURE TO WARN — foreseeable risks that are NOT OBVIOUS. No duty to
warn of open and obvious dangers.

CHAIN OF DISTRIBUTION (WHY THE MBE ALWAYS ASKS "WHO SOLD IT"). Strict liability and implied warranty reach every COMMERCIAL seller in the chain: manufacturer → wholesaler → distributor → retailer. The CASUAL seller (yard sale, Amina selling her Camry) is NOT in the chain — no strict liability there. When a fact pattern names the seller, it is testing the chain.
LIMITS AND DEFENSES: No privity required — for persons injured (Henningsen; MacPherson).
COMPARATIVE FAULT can reduce recovery in many states.
ASSUMPTION OF RISK, PRODUCT MISUSE, and SUBSTANTIAL ALTERATION
after sale are defenses. (The aftermarket brake kit in the worked example: ask whether installation was a substantial alteration.)
For abnormally dangerous activities (blasting — Rylands v. Fletcher),
liability attaches when harm comes from THE VERY RISK that made the activity dangerous. Same "very risk" logic appears in products: the injury must flow from the defect's danger.

chapters.title: Enforceability: Statute of Frauds, Defenses & Parol Evidence
key_rules: SESSION 9 — CONTRACTS II: ENFORCEABILITY — Statute of Frauds, Defenses & Parol Evidence. Phase 1 · Contracts.

CONTRACTS II — ENFORCEABILITY: the Statute of Frauds, the defenses that undo a contract, the parol evidence rule. Practice analyses are held back — send your four letters first, and each one gets checked.

THE FRAME — FORMATION VS. ENFORCEABILITY. Sessions 7–8 asked: does a contract EXIST (offer, acceptance, consideration)? Today asks: even where a contract formed perfectly, can the plaintiff ENFORCE it in court? Three filters decide:
1. THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS — certain contracts are unenforceable (not void) unless in a signed writing.
2. THE DEFENSES — fraud, duress, undue influence, mistake, unconscionability, incapacity, illegality — that make a contract voidable (one party may escape) or void (there never was a contract).
3. THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE — when a final writing exists, what outside evidence may the court hear?

Commonwealth bridge: you know the Statute of Frauds — it is English (1677), and Nigeria inherited it. The American twist is the UCC's goods-specific machinery and the MBE's love of testing the EXCEPTIONS, not the rule.

CORRECTION BANKED (FROM THE 2026-10-13 ENRICHMENT FILE): Session 8's worked example called Amina's car sale "common-law territory." Wrong label — a car is a movable tangible good, so UCC ARTICLE 2 governs (§§2-102, 2-105). The no-contract conclusion still held (counteroffer killed the offer), but on the exam, governing law is always step zero: goods → UCC; everything else → common law.

RETRIEVAL WARM-UP — FROM MEMORY, BEFORE YOU READ FURTHER: 1. State the mirror-image rule and the mailbox rule in one sentence each. (Mirror-image: at common law an acceptance must match the offer exactly — any change is a counteroffer that kills the original offer. Mailbox: acceptance effective on dispatch; revocation effective only when received.)

2. What counts as consideration, and what three things FAIL as consideration? (Bargained-for exchange — something sought in exchange for the promise. Fail: past consideration, pre-existing duty, illusory promises. Promissory estoppel (§90) is the safety net when there is foreseeable reliance but no bargain.)
3. The UBE map, one line. (MBE 200 multiple-choice; MEE 6 essays × 30 min; MPT 2 closed-universe tasks × 90 min; NY pass = 266/400.)

4. New term, defined before any question about it: the STATUTE OF FRAUDS is the rule that certain contracts are unenforceable unless in a signed writing — "frauds" because it was written to prevent perjury about big oral deals.

SPACED REVIEW — SESSIONS 1–8 IN ONE LINE EACH: S2: Intent = purpose or substantial certainty; transferred intent among battery, assault, false imprisonment, trespass; IIED needs extreme-and-outrageous + severe distress.

S3: Trespass to land = unauthorized entry; conversion = full-value interference; defenses roundup (consent, self-defense, defense of property — never deadly force for property alone, necessity, shopkeeper's privilege).

S4: Negligence gates — duty (no general duty to rescue a stranger) → breach (reasonable person; negligence per se) → cause in fact (but-for; Summers v. Tice) → proximate cause (Palsgraf foreseeable plaintiff; eggshell rule; superseding acts).
S5: Premises liability — classify the entrant FIRST; NIED (impact / Dillon v. Legg bystander); contributory = total bar (Maryland still has it); pure vs. modified comparative; assumption of risk.

S6: Strict liability skips the breach fight; products — three theories (strict liability, negligence, UCC warranty), three defects (manufacturing = this unit off-design; design = whole line + feasible safer alternative; failure to warn = non-obvious risks), chain of distribution (commercial sellers; casual yard-sale seller not in the chain).

S7: Formation — offer (objective standard; ads = invitations unless "first come, first served"; counteroffer kills the offer); acceptance (mirror-image at common law; §2-207 battle of the forms for goods; bilateral vs. unilateral; mailbox rule); consideration (bargained-for; past consideration/pre-existing duty/illusory fail; §90 safety net).
S8: Classify FIRST, rule SECOND — the worked-example habit; drill contract live (you attempt, you send the letters, I check each one).

PART 1 — THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS (THE "WRITING" FILTER). WHAT IT DOES. Certain contracts are UNENFORCEABLE by way of action or defense unless there is a signed writing. Note the word: unenforceable, not void. The contract exists; the court just will not enforce it against the party who never signed.
THE COMMON-LAW CATEGORIES — MYLEGS:
M — MARRIAGE: contracts in consideration of marriage (prenuptial agreements). Mutual promises to marry are not the target; bargains trading on the marriage are.

Y — YEAR: contracts that CANNOT POSSIBLY BE PERFORMED WITHIN ONE YEAR of their making. The test is possibility, not likelihood: if there is ANY way to complete performance within a year, the contract is OUTSIDE the Statute. "I will employ you for two years" → inside (cannot finish in one year). "I will employ you for life" → OUTSIDE — death within a year is possible (death ends a lifetime contract; it does not perform a fixed-term one). This is the MBE's favorite Year trap.

L — LAND: contracts for the sale of an interest in real property (and leases longer than one year). Exception: PART PERFORMANCE — payment + possession + valuable improvements can take a land contract out of the Statute.
E — EXECUTOR/ADMINISTRATOR: a promise by an executor to answer personally for the debts of the deceased's estate.

S — SURETYSHIP: a promise to answer for the DEBT OF ANOTHER. Exception: the MAIN-PURPOSE RULE — if the promisor's main purpose is his own economic benefit (not merely guaranteeing another), no writing is needed.

THE UCC'S OWN STATUTE — §2-201 (VERIFIED AGAINST THE STATUTE TEXT TODAY). A contract for the SALE OF GOODS FOR $500 OR MORE is unenforceable unless there is a writing SUFFICIENT TO INDICATE A CONTRACT WAS MADE, SIGNED BY THE PARTY AGAINST WHOM ENFORCEMENT IS SOUGHT (the "party to be charged"), stating a QUANTITY. Four exceptions — the MBE tests these, not the rule:

1. MERCHANTS' CONFIRMATORY MEMO: between merchants, a written confirmation sufficient against the sender binds the receiver too, unless the receiver gives WRITTEN OBJECTION WITHIN 10 DAYS. (Merchant = one who deals in goods of the kind or has special knowledge — defined term, Session 7.)
2. SPECIALLY MANUFACTURED GOODS: not suitable for resale to others, where the seller has made a SUBSTANTIAL BEGINNING OF MANUFACTURE (or commitments for procurement) before repudiation.
3. ADMISSION IN COURT: the party to be charged ADMITS IN PLEADING, TESTIMONY, OR OTHERWISE IN COURT that a contract was made — enforceable only up to the QUANTITY ADMITTED.
4. PART PERFORMANCE: PAYMENT MADE AND ACCEPTED, or GOODS RECEIVED AND ACCEPTED — enforceable ONLY AS TO THAT PORTION (pay $2,000 of an $8,000 oral deal → enforceable to $2,000 of goods).

WHAT THE WRITING MUST CONTAIN. No formal contract needed — a memo, an email, even a signed napkin can do. It must show the essential terms (parties, subject matter; quantity under the UCC) and be SIGNED BY THE PARTY TO BE CHARGED. One signed memo is enough to enforce against the signer. Trap: the plaintiff's signature is irrelevant — only the defendant's matters.
EFFECT, PRECISELY. The defense belongs to the party against whom enforcement is sought. And remember unenforceable ≠ void: if the parties perform anyway, the law has nothing to say.

PART 2 — THE DEFENSES (THE "ESCAPE" FILTER). A clean formation can still be escaped. VOIDABLE = the victim elects to avoid the contract (must act promptly and restore benefits — restitution). VOID = no contract ever existed (illegality; physical duress). These defenses are MEE-essay favorites — the NCBE point sheets reward spotting every defense the facts support.

FRAUD / MISREPRESENTATION. Elements: (1) a FALSE REPRESENTATION OF MATERIAL FACT — past or present fact, not opinion or sales puffery ("best coffee in town" is puffery; an expert's opinion can count as fact); (2) SCIENTER — knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for truth (negligent or even innocent misrepresentation can also make the contract voidable, though damages differ); (3) INTENT TO INDUCE RELIANCE; (4) JUSTIFIABLE RELIANCE; (5) damages. DUTY TO DISCLOSE arises from half-truths, active concealment, or a fiduciary relationship. Remedy: rescission (the contract is voidable) plus damages. FRAUD IN THE FACTUM — deceived about the very nature of what you signed ("I thought it was a receipt; it was a deed") — is VOID, not merely voidable.

DURESS. An IMPROPER THREAT that leaves the victim NO REASONABLE ALTERNATIVE. PHYSICAL DURESS (a gun to the head) = VOID. ECONOMIC DURESS (an improper threat to breach an existing contract unless paid more, victim has no adequate alternative — the classic "pay me double or I walk off the job site") = VOIDABLE. A threat to do what one has a LEGAL RIGHT to do is NOT duress. Three elements to recite: wrongful threat + no reasonable alternative + causation.

UNDUE INFLUENCE. (1) A CONFIDENTIAL OR FIDUCIARY RELATIONSHIP — lawyer-client, doctor-patient, trustee-beneficiary, caregiver-elderly (or de facto dominance), plus (2) UNFAIR PERSUASION producing an unfair deal. The power move: once the relationship and a suspicious transaction are shown, the BURDEN SHIFTS TO THE DOMINANT PARTY TO PROVE FAIRNESS. The MEE's favorite fact pattern is the elderly person deeding property to the caregiver.
MISTAKE.

Mutual (both parties share the same mistaken BASIC ASSUMPTION): the adversely affected party may avoid if (1) the mistake goes to a basic assumption, (2) it MATERIALLY AFFECTS the exchange, and (3) the party did NOT BEAR THE RISK. Sherwood v. Walker — the "barren" cow Rose 2d of Aberlone, actually pregnant: barrenness went to the substance of the thing (breeding cow vs. beef cow), so rescission. No relief for mistakes of VALUE OR JUDGMENT.

Unilateral (only one party mistaken): generally NO RELIEF — UNLESS the other party KNEW OR HAD REASON TO KNOW of the mistake (the math-error bid the other side spotted), or enforcement would be UNCONSCIONABLE.
Conscious ignorance ("we both know we don't know") = assumption of risk — no relief.

UNCONSCIONABILITY (UCC §2-302; Restatement §208). Two prongs on a SLIDING SCALE — a lot of one compensates for less of the other: PROCEDURAL (unfair surprise: fine print, hidden terms, grossly unequal bargaining power, no meaningful choice — the ADHESION CONTRACT, take-it-or-leave-it standard form) + SUBSTANTIVE (terms unreasonably, grossly one-sided). The court may REFUSE TO ENFORCE the contract, SEVER the unconscionable clause, or LIMIT its application. Classic: harsh exculpatory clauses in adhesion contracts.

INCAPACITY (brief, high-yield edges). MINORS: contracts voidable by the minor; disaffirm within a reasonable time after reaching majority; may owe restitution (liable for the reasonable value of NECESSARIES). MENTAL INCAPACITY: the cognitive test (could not understand the nature and consequences) → voidable; the volitional test (could not act reasonably + the other party knew) → voidable (Restatement). INTOXICATION: so drunk as to not understand + the other party had reason to know → voidable.

ILLEGALITY. Subject matter or purpose illegal → VOID, unenforceable by either party (in pari delicto — equally at fault, the court leaves them where it found them). Two outs: the parties were NOT EQUALLY AT FAULT (the exploited party may recover), or the contract is SEVERABLE — the court enforces the legal portion.

PART 3 — THE PAROL EVIDENCE RULE (THE "WHAT EVIDENCE GETS IN" FILTER). WHAT IT IS. When the parties reduce their agreement to a FINAL WRITTEN form (an integration), the parol evidence rule BARS EVIDENCE OF PRIOR OR CONTEMPORANEOUS AGREEMENTS AND NEGOTIATIONS THAT CONTRADICT THE WRITING.
TWO LEVELS OF INTEGRATION:

TOTAL (COMPLETE) INTEGRATION — the writing was intended as the complete and exclusive statement of the deal: bars BOTH contradictory AND consistent additional terms. A MERGER CLAUSE ("this is the entire agreement") is strong evidence of total integration.
PARTIAL INTEGRATION — final as to the terms it includes, but not complete: bars CONTRADICTORY terms, but CONSISTENT ADDITIONAL TERMS may be shown.
WHAT THE RULE DOES NOT BAR — the MBE's real testing ground:
1. Evidence of FRAUD, DURESS, OR MISTAKE IN FORMATION (attacks on whether a contract was really formed get in — the rule protects contracts, not frauds).
2. Evidence of a CONDITION PRECEDENT to the contract taking effect ("we agreed this wouldn't bind until the loan was approved").

3. Evidence to INTERPRET AMBIGUOUS TERMS. And the modern/UCC approach goes further: COURSE OF PERFORMANCE, COURSE OF DEALING, AND USAGE OF TRADE are admissible to explain terms even without ambiguity (UCC §2-202).
4. A COLLATERAL AGREEMENT supported by SEPARATE CONSIDERATION that would not ordinarily be in the writing.
5. SUBSEQUENT modifications — the rule covers only prior and contemporaneous talk. (And under the UCC, a good-faith modification needs no new consideration — §2-209, from the enrichment file.)

THE SOF–PER PAIRING. The Statute of Frauds keeps the whole contract OUT of court without a writing; the parol evidence rule keeps extrinsic evidence OUT of a final writing. Two "writing" doctrines, opposite directions — the MBE loves testing them together.

THE MEE ANGLE. Enforceability is essay gold. The NCBE point sheets repeatedly test: a Statute of Frauds essay (spot the MYLEGS/§2-201 category, then the exceptions), a defenses essay (the elderly grantor + caregiver = undue influence; the threatened breach = economic duress), and parol evidence essays (merger clause + the oral side-promise). On essays, always list EVERY defense the facts could support before arguing the strongest — the investigator's habit: list every charge before choosing the theory.
PRACTICE — This session's drill questions live in the Drills tab, with full explanations for every answer. Attempt each one there before reading its analysis, then send your letters in chat.

TRANSFER CHALLENGE. A contract dispute is a case file. Before arguing the merits, list every defense the other side could raise — the same habit as listing every charge before choosing the theory. Your question: which MYLEGS category would surprise a Nigerian-trained lawyer the most, and why? (My candidate: the Year rule's "any possible way" test — lifetime employment escapes the Statute entirely — because the instinct is to read "one year" as "about a year.")

THE NEXT SESSION. Session 10 closes out Contracts — PERFORMANCE, BREACH, AND REMEDIES: Hadley v. Baxendale foreseeability, expectation damages, the UCC buyer's cover and market damages, the duty to mitigate, liquidated damages, and specific performance for unique goods and land. After that, Criminal Law begins.

chapters.title: Performance, Breach & Remedies
key_rules: SESSION 10 — CONTRACTS III: PERFORMANCE, BREACH & REMEDIES — the contract is alive: who performs, who breaches, who collects. Phase 1 · Contracts.

THE FRAME. Sessions 7–9 answered: does a contract EXIST (formation), and can it be ENFORCED (enforceability filters)? Today the contract is alive and walking: who must perform first, what counts as breach, and what the winner collects. Three questions in order:
1. PERFORMANCE — what each side must do, and which duties depend on the other side's performance (conditions).
2. BREACH — how bad the failure was (material vs. minor), and what happens when a party repudiates early.

3. REMEDIES — the money: expectation damages, the Hadley foreseeability gate, mitigation, liquidated damages, and the equitable fallback (specific performance). Plus the UCC's formula machinery for goods.

Commonwealth bridge — and the insurance bridge you earned: you know Hadley v. Baxendale. It is English, 1854, and Nigerian courts apply it. The American twist is the UCC's formula damages (cover vs. market), the strict foreseeability + certainty + mitigation gates stacked together, and the MBE's love of testing the REMEDY exceptions — liquidated-vs-penalty, lost-volume seller, substantial performance. Also your insurance years pay off here: every insurance policy is a contract built on CONDITIONS PRECEDENT — notice of claim, proof of loss, cooperation. You already think in conditions; today we name the American rules.

RETRIEVAL WARM-UP — FROM MEMORY, BEFORE YOU READ FURTHER: 1. Recite MYLEGS and one exception. (Marriage, Year, Land, Executor, Suretyship. Exceptions: Year — any possible way to perform within a year is outside; Land — part performance (payment + possession + improvements); Suretyship — main-purpose rule.)

2. State the UCC §2-201 rule and the merchants' confirmatory-memo exception. (Goods ≥$500 unenforceable without a writing signed by the party to be charged stating quantity. Between merchants, a written confirmation binds the receiver unless written objection within 10 days.)

3. Name the three mistake categories and their outcomes. (Mutual — avoidable if basic assumption + material effect + no risk-bearing (Sherwood v. Walker); unilateral — no relief unless the other side knew; conscious ignorance = assumption of risk, no relief.)

4. New terms, defined before any question about them: EXPECTATION DAMAGES = the money that puts the nonbreaching party in the position it would have occupied if the contract had been fully performed (the "benefit of the bargain"). CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES = losses beyond the contract's own value — lost profits, downstream costs — recoverable only if foreseeable at formation. MITIGATION = the rule that the injured party cannot recover for losses it could reasonably have avoided. ANTICIPATORY REPUDIATION = a clear statement or act, before performance is due, that a party will not perform.

SPACED REVIEW — SESSIONS 1–9 IN ONE LINE EACH: S2: Intent = purpose or substantial certainty; transferred intent among battery, assault, false imprisonment, trespass; IIED needs extreme-and-outrageous + severe distress.
S3: Trespass to land = unauthorized entry; conversion = full-value interference; defenses roundup (consent, self-defense — never deadly force for property alone, necessity, shopkeeper's privilege).

S4: Negligence gates — duty (no general duty to rescue a stranger) → breach (reasonable person; negligence per se) → cause in fact (but-for; Summers v. Tice) → proximate cause (Palsgraf foreseeable plaintiff; eggshell rule; superseding acts).
S5: Premises liability — classify the entrant FIRST; NIED (impact / Dillon v. Legg bystander); contributory = total bar (Maryland still has it); pure vs. modified comparative; assumption of risk.

S6: Strict liability skips the breach fight; products — three theories (strict liability, negligence, UCC warranty), three defects (manufacturing = this unit off-design; design = whole line + feasible safer alternative; failure to warn), chain of distribution.

S7: Formation — offer (objective standard; ads = invitations; counteroffer kills the offer); acceptance (mirror-image at common law; §2-207 battle of the forms for goods; mailbox rule); consideration (bargained-for; past consideration/pre-existing duty/illusory fail; §90 safety net).
S8: Classify FIRST, rule SECOND — the worked-example habit. CORRECTION BANKED: a car is UCC goods (§§2-102, 2-105), not common-law territory — governing law is always step zero.

S9: Enforceability — Statute of Frauds (MYLEGS; UCC §2-201 ≥$500 writing + exceptions); defenses roundup (fraud 5 elements + scienter; physical duress = void, economic duress = voidable; undue influence → burden shifts; mutual vs. unilateral mistake; unconscionability procedural + substantive; incapacity; illegality); parol evidence rule (total vs. partial integration; 5 exceptions — formation attacks, condition precedent, interpretation, collateral agreements, subsequent modifications).

PART 1 — PERFORMANCE: THE CONDITIONS MACHINE. A CONDITION is an event — not certain to occur — that must happen before a duty to perform arises (or that cuts off a duty). Conditions are the skeleton of performance order: who must act first, and who is excused.

EXPRESS CONDITIONS — STRICT COMPLIANCE. A condition the parties wrote into the contract ("payment due upon architect's certificate") must be STRICTLY satisfied — no "substantial performance" forgiveness. Your insurance policies worked exactly this way: "no coverage unless the insured gives notice within 60 days" — miss the condition, no duty to pay. Courts enforce the parties' bargain — BUT equity softens it in two places:

PREVENTION/HINDRANCE: a party cannot rely on the non-occurrence of a condition it caused. If the owner blocks the architect from inspecting, the owner cannot then refuse to pay for lack of a certificate.

FORFEITURE-AVOIDANCE (RESTATEMENT §229): a court may EXCUSE a non-material condition to avoid extreme forfeiture — e.g., the certificate requirement is excused where the contractor finished the house perfectly and the only missing piece is a ministerial sign-off. The MBE's favorite: the condition must not be a material part of the agreed exchange.

CONSTRUCTIVE CONDITIONS — SUBSTANTIAL PERFORMANCE. Where the contract doesn't spell out the order, the law implies it: performances due at the same time are CONSTRUCTIVELY CONDITIONED on each other (I hand you the car, you hand me the money). The standard here is forgiving: SUBSTANTIAL PERFORMANCE satisfies a constructive condition — the minor breach rule. A builder who finishes the house with trivial defects (wrong-brand pipe of equal quality — Jacob & Youngs v. Kent) has substantially performed: he may recover the contract price minus the small loss in value, and the owner's duty to pay is NOT excused. Only a MATERIAL breach kills the other side's duty.

TIME IS NOT OF THE ESSENCE — unless the contract says so. Late performance is a MINOR breach (damages for the delay), not a failure of condition. "Time is of the essence" language, or circumstances making timing critical (a wedding-cake delivery, commodities), flips this.

SATISFACTION CLAUSES ("subject to buyer's satisfaction"): if satisfaction turns on COMMERCIAL VALUE OR QUALITY (machinery, construction) → OBJECTIVE reasonable-person standard. If it turns on PERSONAL TASTE OR FANCY (a portrait, a custom suit) → SUBJECTIVE good-faith standard — the buyer must be honestly dissatisfied, not merely inventing a pretext. Employment cases (you may fire "if not satisfied with the work") are usually subjective good faith.

THE PERFORMANCE CHECKLIST FOR THE MBE: (1) Is there an express condition? → strict compliance, unless prevention or forfeiture-excuse. (2) Otherwise → constructive condition → substantial performance suffices. (3) Time → not of the essence unless stated. (4) Satisfaction → objective for commercial, subjective for taste.
PART 2 — BREACH: HOW BAD, AND WHAT HAPPENS NEXT. MATERIAL VS. MINOR — THE RESTATEMENT §241 FACTORS. Courts weigh five things to decide whether a breach is total (material) or partial (minor):
1. How much the injured party is DEPRIVED OF THE BENEFIT it reasonably expected;
2. How ADEQUATELY the injured party can be compensated in damages;
3. How much FORFEITURE the breaching party will suffer;
4. The LIKELIHOOD OF CURE; and
5. Whether the breaching party acted in GOOD FAITH.

Consequences: MINOR BREACH → the injured party must still perform, and sues only for damages (the diminished value). MATERIAL BREACH → the injured party may SUSPEND its own performance AND sue for total breach. The builder who walks off with the roof half-done = material; the builder who used the wrong shade of paint = minor.

ANTICIPATORY REPUDIATION. Before performance is due, a party makes an UNEQUIVOCAL statement or commits an act showing it cannot or will not perform ("I will not deliver the wheat in June"). The other party then has a choice: (a) TREAT IT AS A TOTAL BREACH AND SUE IMMEDIATELY, or (b) WAIT, urging performance — but waiting keeps its own duties alive. A repudiation can be RETRACTED (taken back) any time BEFORE the other party materially changes position or signals acceptance of the repudiation. MBE trap: vague grumbling ("times are tough, delivery may be late") is NOT a repudiation — it must be definite and unequivocal.

ADEQUATE ASSURANCE — UCC §2-609. Where a merchant (or any party with REASONABLE GROUNDS FOR INSECURITY) doubts the other's performance, it may DEMAND ADEQUATE ASSURANCE IN WRITING and SUSPEND its own performance meanwhile. If assurance is not given within a reasonable time (NOT EXCEEDING 30 DAYS), that failure IS a repudiation. This is the commercial cousin of repudiation — and a favorite exam pairing with §2-508 cure.

CURE — UCC §2-508. The seller who tenders nonconforming goods may CURE WITHIN THE CONTRACT TIME. Even AFTER the contract time has expired, the seller gets additional reasonable time if it had REASONABLE GROUNDS TO BELIEVE the tender would be acceptable. Pair with the PERFECT TENDER RULE (§2-601): the buyer may reject goods that "fail in any respect to conform" — but that rejection power is bounded by cure, installment contracts (§2-612: reject an installment only if the nonconformity SUBSTANTIALLY IMPAIRS THAT INSTALLMENT'S VALUE and cannot be cured), and waiver.
PART 3 — REMEDIES: THE MONEY, AND WHEN MONEY ISN'T ENOUGH. THE LADDER OF REMEDIES (memorize the ORDER — essays grade it):
1. EXPECTATION (benefit of the bargain) — always first.
2. CONSEQUENTIAL (foreseeable downstream losses) — gated by Hadley.
3. INCIDENTAL (costs of dealing with the breach: inspection, storage, cover expenses).
4. RELIANCE (out-of-pocket expenses) — the fallback when expectation is too speculative.
5. RESTITUTION (value conferred on the breaching party) — available even to a breaching plaintiff.
6. SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE / INJUNCTION — equity, when money is inadequate.

EXPECTATION DAMAGES — THE FORMULA. Put the plaintiff where full performance would have left it: (VALUE OF PROMISED PERFORMANCE) − (VALUE ACTUALLY RECEIVED) − (COSTS AVOIDED BY NOT HAVING TO PERFORM) + (INCIDENTAL + CONSEQUENTIAL LOSSES). For a breached sale: contract price minus the value of what was delivered. Construction classic: COST OF COMPLETION is the measure — UNLESS completion would be ECONOMIC WASTE (tearing down a finished mansion to replace a functionally identical pipe — Jacob & Youngs), in which case the measure is DIMINUTION IN VALUE.

THE HADLEY GATE — FORESEEABILITY AT FORMATION. Hadley v. Baxendale (1854 — English, and you know it from Nigeria): recoverable damages are those ARISING NATURALLY from the breach (general damages) PLUS those REASONABLY IN THE CONTEMPLATION OF BOTH PARTIES AT THE TIME OF CONTRACTING as the probable result of breach (consequential/special damages). The mill's broken crankshaft: the carrier didn't know the whole mill sat idle without it, so the lost profits were NOT recoverable. The modern American statement (Restatement §351): losses are recoverable if the defendant HAD REASON TO FORESEE THEM AS THE PROBABLE RESULT OF BREACH WHEN THE CONTRACT WAS MADE. Tacit-agreement gloss: the defendant must have implicitly assumed the risk of such losses. The MBE's Hadley trap: foreseeability is judged AT FORMATION, NOT AT BREACH — what the breaching party knew when it signed, not when it failed.

CERTAINTY. Damages must be proved with REASONABLE CERTAINTY — no speculation. The NEW-BUSINESS RULE: the majority view bars lost-profits recovery for a business with no track record; the modern/minority trend allows it if proved with sufficient certainty. The MBE tests the majority rule.

MITIGATION (AVOIDABLE CONSEQUENCES). The injured party CANNOT RECOVER FOR LOSSES IT COULD REASONABLY HAVE AVOIDED — but its reasonable EXPENSES OF MITIGATION are recoverable as incidental damages. The wrongfully discharged employee must seek COMPARABLE employment (not any job). Landlord: the traditional rule imposed no duty to re-let; the MODERN TREND (most states, and the MBE's direction) requires REASONABLE EFFORTS TO MITIGATE. Failure to mitigate doesn't bar the suit — it just shrinks the recovery.

LIQUIDATED DAMAGES VS. PENALTY. A clause fixing damages in advance is enforceable IF, AT FORMATION: (1) actual damages were DIFFICULT TO ESTIMATE, and (2) the amount was a REASONABLE FORECAST of probable loss (Restatement §356; UCC §2-718). A term fixing UNREASONABLY LARGE liquidated damages is VOID AS A PENALTY — courts strike the clause and award actual damages instead. UCC §2-718 adds: reasonable in light of anticipated OR actual harm. MBE trap: judge reasonableness AT FORMATION, not with hindsight — and a clause that punishes rather than compensates is a penalty.

RELIANCE AND RESTITUTION. RELIANCE puts the plaintiff in its PRE-CONTRACT position — out-of-pocket expenses incurred in reliance on the contract; used when expectation damages are too speculative to prove. RESTITUTION restores the VALUE CONFERRED on the defendant — and here's the twist: even a BREACHING plaintiff may recover in restitution for benefits conferred, minus the damages its breach caused (Restatement §374).

SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE — EQUITY'S REMEDY. Available when: (1) a valid enforceable contract exists; (2) the plaintiff's conditions are satisfied; (3) the legal remedy is INADEQUATE — the subject matter is UNIQUE (land is ALWAYS unique; rare goods, heirlooms, one-of-a-kind items); (4) enforcement is FEASIBLE; and (5) no equitable defenses apply: UNCLEAN HANDS, LACHES (unreasonable delay), UNCONSCIONABILITY, or undue HARDSHIP. Courts will NOT specifically enforce PERSONAL-SERVICE CONTRACTS (a singer cannot be ordered to sing — 13th Amendment involuntary-servitude wall) — but they WILL grant a NEGATIVE INJUNCTION restraining the performer from working for a competitor (Lumley v. Wagner). INJUNCTIONS more broadly require: irreparable harm, inadequacy of legal remedy, balance of hardships, and (for preliminary relief) likelihood of success.
THE UCC FORMULA MACHINERY — GOODS. This is the American twist on everything above:

BUYER'S REMEDIES: §2-711 (cancel, recover price paid) → §2-712 COVER: buyer covers in GOOD FAITH AND WITHOUT UNREASONABLE DELAY → damages = (COVER PRICE − CONTRACT PRICE) + INCIDENTAL + CONSEQUENTIAL. §2-713 MARKET (buyer does NOT cover): (MARKET PRICE AT THE TIME/PLACE THE BUYER LEARNED OF BREACH − CONTRACT PRICE) + INCIDENTAL + CONSEQUENTIAL. §2-714: breach of warranty on ACCEPTED goods = (value as warranted − value as accepted) at time/place of acceptance. §2-715: INCIDENTAL (inspection, transportation, care, cover costs) + CONSEQUENTIAL — but consequential requires the seller had REASON TO KNOW of the buyer's particular needs AT FORMATION (Hadley for goods).

SELLER'S REMEDIES: §2-706 RESALE: (contract price − resale price) + incidental − expenses saved; resale must be in GOOD FAITH AND COMMERCIALLY REASONABLE. §2-708(1) CONTRACT-MARKET: (contract price − market price at time/place of tender). §2-708(2) LOST PROFITS: where 708(1) is INADEQUATE — the LOST-VOLUME SELLER (a dealer who would have made BOTH sales) recovers LOST PROFIT (contract price − costs saved). §2-709 ACTION FOR THE PRICE: buyer accepted the goods, or goods were lost/destroyed after risk passed, or goods are identified and the seller cannot resell. §2-710: incidental damages.

MEE ESSAY ANGLE. Remedies essays are checklist essays: state the ladder, apply expectation first, gate consequential through Hadley (foreseeable at formation?), check mitigation and certainty, then address any liquidated-damages clause, then ask whether specific performance is available (unique subject matter? personal services?). The examiner rewards the ORDER of analysis.
