chapters.title: Actus Reus & Mens Rea: The Building Blocks
key_rules: SESSION 11 — CRIMINAL LAW I: ACTUS REUS & MENS REA — the guilty act and the guilty mind. Phase 1 · Criminal Law.
THE FRAME. A crime is a prohibited act joined to a prohibited mind. Every crime the exam tests breaks into the same four questions, in order:
1. ACTUS REUS — was there a voluntary guilty act (or a guilty omission where a duty existed)?
2. MENS REA — what guilty mind does the crime require, and did the defendant have it?
3. CONCURRENCE — did the mind and the act coincide in time?
4. CAUSATION — for result crimes (homicide, arson), did the act cause the result?
Miss any one of the four and there is no crime. The examiner's favorite game is hiding which of the four fails.

Commonwealth bridge — and your twenty years carry you here: you know the Nigerian Criminal Code's Section 24 — "a person is not criminally responsible for an act or omission which occurs independently of the exercise of his will." That is actus reus voluntariness, and you have lived it. The American twists are three: the Model Penal Code's precise four-rung ladder of mental states (purpose, knowledge, recklessness, negligence) — recklessness-vs-negligence is the single most-tested boundary; the exam's habit of making you choose between the common-law rule and the MPC rule on the same facts; and mala in se vs. mala prohibita, which you know from police work as "real crime" vs. "regulatory offence." You know this; here is the US twist.
RETRIEVAL WARM-UP — FROM MEMORY, BEFORE YOU READ FURTHER: 1. State the Hadley gate in one sentence. (Consequential damages recoverable only if reasonably foreseeable to both parties AT FORMATION.)

2. UCC §2-712 vs. §2-713 — when does each apply? (§2-712 cover: buyer actually covered in good faith without unreasonable delay → cover − K. §2-713 market: buyer did NOT cover → market-at-learned-of-breach − K.)

3. Liquidated damages vs. penalty — the test and when it is judged. (Enforceable if, AT FORMATION, damages were difficult to estimate and the amount was a reasonable forecast; unreasonably large = void penalty.)

4. New terms, defined before any question about them: ACTUS REUS = the guilty act — the voluntary physical conduct (or duty-based omission) the statute punishes. MENS REA = the guilty mind — the mental state the statute requires. CONCURRENCE = the requirement that the guilty mind and guilty act coincide in time. MODEL PENAL CODE (MPC) = the American Law Institute's 1962 model criminal code — roughly half the states adopted it in whole or in part, and the bar exam tests its rules alongside the common-law rules. MALA IN SE = wrong in itself (murder, theft). MALA PROHIBITA = wrong only because prohibited (regulatory offences like unlicensed driving).

SPACED REVIEW — SESSIONS 1–10 IN ONE LINE EACH: S2: Intent = purpose or substantial certainty; transferred intent among battery, assault, false imprisonment, trespass; IIED needs extreme-and-outrageous + severe distress.
S3: Trespass to land = unauthorized entry; conversion = full-value interference; defenses roundup (consent, self-defense — never deadly force for property alone, necessity, shopkeeper's privilege).

S4: Negligence gates — duty (no general duty to rescue a stranger) → breach (reasonable person; negligence per se) → cause in fact (but-for; Summers v. Tice) → proximate cause (Palsgraf foreseeable plaintiff; eggshell rule; superseding acts).
S5: Premises liability — classify the entrant FIRST; NIED (impact / Dillon v. Legg bystander); contributory = total bar (Maryland still has it); pure vs. modified comparative; assumption of risk.
S6: Strict liability skips the breach fight; products — three theories, three defects (manufacturing/design/failure-to-warn), chain of distribution.

S7: Formation — offer (objective standard; ads = invitations; counteroffer kills the offer); acceptance (mirror-image at common law; mailbox rule); consideration (bargained-for; past consideration/pre-existing duty/illusory fail; §90 safety net).
S8: Classify FIRST, rule SECOND. CORRECTION BANKED: a car is UCC goods (§§2-102, 2-105), not common-law territory — governing law is always step zero.

S9: Enforceability — Statute of Frauds (MYLEGS; UCC §2-201 ≥$500 writing + exceptions); defenses roundup (fraud 5 elements; physical duress = void, economic = voidable; undue influence → burden shifts; mutual vs. unilateral mistake; unconscionability; incapacity; illegality); parol evidence rule (total vs. partial integration; 5 exceptions). Both weak boundaries (one-year finish-vs-end; parol-evidence formation-attack vs. term-adding) now solid — 4/4 on reinforcement.

S10: Performance — express conditions = strict compliance (§229 forfeiture excuse; prevention); constructive = substantial performance; material vs. minor via §241; anticipatory repudiation + retraction; UCC §2-609 assurance / §2-508 cure. Remedies ladder: expectation → Hadley gate at formation → mitigation → liquidated-vs-penalty → specific performance (unique subject, never personal services); UCC cover/market/resale/lost-volume machinery.

PART 1 — HOW AMERICAN LAW CLASSIFIES CRIMES. FELONY VS. MISDEMEANOR VS. INFRACTION. The line is the punishment: a FELONY is punishable by death or imprisonment EXCEEDING ONE YEAR (served in state prison/penitentiary); a MISDEMEANOR carries ONE YEAR OR LESS (usually county jail); an INFRACTION (or violation) carries NO JAIL AT ALL — FINE ONLY (traffic tickets). On the exam, "felony" is a trigger word — felony murder, burglary ("breaking and entering with intent to commit a felony therein"), and accomplice rules all key off it.

COMMON-LAW CRIMES VS. STATUTORY CRIMES. Nearly all American criminal law today is STATUTORY — written codes, not judge-made law. The old common-law labels (murder, larceny, burglary, arson) survive, but as statutory definitions. If a statute doesn't prohibit it, it isn't a crime — no matter how wrongful.

MALA IN SE VS. MALA PROHIBITA. Mala in se — wrong in itself (murder, rape, theft): the moral wrong is obvious. Mala prohibita — wrong only because the law prohibits it (unlicensed driving, selling alcohol after hours): regulatory offences. This distinction drives the strict-liability analysis in Part 4 — strict liability lives almost entirely in the mala prohibita regulatory world.

THE MODEL PENAL CODE. The MPC is the American Law Institute's 1962 model criminal code. Roughly half the states adopted it in whole or in part. The bar exam tests BOTH the common-law rule AND the MPC rule — and its favorite move is a question where they differ. The words "under the Model Penal Code" are your signal to switch rulebooks.

PART 2 — ACTUS REUS: THE VOLUNTARY ACT. THE ACT MUST BE VOLUNTARY. Martin v. State: police found a drunk man in his home, dragged him onto the public street, and arrested him for public drunkenness. Conviction reversed — "being in public while drunk" was not HIS voluntary act; the police put him there. Unconscious conduct never counts: reflexes, convulsions and seizures, sleepwalking, a hypoglycemic episode. Note the trap: VOLUNTARY INTOXICATION DOES NOT MAKE THE ACT INVOLUNTARY — choosing to drink was voluntary. But the actus reus element itself — the conduct the statute punishes — must be voluntary bodily movement.
OMISSIONS: GUILTY ONLY WITH A LEGAL DUTY. A failure to act is an actus reus ONLY if the defendant had a LEGAL duty to act. The five duty sources — memorize them:
1. STATUTE — failure to file taxes, hit-and-run reporting duties.
2. STATUS RELATIONSHIP — parent–child, spouse–spouse.
3. CONTRACT — lifeguard, babysitter, nurse.
4. VOLUNTARY ASSUMPTION / UNDERTAKING — you begin a rescue; you may not abandon it and leave the victim worse off.
5. CREATION OF THE PERIL — you knock someone into the river, even accidentally; you now have a duty to at least attempt rescue or call for help.
The MBE's favorite omission trap is the same as Torts Session 4's nonfeasance rule: NO GENERAL DUTY TO RESCUE A STRANGER. Moral duty is not legal duty.

STATUS CRIMES ARE UNCONSTITUTIONAL. Robinson v. California: California made it a crime to "be addicted to the use of narcotics." Struck down — cruel and unusual punishment (8th Amendment). You may punish the ACT (possessing, using, selling), never the STATUS of being an addict, being homeless, being poor. Powell v. Texas draws the line: appearing drunk IN PUBLIC is conduct — punishable.

POSSESSION COUNTS — THOUGHTS DON'T. Knowing possession (knowledge + control, including constructive and joint possession) satisfies actus reus. Pure thoughts never do — but CONSPIRACY punishes the agreement (the agreement is the act) and ATTEMPT punishes the substantial step. MPC §2.01 states the floor: voluntary bodily movement is required; possession is an act only if the possessor KNOWINGLY PROCURED OR RECEIVED the thing, or was AWARE OF HIS CONTROL of it long enough to have terminated it.

PART 3 — MENS REA: THE FOUR-RUNG LADDER. THE COMMON-LAW BUCKETS. (1) SPECIFIC INTENT — intent to bring about the specific result: first-degree premeditated murder, burglary, attempt, larceny. (2) MALICE — reckless disregard, the "abandoned and malignant heart": second-degree murder, arson. (3) GENERAL INTENT — awareness of doing the act itself: battery, rape. (4) STRICT LIABILITY — no mental state required at all.
THE MPC LADDER (§2.02) — MEMORIZE TOP TO BOTTOM:
PURPOSE — it is his CONSCIOUS OBJECT to cause the result. "That is exactly what I wanted."
KNOWLEDGE — he is AWARE IT IS PRACTICALLY CERTAIN his conduct will cause the result. Lighting a match in a hay-filled barn: he doesn't desire the fire, but he knows it is practically certain.

RECKLESSNESS — he CONSCIOUSLY DISREGARDS A SUBSTANTIAL AND UNJUSTIFIABLE RISK — a gross deviation from the law-abiding person's standard. SUBJECTIVE: he must have perceived the risk and brushed it aside.
NEGLIGENCE — he SHOULD HAVE BEEN AWARE of a substantial and unjustifiable risk — a gross deviation. OBJECTIVE: he didn't see it, but a reasonable person would have.

THE RECKLESSNESS–NEGLIGENCE LINE IS THE SINGLE MOST-TESTED BOUNDARY IN CRIMINAL LAW. Both require a gross deviation — ordinary carelessness is neither. The difference is purely subjective: recklessness = he SAW the risk and disregarded it; negligence = he never saw it but SHOULD have. Drill 2 below lives exactly on this line.

THE SILENCE RULE. Where the statute prescribes NO mental state, the MPC reads in AT LEAST RECKLESSNESS (§2.02(3)). This is the American presumption against strict liability — Morissette v. United States: for crimes derived from the common law, courts presume the legislature meant to require some mens rea; Congress doesn't create serious strict-liability crimes by accident.

TRANSFERRED INTENT — THE TORTS BRIDGE. You know this from Session 2: aim at A, kill B — the intent transfers, and the defendant is guilty of murder OF B. The MPC doesn't use the label but reaches the same result through its causation rules (§2.03).

CONCURRENCE — MIND AND ACT MUST COINCIDE. Thabo Meli v. Regina (Privy Council, 1954): men beat the victim, believed him dead, then rolled the "body" off a cliff — the fall actually killed him. Murder — the whole sequence was ONE CONTINUING TRANSACTION, so intent and the fatal act concurred. The MBE's concurrence trap: D decides to kill V, aims, the gun jams; D abandons the plan; an hour later, driving home with no intent at all, D accidentally runs V over. No murder — at the fatal act there was no guilty mind. (Most exam hypos are saved by the continuing-transaction idea; the trap hypos deliberately break the sequence.)

THE MENS REA CHECKLIST: (1) voluntary act or duty-based omission? (2) What mental state does the statute require — pick the rung (MPC) or bucket (common law)? (3) Did mind and act coincide? (4) Result crime → causation (Part 5).
PART 4 — MISTAKE, AND STRICT LIABILITY. MISTAKE OF FACT — THE RULE CHANGES WITH THE CRIME'S MENTAL STATE:
SPECIFIC-INTENT CRIMES: ANY honest mistake defeats — even an unreasonable one. (Taking a coat he honestly believed was his = no larceny, because larceny needs intent to steal.)
MALICE / GENERAL-INTENT CRIMES: the mistake must be honest AND REASONABLE.
STRICT-LIABILITY CRIMES: mistake is NEVER a defense — not even a reasonable one. Drill 4 tests exactly this.
MISTAKE/IGNORANCE OF LAW — GENERALLY NO DEFENSE. "Everyone is presumed to know the law." Three narrow exceptions the exam loves:

1. LAMBERT V. CALIFORNIA — due process requires fair notice where the conduct is WHOLLY PASSIVE and the defendant had NO NOTICE of the duty (a felon who failed to register in Los Angeles — conviction reversed).
2. REASONABLE RELIANCE ON AN OFFICIAL STATEMENT OF LAW later held invalid (MPC §2.04(3)(b)) — e.g., an attorney general's opinion you followed in good faith.

3. MISTAKE OF LAW THAT NEGATES A REQUIRED SPECIFIC INTENT — "willfulness" crimes like tax evasion (Cheek v. United States): an honest belief you owed no tax, even if unreasonable, defeats willfulness.

STRICT LIABILITY — THE REGULATORY CORNER. Strict-liability crimes punish without any mens rea: selling alcohol to minors, statutory rape AS TO THE VICTIM'S AGE, adulterated food. Morissette sets the boundary: courts read mens rea into serious, common-law-derived crimes; strict liability is tolerated for minor PUBLIC-WELFARE / REGULATORY offences — the mala prohibita world. The MPC confines it further: strict liability is allowed only for "VIOLATIONS" — offences carrying NO IMPRISONMENT (§2.05). Exam habit: if the punishment is serious jail time and the crime is mala in se, strict liability is almost certainly NOT the answer.

PART 5 — CAUSATION (RESULT CRIMES). ACTUAL CAUSE — THE BUT-FOR TEST. "But for the defendant's act, would the result have occurred?" Where two acts are each independently sufficient (two hunters' bullets, two fires), use the SUBSTANTIAL-FACTOR test — your Torts Session 4 bridge (Summers v. Tice).
PROXIMATE CAUSE — FORESEEABILITY, AND THE INTERVENING-ACT ANALYSIS. After but-for, ask: was there an INTERVENING ACT, and what kind?
RESPONSIVE INTERVENERS — the victim flees and is struck by a car; doctors treat the wound negligently; a rescuer acts clumsily. The chain SURVIVES unless the response is GROSSLY ABNORMAL.
COINCIDENTAL INTERVENERS — unrelated events: lightning strikes the victim in the hospital; an unrelated second attacker appears. These BREAK the chain if unforeseeable.
The MPC version (§2.03): no liability where the actual result is TOO REMOTE OR ACCIDENTAL IN ITS OCCURRENCE — too different from what was intended or risked — to have a just bearing on culpability.

THE YEAR-AND-A-DAY RULE IS DEAD. The common law barred homicide prosecution if the victim died more than a year and a day after the act. ABOLISHED IN MOST STATES — the MBE mentions it only to test that it's gone.
THE CAUSATION CHECKLIST: (1) but-for (or substantial factor)? (2) Intervening act? (3) Responsive → chain survives (unless grossly abnormal); coincidental → chain breaks if unforeseeable.

MEE ESSAY ANGLE. Criminal-law essays are ELEMENTS ESSAYS: list each element — actus reus, mens rea, concurrence, causation — apply each to the facts, state the common-law AND MPC rule wherever they differ, and conclude. Graders reward the element checklist and the explicit rule-switch ("At common law…; under the MPC…").
PRACTICE — This session's drill questions live in the Drills tab, with full explanations for every answer. Attempt each one there before reading its analysis, then send your letters in chat.

chapters.title: Homicide: Murder, Manslaughter & the Malice Ladder
key_rules: SESSION 12 — CRIMINAL LAW II: HOMICIDE — the malice ladder: who died, and with what mind. Phase 1 · Criminal Law.

THE FRAME. Session 11 gave you the four-element frame (actus reus → mens rea → concurrence → causation). Homicide is where that frame gets its hardest workout — because the actus reus is identical in every case (a human being died), and the entire legal outcome turns on the mens rea. Murder, manslaughter, negligent homicide: same dead body, different mind.
Climb the ladder from the top:
FIRST-DEGREE MURDER — killing with premeditated intent to kill.
SECOND-DEGREE MURDER — killing with malice aforethought but no premeditation.
VOLUNTARY MANSLAUGHTER — intentional killing in heat of passion upon adequate provocation.
INVOLUNTARY MANSLAUGHTER — unintentional killing by criminal negligence, or during a misdemeanor.
(MPC adds: negligent homicide — death by ordinary negligence.)
Everything below is about drawing these lines. The examiner's favorite game: two fact patterns that look identical, separated by one mental state.

Commonwealth bridge — you have enforced this vocabulary before: the Nigerian Criminal Code you worked under uses the same phrase, MALICE AFORETHOUGHT, and the same doctrine that adequate provocation reduces murder to manslaughter. You know the shape of this ladder. The US twists are three: (1) the common-law exam splits murder into first and second degree around PREMEDITATION, and the exam loves testing that premeditation can form in an instant; (2) the FELONY-MURDER RULE has sharper limits than most Nigerian-trained lawyers expect — the merger doctrine in particular; and (3) the MPC rewrites the whole ladder with its own names, and "under the Model Penal Code" is your signal to switch rulebooks.

NEW TERMS, DEFINED BEFORE ANY QUESTION ABOUT THEM: HOMICIDE — the killing of a human being by another human being. Only unlawful homicide is criminal; justifiable homicide (lawful self-defense, execution of a lawful sentence) is not a crime at all.

MALICE AFORETHOUGHT — the mental state that makes a killing murder. A term of art: it does NOT mean "planned in advance." It means the defendant acted with (1) INTENT TO KILL, (2) INTENT TO INFLICT SERIOUS BODILY INJURY, (3) DEPRAVED HEART (EXTREME RECKLESSNESS), OR (4) DURING A FELONY (FELONY MURDER). Memorize all four.
PREMEDITATION — thinking about the killing beforehand; required, with deliberation, for first-degree murder. It can be formed in moments — no lengthy planning needed.
DEPRAVED HEART — an act of extreme recklessness creating a very high risk of death, done with extreme indifference to human life ("abandoned and malignant heart").
FELONY MURDER — a killing committed during an inherently dangerous felony; malice is implied from the felony itself.
HEAT OF PASSION — the sudden intense emotional state (rage, terror) that, when caused by adequate provocation with no cooling time, reduces murder to voluntary manslaughter.
EMED — the MPC's broader version: extreme mental or emotional disturbance with a reasonable explanation, viewed from the defendant's situation.
RETRIEVAL WARM-UP — FROM MEMORY, BEFORE YOU READ FURTHER: 1. State the four elements of a crime, in order. (Actus reus → mens rea → concurrence → causation. Miss one, no crime.)

2. Recite the MPC mens rea ladder top-down, with the one-word essence of each. (Purpose = conscious object; knowledge = practically certain; recklessness = conscious disregard — SUBJECTIVE; negligence = should have known — OBJECTIVE.)
3. Name the five sources of a legal duty to act (omission actus reus). (Statute; status relationship; contract; voluntary undertaking; creation of the peril.)
4. Mistake of fact — state the rule for each bucket. (Specific intent: any honest mistake; malice/general intent: honest + reasonable; strict liability: never a defense.)

SPACED REVIEW — SESSIONS 1–11 IN ONE LINE EACH: S2: Intent = purpose or substantial certainty; transferred intent among battery, assault, false imprisonment, trespass; IIED needs extreme-and-outrageous + severe distress.
S3: Trespass to land = unauthorized entry; conversion = full-value interference; defenses roundup (consent, self-defense — never deadly force for property alone, necessity, shopkeeper's privilege).

S4: Negligence gates — duty (no general duty to rescue a stranger) → breach (reasonable person; negligence per se) → cause in fact (but-for; Summers v. Tice) → proximate cause (Palsgraf foreseeable plaintiff; eggshell rule; superseding acts).
S5: Premises liability — classify the entrant FIRST; NIED (impact / Dillon v. Legg bystander); contributory = total bar (Maryland still has it); pure vs. modified comparative; assumption of risk.
S6: Strict liability skips the breach fight; products — three theories, three defects (manufacturing/design/failure-to-warn), chain of distribution.

S7: Formation — offer (objective standard; ads = invitations; counteroffer kills the offer); acceptance (mirror-image at common law; mailbox rule); consideration (bargained-for; past consideration/pre-existing duty/illusory fail; §90 safety net).
S8: Classify FIRST, rule SECOND. CORRECTION BANKED: a car is UCC goods, not common-law territory — governing law is always step zero.

S9: Enforceability — Statute of Frauds (MYLEGS; UCC §2-201 ≥$500 writing + exceptions); defenses roundup; parol evidence rule (total vs. partial integration; 5 exceptions). Both weak boundaries solid — 4/4 on reinforcement.

S10: Performance — express conditions = strict compliance (§229 forfeiture excuse; prevention); constructive = substantial performance; §241 material-vs-minor; anticipatory repudiation + retraction; UCC §2-609 assurance / §2-508 cure. Remedies ladder: expectation → Hadley gate at formation → mitigation → liquidated-vs-penalty → specific performance (never personal services); UCC cover/market/resale/lost-volume machinery.

S11: Four-element crime frame; actus reus voluntariness (Martin v. State); omissions need one of five duty sources; status crimes unconstitutional (Robinson); MPC ladder purpose/knowledge/recklessness(SUBJECTIVE)/negligence(OBJECTIVE); mistake-of-fact buckets; strict liability = regulatory mala prohibita only; causation but-for + too-remote (MPC §2.03).
PART 1 — MURDER = KILLING + MALICE AFORETHOUGHT. THE FORMULA. Common-law murder = THE UNLAWFUL KILLING OF A HUMAN BEING WITH MALICE AFORETHOUGHT. Break it open:
UNLAWFUL KILLING — not justified (lawful self-defense, war, execution) and not excused. Actus reus + causation from Session 11 do this work.

OF A HUMAN BEING — at common law, the victim must have been BORN ALIVE. A fetus is not a "human being" at common law (modern statutes create separate feticide offenses; the MPC defines human being as born and alive — §210.0).
WITH MALICE AFORETHOUGHT — the mental state, and here is the part that fails students: "malice aforethought" is a TERM OF ART meaning any one of four mental states:
1. INTENT TO KILL (express malice) — "I meant for him to die."
2. INTENT TO INFLICT SERIOUS BODILY INJURY (implied malice) — "I didn't mean to kill him, but I meant to hurt him badly." The death that follows a meant beating is murder.
3. DEPRAVED HEART — extreme recklessness manifesting extreme indifference to human life (Part 3).
4. FELONY MURDER — killing during an inherently dangerous felony (Part 4).

Any ONE of the four = malice aforethought = murder. The word "aforethought" does not mean the defendant thought about it beforehand — that is PREMEDITATION, a separate concept that divides first from second degree.
DEGREES OF MURDER. Most American jurisdictions grade murder:

FIRST-DEGREE MURDER = a killing that is DELIBERATE AND PREMEDITATED, plus (in most statutes) felony murder. DELIBERATE = the defendant weighed it — considered the pros and cons, however briefly. PREMEDITATED = thought about it beforehand — and the exam's golden trap: PREMEDITATION CAN BE FORMED IN AN INSTANT. There is no minimum thinking time. A defendant who, mid-argument, decides "I'm going to kill him," reaches for a weapon, and fires, has premeditated — seconds are enough. What defeats premeditation is not speed but heat of passion (Part 5).

SECOND-DEGREE MURDER = every other murder — all malice killings without premeditation and deliberation. Intent to kill formed in the moment but acted on with cool reflection absent? That is the first/second boundary the exam probes.
THE TWO-STEP CLASSIFICATION METHOD (USE ON EVERY HOMICIDE QUESTION):
1. Is it murder at all? — check malice aforethought (the four routes). If none of the four fits, it is manslaughter or no crime.
2. If murder, which degree? — deliberate + premeditated = first; everything else = second.

PART 2 — DEPRAVED HEART: MURDER WITHOUT MEANING IT. THE RULE. An unintentional killing is still MURDER — second degree — when the defendant acted with EXTREME RECKLESSNESS MANIFESTING EXTREME INDIFFERENCE TO THE VALUE OF HUMAN LIFE: the "abandoned and malignant heart." The act must create a VERY HIGH RISK OF DEATH OR SERIOUS BODILY INJURY — not just an unreasonable risk (that would be negligence), but a risk so grave that the conduct shows the defendant simply did not care whether someone died.

CLASSIC EXAMPLES: firing a gun into an occupied house or a crowd; driving a car onto a crowded sidewalk; throwing a heavy rock off an overpass into traffic; playing Russian roulette with another person.

WHERE IT PLUGS INTO SESSION 11. This is the MPC ladder's RECKLESSNESS rung pushed to its extreme. Remember the line: recklessness is SUBJECTIVE — the defendant must have consciously disregarded the risk. Depraved heart = conscious disregard of a very high risk of death. Contrast:
DEPRAVED HEART (extreme recklessness) → second-degree murder.
ORDINARY RECKLESSNESS causing death → involuntary manslaughter (common law).
CRIMINAL NEGLIGENCE (gross deviation, objective) causing death → involuntary manslaughter.
ORDINARY NEGLIGENCE causing death → tort liability, and under the MPC, negligent homicide (a misdemeanor) — but at common law, no crime at all.
That four-way split is one of the most-tested distinctions on the MBE. Drill it until it is reflex.

PART 3 — FELONY MURDER: THE STRICT-LIABILITY MURDER. THE RULE. A killing committed DURING THE COMMISSION (OR ATTEMPTED COMMISSION) OF AN INHERENTLY DANGEROUS FELONY is murder — and the prosecution need not prove any intent to kill. The malice is implied from the felony itself. The accidental discharge during an armed robbery that kills the clerk = murder, even though the robber never meant to fire.
THE LIMITS — THE EXAM TESTS THE LIMITS, NOT THE RULE. Five of them; memorize:

1. INHERENTLY DANGEROUS FELONY. The classic list: burglary, arson, rape, robbery, kidnapping. Some jurisdictions add a statutory list; others ask whether the felony was dangerous as committed. A non-dangerous felony (e.g., forgery) generally cannot support felony murder.

2. MERGER DOCTRINE (THE BIG ONE). The underlying felony must be INDEPENDENT OF THE KILLING ITSELF. You cannot bootstrap the very assault that caused the death into a felony and then call the death felony murder — the assault merges into the homicide. So: beating a victim to death during an aggravated assault = NOT felony murder. It is still SECOND-DEGREE MURDER — via malice route #2 (intent to inflict serious bodily injury). The merger doctrine kills the felony-murder theory, not the homicide charge. But armed robbery of a store where the clerk is shot = felony murder stands, because robbery is independent of the assault on the clerk.

3. AGENCY THEORY (MAJORITY RULE). Only deaths CAUSED BY THE FELON OR HIS AGENT count. If, during the robbery, the store guard or a police officer shoots back and kills a bystander — or kills one of the robbers — that is NOT felony murder (People v. Redline logic: the killing was by someone resisting the felony, not by a felon). A minority of jurisdictions extend felony murder to any foreseeable death during the felony, even caused by resisters — but majority = agency, and the exam defaults to majority unless told otherwise.

4. RES GESTAE — "IN THE COURSE OF." The killing must occur during the felony's natural scope: attempt, commission, and IMMEDIATE FLIGHT. The flight continues until the felon reaches a POINT OF TEMPORARY SAFETY. A killing during the getaway chase = felony murder. A killing the next day, after the felon is home safe, = separate homicide, not felony murder.
5. FORESEEABLE MANNER OF DEATH. The death must be a foreseeable consequence of the felony. A bizarre, freakish causal chain can break felony murder just as it breaks proximate cause.

THE MPC VERSION (§210.2). The MPC has NO INDEPENDENT FELONY-MURDER RULE. Instead, committing (or attempting) robbery, rape, arson, burglary, kidnapping, or felonious escape creates a REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION of recklessness manifesting extreme indifference — i.e., the MPC reaches the same result (murder) but through the depraved-heart route, and the defendant can rebut it. When the question says "under the Model Penal Code," reason it through §210.2, not through common-law felony murder.

PART 4 — VOLUNTARY MANSLAUGHTER: MURDER, MINUS THE MALICE, BECAUSE OF PROVOCATION. THE RULE. An INTENTIONAL KILLING committed in HEAT OF PASSION UPON ADEQUATE PROVOCATION is VOLUNTARY MANSLAUGHTER, not murder. The provocation negates malice — the defendant still meant to kill, but the law treats the inflamed mind as less culpable. Think of it as murder with a partial defense built in.
THE FOUR ELEMENTS (COMMON LAW) — MEMORIZE:

1. ADEQUATE PROVOCATION — the provocation must be such as would arouse SUDDEN AND INTENSE PASSION IN A REASONABLE PERSON. The classic adequate provocations: catching one's spouse in the act of adultery; a violent assault or battery on the defendant; witnessing a violent attack on a close relative. MERE WORDS, HOWEVER INSULTING, ARE NOT ADEQUATE PROVOCATION (majority rule) — insults do not reduce murder to manslaughter. (A minority treats informational words — e.g., being told of the adultery — as adequate; know the majority rule for the MBE.)
2. ACTUAL SUBJECTIVE PASSION — the defendant must actually have been in the heat of passion. A cold, calculated revenge killing after provocation = murder.

3. NO COOLING TIME — the killing must follow the provocation before a reasonable person would have cooled. This is judged OBJECTIVELY. Hours of brooding, leaving the scene and returning with a weapon = cooling time = murder. Seconds or minutes of continued rage = manslaughter.
4. CAUSAL CONNECTION — the provocation must have caused the passion that caused the killing.
TWO FINE POINTS THE EXAM LOVES:

MISDIRECTED RETALIATION: the enraged defendant aims at the provocateur but kills a bystander. Still voluntary manslaughter — transferred intent (Session 2) carries the mitigated mental state along with it.

BURDEN AND PLEADING: the prosecution proves murder; the defendant raises provocation as mitigation. And note the asymmetry — provocation mitigates intentional killing to manslaughter, but it does NOT help a defendant whose conduct was depraved-heart or felony murder.

THE MPC VERSION (§210.3) — EMED. A homicide that would be murder is manslaughter when committed UNDER THE INFLUENCE OF EXTREME MENTAL OR EMOTIONAL DISTURBANCE FOR WHICH THERE IS A REASONABLE EXPLANATION OR EXCUSE, judged from the viewpoint of a person in the defendant's situation. This is BROADER than common law: no rigid cooling-time requirement, and the "situation" includes the defendant's personal characteristics as the jury sees them. Classic exam use: the battered spouse who kills after years of abuse — no adequate common-law provocation, no heat of the moment, but a strong EMED argument.
PART 5 — INVOLUNTARY MANSLAUGHTER: THE UNINTENTIONAL KILLINGS. TWO ROUTES, BOTH UNINTENTIONAL:

1. CRIMINAL NEGLIGENCE — death caused by GROSS negligence: a gross deviation from the standard of care, more than ordinary tort negligence. The drunk driver who kills a pedestrian; the parent who leaves a loaded gun where a toddler reaches it. (Ordinary civil negligence causing death = no crime at common law; under the MPC = negligent homicide, a misdemeanor — §210.4.)

2. MISDEMEANOR MANSLAUGHTER (UNLAWFUL-ACT DOCTRINE) — death caused during the commission of a MISDEMEANOR OR NON-DANGEROUS FELONY. The mirror image of felony murder, one rung down: dangerous felony + death = murder; misdemeanor + death = involuntary manslaughter. Merger applies here too — the misdemeanor must be independent of the killing (a simple assault that kills is not "misdemeanor manslaughter" via merger; it is analyzed under criminal negligence instead).
THE RECKLESSNESS LINE, ONE MORE TIME — because the MBE will make you draw it under pressure:
Extreme recklessness (depraved heart) + death = SECOND-DEGREE MURDER
Ordinary recklessness + death = INVOLUNTARY MANSLAUGHTER (common law) / MANSLAUGHTER (MPC §210.3(1)(a))
Criminal (gross) negligence + death = INVOLUNTARY MANSLAUGHTER
Ordinary negligence + death = NO CRIME (common law) / NEGLIGENT HOMICIDE (MPC §210.4)
PART 6 — CAUSATION IN DEATH CASES: THE TRAPS. Session 11 built causation (but-for + proximate; responsive vs. coincidental interveners; MPC §2.03 "too remote"). In homicide the traps are:
SUBSEQUENT MEDICAL NEGLIGENCE IS FORESEEABLE — the victim shot, then dies from a botched surgery: the shooter still caused the death (responsive intervener).

THE VICTIM'S OWN CONDUCT RARELY BREAKS THE CHAIN — refusing medical treatment on religious grounds, or a pre-existing condition (eggshell-skull in criminal dress: the victim's thin skull does not save the defendant).

YEAR-AND-A-DAY RULE: ABOLISHED IN MOST JURISDICTIONS. At common law, the victim had to die within a year and a day of the act for homicide. The modern rule — and the MBE's trap answer — is that the rule is abolished; a death two years later from the original wound is still homicide (proximate cause permitting).

CONCURRENCE IN HOMICIDE: Thabo Meli — defendants struck the victim, believed him dead, threw the "body" off a cliff; he was actually alive and died from exposure. One continuing transaction — actus reus and mens rea concurred. Murder stands.

PART 7 — DEFENSES AGAINST A HOMICIDE CHARGE (ROUNDUP): SELF-DEFENSE (Session 3's privilege, now with deadly stakes): deadly force is lawful only against an IMMINENT threat of DEATH OR SERIOUS BODILY INJURY. No deadly force for property alone. DUTY TO RETREAT before using deadly force in a minority of jurisdictions (if safe retreat is possible); NO DUTY TO RETREAT in the majority — and never in one's own home (CASTLE DOCTRINE). The INITIAL AGGRESSOR cannot claim self-defense unless he clearly withdraws and communicates it. IMPERFECT SELF-DEFENSE — an honest but unreasonable belief in the need for deadly force — does not acquit; it reduces MURDER TO VOLUNTARY MANSLAUGHTER.

INSANITY, INTOXICATION, MISTAKE — Session 11's rules apply unchanged; note that voluntary intoxication can negate specific intent (including premeditation — reducing first-degree to second) but never supplies a full defense.
CONSENT — never a defense to homicide. (Dueling deaths are murder on both sides' survivors.)
